News.title: Family of British woman shot dead by dad in Texas ask UK police to help with 'new evidence'
News.content:
Family of British woman shot dead by dad in Texas ask UK police to help with 'new evidence'

The family of Lucy Harrison, a 23-year-old British woman who was shot dead by her dad in the US, have asked Cheshire Police to help obtain new evidence

View 3 Images Lucy Harrison, 23, died on January 10, 2025 (Image: Liverpool Echo)

The family of a 23-year-old British woman who was unlawfully killed by her dad in Texas have asked a UK police force to help obtain new evidence after US authorities closed the case without bringing criminal charges.

‌



‌



Lucy Harrison, a fashion buyer from Warrington, was shot through the chest by Kris Harrison at his home in Prosper on January 10, 2025 - the day before she was due to fly home to the UK.

‌



Ms Harrison's family contacted Cheshire Police to ask them to examine evidence that has not yet been investigated, including messages recently found on her phone.

‌



The family said they have "serious concerns" about the investigation by US authorities, which ended with no charges brought against Mr Harrison. The UK force said it has "no lawful authority" to intervene in the case.

View 3 Images Lucy Harrison's mum Jane Coates (centre), her friend Ella Gowing (left) and boyfriend Sam Littler outside Cheshire Coroner's Court following her inquest (Image: PA)

A grand jury in Collin County, Texas, decided there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges after Mr Harrison claimed his handgun had discharged accidentally while he was showing it to his daughter.

‌



In February this year, a coroner in England concluded Ms Harrison had been unlawfully killed, finding that her father's actions amounted to gross negligence manslaughter under UK law.

Despite the ruling, Cheshire Constabulary said "significant operational, evidential and jurisdictional barriers" prevent the force from getting involved.

‌



In a letter to Ms Harrison’s family, Deputy Chief Constable Mike Evans said: "Whilst we may share the family’s concerns and understand their desire for further scrutiny, we have no lawful authority to intervene in [the] decision taken by those agencies."

He added: "I hope the family can be assured that Cheshire Constabulary has never viewed this matter with indifference.

‌



"We recognise the profound loss they have suffered and understand why they continue to seek answers.

"However, whilst we have great sympathy for the family’s position, we are ultimately constrained by legal, jurisdictional and practical realities that significantly limit what any police force in England and Wales can do in relation to a death that occurred in the United States."

‌



Radd Seiger, a spokesperson for Ms Harrison's family in the UK, insisted they are not asking the force to take over the investigation.

View 3 Images Lucy Harrison with her mum, Jane Coates, on Christmas Day 2024, just weeks before her death (Image: Jane Coates/Liverpool Echo)

‌



In a statement, he said the family believe messages recovered in a recent download of Lucy's phone are "relevant to understanding the circumstances leading up to her death".

"This is evidence that the family believe should have been obtained and examined as part of the original investigation in Texas," Mr Seiger added.

‌



Ms Harrison’s family have asked police to reconsider their position in light of the newly uncovered messages, and to help secure and share the evidence with law enforcement authorities in Texas.

Mr Seiger said: "The family have spent nearly two years trying to get answers about Lucy’s death and justice for her. They are not prepared to accept that the investigation is complete simply because the American authorities have decided not to take the matter further.

‌



"They want the evidence properly examined, the unanswered questions addressed and the authorities to make their decisions on the basis of all the relevant information, rather than evidence which is so obviously incomplete.

"That is all the family are asking for. A proper examination of the evidence, and a fair opportunity for the outstanding questions surrounding Lucy’s death to be answered."

‌



Senior coroner Jacqueline Devonish ruled in February that Mr Harrison's conduct had been "reckless".

The inquest heard that he had been drinking wine before taking a loaded Glock pistol from his bedside cabinet.

Article continues below

The coroner concluded the gun could only have been fired after it was pointed at Ms Harrison. The inquest also heard that police officers in Texas did not carry out an alcohol test, despite smelling alcohol on Mr Harrison's breath.

News.title: Turkish cosmetics firm upsells potentially deadly BBL surgery to unsuspecting Brits in Mirror probe
News.content:
Turkish cosmetics firm upsells potentially deadly BBL surgery to unsuspecting Brits in Mirror probe

EXCLUSIVE: The surgeon even suggested that our reporter should “gain some weight” if she opted for the BBL so she had enough fat to carry out the procedure

2SITE_SASKIA_-compressed

A cosmetics firm has been upselling potentially deadly operations abroad to unsuspecting Brits, it's been revealed.

‌



‌



A company hawking the risky operation was recorded offering discounts to lure in folk. Experts warned of cosmetic tourism’s dangers as our undercover probe exposed “deeply troubling” practices at a conference where Turkish firms touted their wares.

‌



Two of our reporters - one male, one female - recorded a sales representative saying he could “guarantee” convenience and promised a “really good discount". Then in a follow-up consultation call - which lasted just 14 minutes and took place over Whatsapp - with a surgeon in Turkey, we discussed a potential liposuction procedure to “tone hips and tummy".

‌



Within seconds he “recommended” an additional “skinny Brazilian Butt Lift (BBL)” treatment to inject the harvested fat into the “gluteal area”. He even suggested taking “gainers” or “supplements” to bulk up before the op so the fat could be removed and pumped into the buttocks.

We shared our footage and audio recordings to industry experts who described the practices as "deeply troubling". They said our findings demonstrate the dangers facing patients travelling abroad.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



View 9 Images Our reporters attended the ALZ Health Tourism Expo in Manchester

Mum left hours from death after disaster BBL says the love for her son kept her alive READ MORE :

Ricardo Ribeiro, whose daughter Morgan, 20, died after gastric sleeve surgery in Turkey, said it was “disturbing”. He said: “It just shows that this is about nothing but profit - health wasn’t in their minds in any way shape or form.” Ashton Collins of Save Face, the UK’s leading Government-approved register, said she was “appalled".

‌



And Anthony MacQuillan, the president of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons - known as BAAPS - said the footage raised serious concerns about “commercially-driven” consultations. He told us: “There is no such thing as surgery that doesn’t have risk attached to it.

“But it’s even more dangerous when the people involved are obviously not examining the patient properly and really not acting in the patient’s best interests. They’re just acting in a really irresponsible manner and it’s because it’s driven by commercial interests.”

‌



The Foreign Office says at least 28 British people have died since 2019 due to complications from elective medical procedures performed in Turkey. Seven British nationals lost their lives in the country in 2025 alone following medical procedures. And analysis suggests the NHS is burdened with costs of nearly £20,000 per patient when cosmetic and obesity surgery abroad goes wrong.

View 9 Images Melissa Kerr died after a surgical BBL in Turkey (Image: Natasha Kerr / JustGiving)

‌



Morgan went into septic shock in January 2024 after surgery by a different medical provider on her flight back to the UK. The plane was diverted to Belgrade, but Morgan died in a hospital in the Serbian capital days later.

Melissa Kerr, 31, died on the day she had BBL surgery at the private Medicana Kadikoy Hospital in Istanbul in 2019 carried out by a different medical provider. A coroner raised concerns that she and others were not given enough information to help them make safe decisions before they went abroad to go under the knife.

‌



Despite the tragedies, the UK market for private Turkish clinics is thriving. Dozens of companies proudly sold their services at the Manchester International Health Tourism Expo.

Our undercover reporter - who, at 7.5st and standing 5ft 5in tall, is already a healthy weight by NHS standards - spoke with a representative from Turkish firm Medical Point named Ahmed Altun. He suggested it was unlikely she would experience complications in potential liposuction treatment because she was “not overweight”.

‌



View 9 Images Morgan Ribeiro died after gastric sleeve surgery in Turkey (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

When asked how long it would take, he said: “It depends if there are any side effects. Since you are not overweight I would say, between seven to 10 days max. You will be in the hospital for just two days, then you will just have a follow-up once then you will fly back home.”

‌



Asked if she would be left with scarring, he said they use “special” equipment, adding: “They will give you some creams, the scar will be gone in a couple of months.” In a bid to reassure our reporter about the "outcomes", Mr Altun produced a WhatsApp message from a recent Nigerian patient. The woman - who had undergone “liver surgery” before opting for liposuction - seemed to praise the care. The representative told our reporter: “She’s really satisfied with the results.”

When asked about costs, the representative said we would need to have an online consultation before saying: “I will try my best to do a really good discount. If you ask other places, [our care] would be more convenient. I can guarantee that.”

‌



After sending images to a consultant in Turkey, we had a WhatsApp call with a surgeon who told us: “Using your own fat, we can reshape the gluteal area and the hips.” He added: “The other name we can use is a Brazilian Butt Lift if we perform that... the combined liposuction 360 and fat transfer for the glutes and the hips.”

View 9 Images Representative Ahmed Altun suggested it was unlikely our reporter would experience complications

‌



The surgeon even suggested that our reporter should “gain some weight” if she opted for the BBL so she had enough fat to carry out the procedure. He said: “One of the main issues is you should have enough fat because we are reshaping those areas, the hips and the gluteal areas using your own fat. So if you don’t have enough fat, it would be better to gain some weight until the surgery if you are considering this kind of procedure.”

He added: “We are getting the fat from the tummy, sides, back and sometimes from the inner thighs and after preparing them, I am injecting them...” He suggested using powdered “gainers” to add fat before the procedure. At no point did he ask a single question about our reporter’s medical history.

‌



He said: “Some of our patients like this... like your body... with a skinny BBL... you can use some gainers, this supplement, it’s a kind of supplement in different brands. You can use them so that the supplement includes a lot of calories and you can gain a lot of calories and fat in this kind of supplement.”

BBLs are not illegal in the UK or Turkey, but they are unregulated and are considered to be the most dangerous and life-threatening form of cosmetic surgery. Asked if there were any risks, the surgeon said: “Surgery has some unique risks, even simple and basic procedures includes risk but we can minimise those risks especially for the liposuction with using power-assisted liposuction device. I’m using that routinely.

‌



View 9 Images Save Face's Ashton Collins was “appalled" by our findings (Image: BBC)

“And for the fat grafting, the Brazilian Butt Lift surgery, I’m using an ultra-sound device to check the fat grafting areas to stay above the muscle to prevent any complications.” He added: “We should do the liposuction and BBL procedures at the same time. We need your fat to use for that.

‌



“First of all I will harvest the fat and get the fat grafts from your body and then after preparing them I will inject them into those areas freshly. We cannot keep them for days, we should inject them during the same surgery.”

The surgeon suggested recovery would take between four to six weeks and said they would provide a “corset” or “compression garment". He said: “We will start to see the final results in a couple of months. For the first weeks there may be bruising, swelling as you know. You will get better day-by-day and week-by-week. We will start to see the final definition and the shape. You can go back to your work by seven to 10 days after surgery.”

‌



Asked if the surgery would likely have a “good outcome”, he said: “The main goal of that surgery is this, because you don’t need the tummy tuck. You don’t have saggy skin or excess skin, just need liposuction and skin tightening to achieve a more defined appearance.”

View 9 Images BBLs are not illegal in the UK or Turkey but they are considered to be the most dangerous form of cosmetic surgery (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

‌



Medical Point was among dozens of foreign health firms selling treatments abroad at Manchester’s two-day ALZ Health Tourism Expo. Ashton Collins of Save Face said: “I was appalled by the casual way the surgeon spoke to this patient. There was no adequate discussion of risks or potential complications, and no proper basis for informed consent.

“Using virtual consultations to fast-track bookings or pressure people into major surgery is unacceptable. Surgery should never be treated as a purchase to be hurried through a sales process. What we saw falls seriously short of the standard patients should expect from a responsible surgeon.

‌



“No one should be encouraged towards an irreversible procedure before their suitability has been properly assessed and they understand the risks, alternatives and recovery involved.” Mr Ribeiro said: “The fact that you inquired about liposuction and they immediately offered a BBL dumbfounds me.

“At a healthy weight of seven-and-a-half stone, they should have told you that liposuction wouldn’t be appropriate, rather than allowing you to have it and then trying to upsell you a skinny BBL. They could have offered a million other alternatives like seeing a dietitian, but instead they jumped straight to surgery.” He added: “I’m speaking out because I don’t want any other family to go through what we’ve been through.”

‌



View 9 Images BAAP's Dr Anthony MacQuillan said the surgeon should have conducted a medical consultation (Image: anthonymacquilliam.com)

Mr MacQuillan, from BAAPS, said “upselling” introduced a new level of danger to patients and raised concerns about “good medicine”. He said: “You listen to the patient and ask what their problems are, what their needs are, not basically what what you think you can get out of them or get them to do.

‌



“I don’t believe that the whole thing should start with the sales process. It should start with the medical consultation and not involve remote consultations for surgery without actually seeing the patient.

“Every time you do something additional to the patient, it increases risk. As soon as you start upselling, you’re introducing more risk to the patient for procedures they weren’t actually asking for. That surely isn’t a good thing. You would hope most responsible doctors are not behaving in that manner. The thing about people going abroad for surgery, it’s not intrinsically bad. There are world class surgeons in Turkey. But you will also pay world class prices to go and see them.”

‌



View 9 Images Medical Point hospital is in Izmir, Turkey (Image: mph.com.tr)

Cosmetic cowboys who deliver botched procedures to face crackdown, Yvette Cooper vows READ MORE :

Consultant plastic surgeon Dr Simon Lee said: “On the face of it, the consultation may seem reasonable. The patient asked about achieving more definition, so it was appropriate to discuss fat grafting to areas such as the hip dips, abdomen and gluteal region. The surgeon also referred to using ultrasound during a Brazilian butt lift to reduce risk.

‌



“But the most striking omission is any meaningful discussion of risk. Patients need to understand the potential complications of surgery, including those that can arise in the early post-operative period, as well as serious risks such as blood clots and thromboembolism. For gluteal fat grafting, the possibility of a life-threatening fat embolism must be addressed clearly and specifically.

“Questions about flying after surgery should not be brushed aside as an administrative matter for a patient coordinator. That advice has medical implications and should be given by an appropriately qualified clinician. More fundamentally, there appears to have been no proper assessment of whether surgery was necessary or suitable, and no adequate discussion of its consequences.

‌



“In the UK, patients should expect a full medical history to be taken and a clinician to take responsibility for their care. That means giving honest advice, explaining risks and alternatives, and making sure the patient’s consent is informed and genuinely voluntary. What I find most disturbing is the apparent absence of that care.”

View 9 Images Plastic surgeon Dr Simon Lee was shocked by our findings (Image: simonleeplasticsurgeon.co.uk)

‌



Last year an inquest was told that mother-of-one Ruby Khan, from Oldham, had suffered a cardiac arrest on the operating table during a liposuction and tummy tuck procedure at the Izmir Medical Point clinic, in İzmir. Consultant histopathologist Dr Sami Titi conducted a postmortem at the Royal Oldham Hospital when Ruby’s body was transferred back home from Turkey.

He said he “didn’t think there was an indication that the procedure itself was faulty, nor the aftercare." In fact, he said, the cardiac arrhythmias experienced by Ruby are “common causes of death in these types of procedures”.

Article continues below

The pathologist said it appeared the same “standard procedures” for a patient in the UK having those procedures had been followed. He added: “These complications are rare but do take place in some instances.”

Medical Point and expo organiser ALZ were contacted for comment. There is no suggestion that they have broken the law.

News.title: We have a bold plan to turn things around and bring big brands – and new life – back to the nation’s high street
News.content:
This week, we’re celebrating a momentous new era for Oxford Street, as the nation’s high street goes traffic-free – just in time for the busy Christmas shopping period. On Monday morning, I did ­something I’ve done countless times since my teenage years – I left my home in Tooting and headed into central London.

It was a typical wet and windy autumn morning. But, under an ­overcast sky, a new dawn was breaking for our city’s most famous street. For the first time in its history, Oxford Street was closed to traffic – not for hours or days, but for good.

It felt like a different place. Without the roar of engines, you could hear people talking and laughing. Free from exhaust fumes, the air felt cleaner. You didn’t have to jostle for your place on the pavement, because you could walk anywhere you liked.

The Londoners and visitors I met were already making the most of it. On the first day of the school holidays, Oxford Street was full of families who’d come for a day out.

‌



Watching them make their way down the street, I remembered what it was like to take my own daughters shopping on Oxford Street when they were much younger – and how I had to hug them close to protect them from passing buses and taxis. Thanks to pedestrianisation, those days are finally over.

This is a massive moment for both the capital and the country. To say that Oxford Street is solely London’s high street would be well wide of the mark. Recent data shows it generates 1% of the UK’s total economic output.

View 6 Images (Image: Carlos Jasso/AFP via Getty Images)

And yet, in recent years, it has ­struggled. The rise of online shopping was already a colossal challenge, but the impact of the pandemic made the situation much worse. As footfall fell, good shops shut – only to be replaced by stores selling vapes and cheap American candy.

‌



Oxford Street is hardly alone in this respect. Its story is one of thousands unfolding in communities across the country, where – as Andy Burnham has put it – high streets have been hollowed out after decades of decline.

But we have a bold plan to turn things around and bring big brands – and new life – back to the nation’s high street. When we talk about our town centres, it’s easy to be nostalgic. But the truth is that times have changed. When you can order whatever you want, whenever you want, from wherever you want in a couple of clicks, sprucing up some shopfronts isn’t going to be enough to get people off the sofa.

View 6 Images (Image: NEIL HALL/EPA/Shutterstock)

If our high streets aren’t places you have to go, they’ve got to be places you want to go. And they’ve got to offer people an experience they can’t get online.

‌



I want Oxford Street to be a place that people choose to come back to again and again, and closing it to traffic is just the start. Now, we can begin transforming Oxford Street into a truly world-class destination for Londoners and visitors alike – a space that hosts the biggest names in retail alongside exciting events that offer crowds culture and connection. Household names like Ikea, Puma and Clarks have already invested in new stores, but this is only the beginning.

Oxford Street has been known for many things in its time, but standing still isn’t one of them. Once a Roman road, then a street famous for being the route to the Tyburn Gallows, it was Oxford Street where the modern-day department store was born.

View 6 Images (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

And it was Oxford Street where, after the destruction of the Blitz, London began to rebuild itself. The way I see it, pedestrianisation is just the latest chapter in Oxford Street’s long history of change and it couldn’t have come soon enough. In a world evolving as rapidly as ours, business as usual won’t cut it.

‌



In my 10 years as Mayor, plenty of people tried to tell me that ­pedestrianising Oxford Street couldn’t be done. My predecessor once said that it would be “foolish”. But, if the last few days are anything to go by, the naysayers are wrong.

For me, this comes down to one thing: pride. I still remember the first time I went to Oxford Street without my parents like it was yesterday. It felt like the whole world was right there – in the beating heart of the greatest city on Earth.

See all the latest stories from your Real Britain columnist Ros Wynne-Jones here

But Brits today no longer feel that way. They’ve lost their sense of pride in Oxford Street, because it no longer shows our capital city at its brilliant best.

‌



My message to the country this week is clear: you won’t have to feel that way for much longer. New York has got Times Square, Paris has got the Champs Élysées, and Barcelona has got La Rambla.

Now, we’re going to turn Oxford Street into something even better, by creating a place every Brit can be proud of. You don’t have to take my word for it. With Christmas around the corner, now’s the perfect time to come and see it for yourself.

Ensure Real Britain always appears at the top of your Google Search by making The Mirror a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as your Preferred Source in your Google search settings.

In safer hands tackling crime

If you’ve been on social media, the chances are you may have seen a story about “lawless London”. Look past the lies being spread online and you’ll see the truth is very different.

‌



Neighbourhood crime is falling across our city, with phone theft and robbery at their lowest level in years. Our success reflects the fact we’re not just being tough on crime, by providing record police funding from City Hall. We’re being tough on its complex causes too.

I set up England’s first Violence Reduction Unit in 2019 to provide young people with positive opportunities to prevent them from being caught up in crime. Since then, it’s reached over one million Londoners, and hospital admissions of young people for knife assault have fallen by 55%. Last year, London’s per capita homicide rate was the lowest in history.

There’s always more to do. But the evidence shows we’re headed in the right direction – and London’s a lot safer than the scaremongers say.

Can’t compete with our Kane

View 6 Images (Image: FRANCK FIFE / AFP via Getty Images)

‌



I was delighted to see England captain Harry Kane crowned the winner of the Ballon d’Or in London.

Kane is fully deserving of the prestigious award for the world’s best footballer after scoring an astonishing 73 goals for club and country last season.

England fans like me will never forget the starring role he played at this summer’s World Cup. Seventy years after the inaugural Ballon d’Or was won by England’s Sir Stanley Matthews, it was fitting that the ceremony should come to London for the first time and Kane honoured. He is now – officially – one of the greatest of all time.

‌



Stratford

View 6 Images (Image: PA)

Home of the Olympics, Stratford has become one of Europe’s biggest regeneration projects. After this week’s budget, we’re writing the next chapter of this East London success story. By bringing cross-channel trains to Stratford International station, it gets a direct connection to the Continent, benefiting the whole country.

News.title: Missing nine-year-old boy in Bristol found 'safe' after call from member of public
News.content:
Missing nine-year-old boy in Bristol found 'safe' after call from member of public

A nine-year-old boy who went missing in south Bristol has been found 'safe and well', Avon and Somerset Police said

View Image Police thanked everyone who came forward with information (file image) (Image: Getty Images)

A nine-year-old boy who went missing in south Bristol has been found "safe and well" following a call from a member of the public.

‌



‌



Abbullah was last seen in the Totterdown area at 11.30am on Saturday. Avon and Somerset Police launched an appeal as officers searched the streets and parks in the area to find him.

‌



In an update shortly before 5.30pm, a force spokesperson said: "We're very pleased to update you that Abbullah, nine, who was missing from Totterdown in Bristol, has been found safe and well within the last few minutes."

Article continues below

They added: "He was found after a call from a member of the public. We're very grateful to everyone who contacted us with information."

Police had earlier said the boy was thought to be on foot in the Totterdown area.

News.title: Laura Kuenssberg: Healey risks breaking minimum wage promise for younger workers
News.content:
The Chancellor, John Healey, has suggested that younger workers might not receive the same minimum wage as others before the next election, potentially breaking a Labour manifesto promise.

In 2024, Labour said it would remove "discriminatory age bands", vowing to end the gap between the adult minimum wage and pay for 18 to 20-year-olds.

But in last week's Budget, Healey said that younger workers would see the same increase as older workers, leaving a gap between the two rates this year.

Pay for 18 to 20-year-olds in 2026 will rise to Â£11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of Â£13.21 an hour.

In a BBC interview to be broadcast on Sunday, Healey was asked if younger workers would be paid the same as older workers, when it comes to the minimum wage, by the time of the next election?

"We'll take one step at a time," he said, suggesting that Labour might abandon its plan to close the gap before the next election.

It is a change that is likely to anger the unions and some on the left of the party.

Healey added that Labour was still committed to the ambition, but hinted the plan to equalise wages might be delayed, partly to encourage businesses to employ younger workers.

"There is no question about whether or if, it's a question of when - it's a question of how fast," he said.

"I want to make sure we can look hard at those trade-offs that are there between jobs and wages."

"I want to take business, I want to take trade unions with me, and with the government, because together we have to get into what at the moment is a moral shame on this nation. A million youngsters - written off without any prospect of being helped into work and making contributions to this country for the future."

News.title: King to address slavery during Commonwealth speech in Antigua on final leg of Caribbean tour
News.content:
King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.

The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech which will touch on the issue.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.

It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.

The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.

Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.

The King will make his speech at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said.

"You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow, and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."

When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to "the UK Government's position".

The Caribbean tour has again thrust King Charles into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.

On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech where he spoke of the "suffering of the past".

In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.

News.title: Who are the real winners of Celebrity Traitors?
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from The Celebrity Traitors final

In some ways, all the players on the Celebrity Traitors can be seen as winners.

They all got to appear on a hugely popular TV show, rubbing shoulders with other stars and gaining new fans along the way.

But there are certain celebrities, such as Miranda Hart, King Kenny, Maya Jama and Joanne McNally, who have been tipped by industry experts as getting the biggest career boost after the show.

Sebastian "Bash" Croft - who won the game, alongside Romesh Ranganathan - could also now be in line for greater roles.

We've taken a look at the breakout stars of the series and what might lie ahead for them.

News.title: Hamilton takes first pole for Ferrari at Mexico City Grand Prix
News.content:
Russell, who said he was happy to have ended a run of difficult form but could not explain why, took a unilateral decision not to do a preparation lap after his out lap on his final run.

He said he had a "gut feeling" that it was the best approach, but the team had insisted on a prep lap and had fuelled the car for the extra mileage.

"[The time loss for the extra fuel weight is] such a small number," said Russell, "but it's bigger than the gap to pole. Nevertheless, I'm just happy to be up here."

Verstappen said traffic with another car is what led to his loss of time.

"Already going into (Turn) 12 I had a car very close to me and I already lost time there with the dirty air," he said.

"And then going into the hairpin, instead of going on the left, I had one car on my right where you normally want to open up the corner. So its a bit of an awkward angle you have to go into the hairpin.

"Plus you lose your reference on the right-hand side where you are constantly looking. It's a difficult corner to get right, that killed my lap. The most promising thing is how we turned it around as in practice I was not that happy and we turned it around, I was in the fight for pole."

McLaren's Lando Norris had looked in contention for pole, fastest in the second session and on the first runs in the final session, when he was third fastest behind Leclerc and Verstappen.

But he failed to improve on his final lap and had to be satisfied fight sixth.

"Just not quick enough that's all," said Norris. "The lap was incredible in Q2 to put me P1. That was very unrealistic in terms of achieving that again in Q3.

"I am pretty happy with P6, can't ask a lot more and pretty happy with the job I did with the car I have."

Red Bull's Isack Hadjar, Racing Bulls pair Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad and Alpine's Pierre Gasly completed the top 10.

Lawson was later disqualified from qualifying for an Infringement of the technical regulations regarding the usage of the electrical deployment of the power unit and will start from the back.

Fernando Alonso looked to be in contention for his best qualifying of the year for Aston Martin when he went fastest on his first lap of the session ahead of a number of cars that for most of the season have been ahead of him.

But his engine suffered a water leak in the energy recovery system as he started his second attempt, when he was still lying third, and he was ordered to stop the car on track.

Alonso's frustration after a year of poor performance and reliability from the Honda engine was clear in an interview with the official television channel afterwards, when he said a total of nine words in answer to four questions.

In those words, he confirmed it had been an engine problem, said "it was" a good opportunity and it was "correct" that the car has been looking good all weekend - but that he could not do anything in the race "from the back".

News.title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
News.content:
When Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess.

Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage.

But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.

"It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes.

She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher.

News.title: I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly home
News.content:
When Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific.

The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged".

Ranasingha had been hoping to settle in New Zealand.

After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa.

Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka.

Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed.

As a result, she has no feasible way of leaving.

"My son - my only child - is getting married in November and I really want to be there for his wedding. My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she says through tears.

"I will do anything they ask of me - I just want to go home."

News.title: Why did this Korean content creator throw a divorce ceremony?
News.content:
Single mother and content creator Cho Seung-yeon, 37, marked the end of her marriage by throwing a divorce ceremony.

Instead of treating her divorce as a failure, she gathered her close friends to mark the end of her former life and the beginning of her next chapter. However, Cho received a backlash after posting about the ceremony online.

She told the BBC that she wants to fight the stigma surrounding divorced women and reclaim her identity beyond marriage.

News.title: The Papers:  'PM lets down the King' and 'Kenny's secret night at Maya's'
News.content:
Image caption,

Several Sunday papers are running with stories following Prime Minster Andy Burnham's comments that he was open to discussions around the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade. The Sunday Express headlines with "PM 'lets down the King' over slavery apology" and says Burnham has been "accused of 'irresponsible' blunder" as King Charles III tours the Caribbean.

News.title: Thick fog to create hazardous driving conditions into next week
News.content:
Dense fog will blanket parts of the UK on Sunday and into next week, causing dangerous driving conditions.

England and Wales are most likely to experience the foggy conditions on Sunday, before the threat shifts northwards into next week.

It comes after the Met Office issued a yellow weather warning for parts of England and Wales early on Saturday morning with visibility on roads predicted to drop to less than 100m in places.

Further warnings could be issued in the coming days as the waning strength of the late autumn sun means mist, fog and patches of low cloud are slow to clear.

News.title: Second night of drone disruption at Jersey Airport
News.content:
People at Jersey Airport have said they are frustrated and angry that "unauthorised drone" activity caused more flight cancellations for a second night in a row.

At 20:05 on Saturday Jersey Airport said it was "experiencing disruption.... affecting inbound flights as a result of further drone activity in the vicinity of the airfield".

States of Jersey Police are investigating the incidents and officers have appealed to anyone with information about who is responsible to come forward.

Insp Rob McCallum said it was believed "two or three" drones had entered the restricted airspace, but they were not thought to be linked to terrorism.

News.title: Europe can no longer rely on US to 'bankroll' its defence, Starmer says
News.content:
Sir Keir Starmer has said Europe should build a common security framework, warning the change in its defence relationship with the US is permanent rather than "an aberration of the Trump presidency".

The former prime minister was speaking at a British Irish Chamber of Commerce (BICC) dinner in Dublin, external on Friday evening.

Sir Keir said a "common security framework" for Europe was needed as much as a common market, with the UK at its centre.

He warned that "things will not go back to the way they were," adding that the US had made clear it will no longer "bankroll" its European allies.

Press Association reported that he told the crowd in Dublin City Hall his comments did not mean "the US relationship is no longer important".

Rather he said the UK-USA military, security and intelligence alliance was "far too strong for that".

But he said Europe must be enabled to "take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security".

"Europe has twice been caught asleep â failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events," he said.

"First when Russia's attack on Ukraine exposed long-standing European weaknesses on defence and security; and second when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up," he added.

He added: "I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.

Sir Keir was at the dinner to be awarded an honorary life membership from the BICC.

News.title: 'It's been killing me!' Celebrity Traitors winners relieved the secret is out
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors final

The winners of Celebrity Traitors have said they are relieved that they no longer need to keep the biggest secret in British TV, as they reunited to celebrate their victory.

Actor Sebastian Croft and comedian Romesh Ranganathan were the last ones standing, with the two faithfuls splitting the Â£83,000 prize pot between their chosen charities.

"I am feeling good, it's so nice to finally be able to talk about it properly," Croft, known to pals as Bash, told BBC Newsbeat.

The second series of the hit BBC One show finished on Friday, after the original 21 celebs were whittled down to seven finalists.

Reuniting with Ranganathan on the comedian's BBC Radio 2 show on Saturday morning, Croft said they had been worried about being seen together in public before the final.

"We were having dinner and we're not exactly a likely duo and the whole restaurant was like, 'we like you on Traitors and hope you win'," he said.

Croft added that he had woken up on Saturday "with a light sense that I don't have to keep the secret anymore. It's been killing me".

Ranganathan, 48, started his show by saying: "Last night, I don't know if you're aware, was the finale of The Celebrity Traitors and I won."

He said he was "delighted to win" but admitted he probably wouldn't have done so without Croft convincing him to banish the last remaining traitor, King Kenny.

"It's taken the gloss off it slightly that everybody's saying, 'you better thank [Croft] every day for the rest of your life'," he added, with his typical deadpan-humour.

But 24-year-old Croft said he thought Ranganathan had played the game in a "lovely" way.

"People are seeing how smart you are and how you're actually so on it, and you're such a good judge of character," he praised.

News.title: Fireworks and fancy dress at Derry's 40th Halloween festival
News.content:
The 40th anniversary of Londonderry's Halloween festival has come to a spectacular close, with a carnival parade and fireworks display lighting up the skies over the River Foyle.

From its humble beginnings in the 1980s, the festival has grown to become what organisers have called Europe's largest Halloween celebration.

This year, Derry marked four decades of the festival with events inspired by folklore, mythology and the traditions of Samhain, the ancient Celtic festival from which Halloween has its roots.

Now a major fixture in the city's calendar, the final day of the festival attracted visitors from around the world, who joined in the celebrations with all of the ghosts, ghouls and goblins.

News.title: Mahmood expected to announce changes to rules around indefinite leave to remain
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is expected to announce her final decision on immigration rules for legal migrants next week.

She had proposed to extend the wait for permanent settlement from the current five years to 10 with some lower-paid migrants facing a 15-year wait. The BBC understands the proposals are likely to be revised for most of those currently working in social care.

The home secretary was concerned about the number of people who would be eligible for permanent residency after a period of very high net migration under the previous government.

Mahmood has faced opposition from within the government for proposing to impose new rules on migrant workers already in the UK.

Before she rejoined the cabinet, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner described the proposals as "un-British" because they sought to change the rules for people who had come to the UK in good faith.

In particular, many lower-paid social care workers were facing a wait of up to 15 years rather than five.

But the BBC understands that social care workers already in the UK are now likely to be exempt from the longer wait.

But as originally proposed, it is likely most other workers will have to live and work in the UK for 10 years before being eligible for permanent settlement. That can be reduced if they contribute to their local communities or have higher incomes.

The government's consultation on the proposed reforms has drawn 200,000 responses.

The Home Office will not comment on Mahmood's final decisions until they are presented to Parliament in the coming week.

In September, a Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain."

"This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low wage migrants."

Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

News.title: Everton striker's relief family not home during burglary
News.content:
Everton striker Thierno Barry has said he was relieved that his family were not at home when it was burgled while he played in a cup match.

His home in Greater Manchester was targeted while he was playing for Everton against Newcastle United in a Carabao Cup tie at the Hill Dickinson stadium on Thursday.

The Frenchman, 24, posted on Instagram "things could have been much worse" had his partner and toddler not been in the stands.

A spokesman for Greater Manchester Police said an investigation was ongoing.

Barry posted that he would not put his family "at risk" in the future by posting about his life on social media.

He said: "Maybe I've been too open about my family's life and mine, potentially putting them at risk, all just to show my lifestyle and inspire others through my journey and success, hoping to motivate them to do the same.

"My childhood was never easy, but I've always believed that when you give yourself the best possible chances, there is always hope.

"Unfortunately, in life, there are people and things beyond our control."

News.title: UK has 'no authority' over case of woman killed by father in US
News.content:
The mother of a British woman who was shot and killed by her father in Texas has been told that police in the UK have "no lawful authority to intervene" as the family tries to find answers.

Lucy Harrison, 23, from Warrington was shot in the chest on 10 January 2025 in Prosper, Dallas - found by a UK coroner to be an unlawful killing.

However, no criminal case was brought against her father Kris Harrison, after a grand jury in Collin County declined to indict him.

Lucy's mother Jane Coates wrote to Cheshire Police urging them to "gather evidence" here locally, and then "liaise" with US authorities - but the force has responded and said it was "constrained" by law and jurisdiction.

In a letter to Coates, Deputy Chief Constable Mike Evans said: "Whilst we may share the family's concerns and understand their desire for further scrutiny, we have no lawful authority to intervene in decisions taken by those agencies."

Last month, Coates flew to Texas in a bid to meet the district attorney in Collin County and to call on him to reinstate the investigation but was told he would not speak to her.

News.title: Police hunt masked men after Halloween party stabbing leaves teen hospitalised
News.content:

Police have launched a manhunt for a group of masked men after a teenager was stabbed multiple times at a Halloween party in London.

Emergency services were called to a community centre on James Close in Newham at around 7:45pm on Wednesday after reports eight to 10 masked men stormed a Halloween party and stabbed an 18-year-old in the torso and arms in a “violent attack”.

He was rushed to hospital where he remains in a stable condition with potentially life-changing injuries, the Metropolitan Police said. Detectives have since launched an attempted murder investigation and are urging anyone with any information to come forward.

Police are urging anyone with information to come forward ( Getty/iStock )

No arrests have been made at this time, but police have issued an appeal asking any young people who fled the party when the stabbing happened to speak to officers.

Detective Inspector Sam Lockstone, who is leading the investigation, said: “We are grateful to those who have come forward so far. However, there were a lot of young people at the party who fled when the stabbing happened, and it is really important that they contact police and offer any information they can to help with our enquiries.

“The victim was subject to a violent attack, and we want to know if you have any video footage taken during or after the party or witnessed anything that could help with our investigation. If you don’t want to contact police directly, you can pass information anonymously onto Crimestoppers.”

Police said those with information can contact police via 101, quoting CAD 6525/28OCT26, or call the independent charity Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

News.title: How Canelo Alvarez kept his career alive with vital win against Christian Mbilli
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Canelo Alvarez scored a crucial win over Christian Mbilli on Saturday, rebounding from a loss to Terence Crawford after 13 months out of the ring.

Alvarez outpointed Mbilli to take the WBC super-middleweight title from the Cameroonian, earning scorecards of 115-112, 116-111, and 117-110.

Those scores factored in a docked point for Mbilli in round eight, after the champion landed one low blow too many for the referee’s liking, but it would have been a comfortable win for Canelo regardless.

open image in gallery Canelo Alvarez (left) during his win over Christian Mbilli ( Reuters )

The Mexican icon was much more active than he had been in recent performances, starting well and – at times – matching the volume punching of Mbilli, who is known for his activity and had never lost before.

Mbilli, 31, allowed that activity to dip here and there on Saturday, and Canelo, 36, capitalised well. The four-weight world champion varied his shots well, landing hard right hooks early on and mixing in uppercuts in the later rounds.

Canelo appeared emotional afterwards, as he regained super-middleweight gold after losing his undisputed status against Crawford last year.

Crawford claimed all the major belts by outpointing Canelo, before retiring from boxing in December. Upon the American’s retirement, Mbilli’s interim WBC belt was upgraded.

But the Cameroonian’s first defence of the official title ended in disappointment, as Canelo got back to winning ways in Riyadh, which has been subjected to deadly attacks in recent weeks.

The Yemen-aligned Houthis had launched numerous strikes on the Saudi city, injuring hundreds of people and killing more than 20, per local authorities.

Still, Saturday’s boxing event went ahead at ANB Arena, where Canelo said after winning: “It’s so difficult to explain [my emotions]. It’s something unbelievable.

“This feels like my first title, now after 21 years as a professional; 16 years ago I won my first title, now I won the title again. I’m so proud, so proud of my team. [They] made me the champion I am.”

“No, [nothing surprised me]. I knew he’s a strong fighter, and he didn’t throw a lot of punches because it’s difficult to throw punches with me. I did perfectly.”
