Sports.title: Canelo Alvarez Calls For Terence Crawford Rematch After Win
Sports.content:
Canelo Alvarez made his priority clear right after taking down Christian Mbilli in Riyadh to grab back the WBC super middleweight strap: he wants another shot at Terence Crawford.

In his post-fight interview, Canelo didn’t hide his intentions when asked about coaxing Crawford out of retirement.

“Hopefully, yes. Hopefully, yes. We would honestly love to have that rematch, like I’ve told you. If not, we’ll keep moving forward with our career, but hopefully that fight can happen,” Canelo said.

The desire is there. The evidence of meaningful improvement is harder to find. Beating Mbilli restores Canelo’s position as a champion, but defeating a pressure fighter does not demonstrate that he would fare better against Crawford’s movement, timing, and ability to control distance.

Whether the Mexican star cares about the potential of losing again is unclear. Assuming Turki is on board with financing a second fight, the money Canelo would get would make it worthwhile.

The appetite from fans for a sequel is lukewarm at best, and for good reason. The first bout settled whatever competitive debate existed. Crawford put on a clinic in ring generalship, using distance, a sharp jab, lateral movement, and timely ties inside to neutralize Canelo. While purists could appreciate Crawford’s discipline, it was a pedestrian viewing experience for the casual paying crowd.

Fans remember twelve rounds of Canelo plodding forward, swinging at air, unable to cut off the ring, while Crawford played keep-away and banked rounds on the outside. Rematches of fights like that rarely produce fireworks; they usually produce a carbon copy.

Boxing fans would far rather see matchups that guarantee genuine action and modern divisional relevance: A unification clash with Osleys Iglesias gives hardcore fans an intriguing, high-risk clash against a dangerous, prime southpaw puncher holding the missing IBF strap.

Even a bout against Dmitry Bivol at light heavyweight would hold more competitive curiosity than watching Crawford stick and move his way to another lopsided decision.

The only real driver behind a Crawford rematch is pure business. Turki Alalshikh has the deep pockets to bankroll a massive spectacle, and both fighters stand to collect generational checks. The promotional build would lean on celebrity hype and pageantry, but inside the ring, the paying audience knows exactly what it would look like: twelve more rounds of perimeter defense and frustration.

Sports.title: Alvarez victorious over Mbilli, captures WBC super middleweight title
Sports.content:
Canelo Álvarez (64-3-2, 39 KOs) reclaimed the WBC super middleweight title with a twelve-round unanimous decision over Christian Mbilli (29-1-1, 24 KOs) on Saturday at Kingdom Arena in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Canelo’s cleaner counters and defensive work earned him scores of 115-112, 116-111 and 117-110 in the DAZN PPV main event.

Returning from a thirteen-month absence following his loss to Terence Crawford, Álvarez landed in bursts while Mbilli pressed forward without consistently connecting cleanly.

Mbilli had success when he sustained his attacks, but too often backed away after throwing, allowing Álvarez time to choose his counters. Canelo’s jab, hooks and uppercuts supplied the more accurate work, although Mbilli’s activity kept several rounds competitive.

In the eighth, referee Hector Afu deducted a point from Mbilli following an illegal punch. Álvarez had repeatedly drawn the referee’s attention to Mbilli’s fouls before the penalty.

Mbilli continued pressing late but could not produce the breakthrough he needed. Álvarez finished effectively in the final two rounds, securing the decision without either fighter scoring a knockdown.

WBA super middleweight champion Jaime Munguía (47-2, 35 KOs) had a much harder evening than the scorecards suggested against Russian southpaw Nikita Zon (12-1-1, 10 KOs). Munguía retained his title by unanimous decision, winning 116-112 and 117-111 twice after twelve competitive rounds.

Their sixth round produced furious action, with both fighters hurt and Munguía in serious danger before recovering. The Mexican’s combinations and greater output helped him through the later rounds, but Zon remained dangerous until the finish.

Munguía’s defensive lapses made this an uncomfortable first defense against an opponent making his first twelve-round appearance.

Rafael Espinoza (29-0, 25 KOs) retained his WBO featherweight title with a third-round TKO over Ricardo Blandón. The ringside doctor stopped the scheduled twelve-round contest at 1:22 because of a severe cut over Blandón’s eye.

Espinoza controlled the action with his jab and pressure. The medical intervention brought an abrupt ending before the challenger’s corner could attempt further treatment between rounds.

Carl Jammes Martin (29-0, 21 KOs) overcame a seventh-round knockdown to take the WBC Silver featherweight title from David Picasso (33-2-1, 18 KOs) by split decision over ten rounds.

Martin bloodied Picasso’s nose with a left hand in the third. Picasso answered in the seventh with a left hook that dropped the Filipino southpaw, who rose quickly and continued.

Martin’s strong final round helped him secure scores of 95-94 and 96-93, while the third judge favored Picasso 95-94.

Super featherweight Reito Tsutsumi (6-0, 5 KOs) stopped Raymundo Rojas García (16-3, 11 KOs) at 2:27 of the second round. The Japanese southpaw scored two knockdowns in the second before a follow-up attack prompted the referee to stop the scheduled ten-round bout.

Bek Nurmaganbet (17-0, 15 KOs) knocked out Marcos Vázquez Rodríguez (21-4-1, 10 KOs) at 2:57 of the opening round in their scheduled ten-round contest. Nurmaganbet scored an initial knockdown with approximately a minute remaining, then finished the Mexican southpaw with a combination that sent him onto his back.

Brayan León (13-0, 9 KOs) earned an eight-round unanimous decision over Hector Aguirre (7-1, 3 KOs) in a lively super middleweight contest. León landed the heavier punches early, but Aguirre rallied and kept the fight competitive.

Both men landed well in the closing rounds before León received scores of 77-75 and 78-74 twice.

Emiliano Rojo (22-0, 9 KOs) stopped Flavius Biea (24-4, 12 KOs) in the fourth round of their scheduled eight-round bout. Rojo’s pressure and body punching wore down the Romanian veteran, bringing the stoppage midway through the fourth.

Sultan Almohammed (6-0, 4 KOs) defeated Erick Jahir Urvina Villegas (5-3-3, 1 KO) by unanimous decision over six rounds. The eighteen-year-old scored a final-round knockdown with a left hand to the chin and won by scores of 60-54 and 59-55 twice.

Sports.title: Canelo Alvarez Defeats Christian Mbilli by Unanimous Decision to Reclaim WBC Title
Sports.content:
Canelo Álvarez (64-3-2) reclaimed the WBC super middleweight title by making Christian Mbilli miss and punishing his approaches, winning a unanimous decision after twelve rounds on Saturday. Returning from thirteen months out following his defeat to Terence Crawford, Canelo showed that pressure alone was not enough to overwhelm him.

The judges scored it 115-112, 116-111 and 117-110, with Boxing News 24 scoring it 116-111. Mbilli (29-1-1) supplied the greater activity in stretches, but Canelo’s cleaner counters, jab and defensive work gave him the stronger scoring punches across enough rounds to secure the victory.

Canelo established that difference early. Mbilli came forward with energy and tried to force a fast pace, only to find that much of his offense struck the guard or missed. Canelo answered selectively, catching the champion as he entered rather than trying to match every burst with an equally long combination.

The opening three rounds favored Canelo’s accuracy on our card. His jab helped him judge the distance, while his counters discouraged Mbilli from attacking without caution. The champion was working hard, but the effort did not consistently produce clean connections.

Mbilli improved in the fourth, landing more frequently and forcing Canelo into a largely defensive role. That was the approach he needed to sustain: make Canelo respond to several attacks rather than give him time to select a single counter. When Mbilli kept the work coming, the rounds became considerably harder to separate.

The sixth provided another productive spell for the champion. Canelo spent time backing up and near the ropes, answering with occasional body shots and counters while Mbilli supplied the steadier offense. Those passages kept the fight competitive and showed why Canelo could not afford to rely entirely on isolated punches.

Canelo responded in the seventh with one of his better rounds. A stiff jab interrupted Mbilli’s output, and a sharp right uppercut caught him coming forward. Canelo also mixed in body work, giving the champion more to consider before launching his next attack.

The eighth brought a costly point deduction against Mbilli from referee Hector Afu. Canelo’s cleaner work earned him the round on our card, making it 10-8 after the penalty. That gave the challenger additional breathing room without either fighter having scored a knockdown.

Mbilli continued competing rather than allowing the deduction to end his effort. His activity narrowly earned him the ninth and tenth on our card, as Canelo left enough gaps between attacks for the champion to collect points. Canelo remained accurate, but accuracy still needed sufficient output to win those rounds.

The closing two rounds settled matters. Canelo beat Mbilli to openings in the eleventh and finished behind his jab and counters in the twelfth. Mbilli could not generate the sustained late attack needed to threaten a reversal, and Canelo reached the final bell without a serious scare.

This was a successful return built on skills that survived the layoff: timing, punch selection and the ability to defend while remaining close enough to answer. Mbilli made him work and earned rounds through persistence, but never consistently solved the difference between getting Canelo to the ropes and landing effectively once he had him there.

Canelo did not deliver a stoppage, extending his run of distance fights, but he earned the belt with the more precise boxing. Mbilli brought the pressure expected of him; Canelo repeatedly supplied the better answer.

Sports.title: Canelo vs Mbilli Live Results: Round-by-Round Updates and DAZN Coverage
Sports.content:
Jaime Munguía (47-2, 35 KOs) retained his WBA super middleweight title with a unanimous decision over Nikita Zon (12-1-1, 10 KOs), but looked alarmingly poor in a fight closer than the scores suggested. The judges returned cards of 117-111, 116-112 and 117-111, margins that flattered the champion after a difficult twelve rounds.

Zon repeatedly found openings for his southpaw power shots, exposing Munguía’s loose defense and hurting him badly during a furious sixth round. Munguía survived that crisis and answered with volume and combinations, but never produced the commanding performance expected against such an inexperienced challenger.

The referee also appeared to miss two potential knockdowns against Munguía, allowing him to escape counts that could have materially affected the scoring. A clear rabbit punch from Munguía went without a point deduction, another officiating failure that favored the champion. Munguía left with the belt, but his defensive mistakes and reliance on outworking Zon made this an unsettling defense rather than a reassuring victory.

Featherweight champion Rafael Espinoza (29-0, 25 KOs) retained his WBO title with a third-round TKO over Ricardo Blandón (21-7, 14 KOs) after a severe cut over the challenger’s eye forced a medical stoppage.

Espinoza controlled the early action with his jab and reach, keeping Blandón under pressure. The Nicaraguan struggled to get past the champion’s long punches and establish an attack of his own. The cut worsened enough for the ringside doctor to intervene, ending the scheduled twelve-round contest.

Blandón had accepted the fight on roughly a week’s notice after Lorenzo Parra was ruled out, and the gap in preparation accompanied a substantial difference in class. Espinoza was comfortably in charge, although the medical ending denied him the chance to produce a more decisive finish with his punches. It was a straightforward retention for the champion, but a brief and unsatisfying title fight against a replacement challenger.

Super featherweight Reito Tsutsumi (6-0, 5 KOs) overwhelmed Raymundo Rojas García (16-3, 11 KOs) for a second-round TKO in their scheduled ten-round bout. The Japanese southpaw took charge early, using his speed to land clean combinations before Rojas could establish himself.

Rojas struggled to cope with the quicker, more polished prospect and could not slow his attack. Tsutsumi kept pressing, turning his technical advantage into damaging offense rather than allowing the Mexican time to recover.

The second-round stoppage completed a one-sided performance and gave Tsutsumi his fifth consecutive knockout victory. Rojas brought regional experience and respectable punching power, but neither was enough to bridge the difference in speed and technique. Tsutsumi looked ready for a sterner test after another opponent failed to take him beyond the early rounds.

Carl Jammes Martin (29-0) upset David Picasso (33-2-1, 18 KOs) by split decision over ten rounds to claim the WBC Silver featherweight title. The Filipino southpaw started quickly, using his speed and cleaner power shots to prevent the taller favorite from settling.

Picasso had substantial height and reach advantages but too often allowed Martin to dictate the pace rather than keeping him outside. Martin’s busier work and heavier-looking punches gave him the stronger argument in rounds where neither fighter sustained control.

Picasso had his successes in a competitive fight, but his quieter stretches left openings for Martin to seize the initiative. Two judges favored the unbeaten challenger, rewarding a performance built on activity and effective aggression against a more established opponent. Moving up in weight, Martin earned a significant victory while Picasso paid for failing to make his physical advantages count.

Super featherweight Sultan Almohammed (6-0) scored a sixth-round knockdown on his way to a unanimous decision over Erick Jahir Urvina Villegas after six rounds. The 18-year-old Saudi prospect dictated the action with persistent pressure, making the Mexican fight at his pace.

Almohammed maintained his intensity throughout, but Urvina Villegas proved tougher to finish than some of the teenager’s earlier opponents. The Mexican kept battling despite being outworked, forcing the heavy favorite to go the distance.

Almohammed closed strongly, putting Urvina Villegas down in the final round to underline his superiority. The knockdown capped a clear victory, even if the prospect could not produce another early stoppage. Six rounds against an opponent who kept competing gave Almohammed useful work beyond the quick finishes that had marked his early career.

Super middleweight Bek Nurmaganbet (17-0, 15 KOs) demolished Marcos Vázquez Rodríguez (21-4-1, 10 KOs) with a first-round knockout, ending their scheduled ten-round fight at 2:57. The unbeaten Kazakh attacked early with heavy, accurate punches, giving the Mexican veteran little opportunity to settle.

Nurmaganbet scored two knockdowns as his southpaw power proved too much for the 37-year-old. The violent finish immediately drew Knockout of the Year talk from DAZN.

Vázquez Rodríguez’s experience offered little protection once Nurmaganbet began landing, and he was overwhelmed before the opening round was over. This was a destructive performance, although beating an older opponent coming off a defeat leaves tougher tests ahead. Nurmaganbet supplied the kind of emphatic finish expected from a heavy favorite and delivered one of the early undercard’s biggest moments.

Emiliano Rojo stopped Flavius Biea at 1:37 of the fourth round, securing Team Mexico’s first victory of the night in their super middleweight bout. The 20-year-old controlled the middleweight bout with steady pressure, walking down his Romanian opponent and making him work at Rojo’s pace. Biea (24-4, 12 KOs) struggled to halt the younger fighter’s advance as Rojo’s activity gradually wore him down.

Rojo (22-0, 9 KOs) looked comfortable taking the initiative against the more experienced veteran, keeping the pressure on until the referee intervened. It was an effective performance, although Biea’s recent stoppage defeats limit how much can be read into the result. The 20-year-old Rojo did what a heavy favorite needed to do, finishing an opponent whose career was already heading downhill.

Super middleweight prospect Brayan León (13-0, 9 KOs) defeated Hector Aguirre by an eight-round unanimous decision, but the unbeaten Cuban had to work for it. Aguirre pressed León and forced him into a tough, competitive fight that exposed some flaws in the favored prospect.

León started rounds well, only to let his work rate drop and allow Aguirre to back him up. Those lapses gave the Mexican opportunities to keep the action close rather than letting León take control.

Aguirre lacked the punching power to make those stretches more costly, but he pushed León through the full eight rounds before suffering his first professional defeat.

Sports.title: Jaime Munguia Survives Sixth Round Scare to Outpoint Nikita Zon
Sports.content:
Jaime Munguía (47-2, 35 KOs) retained his WBA super middleweight title against Nikita Zon (12-1-1, 10 KOs), but his dreadful defense and a dangerous sixth round made the unanimous decision far less comfortable than the scorecards suggested. The champion won by scores of 117-111, 116-112 and 117-111 after twelve rounds that exposed how easily he can still be hurt.

Zon arrived with limited experience and no previous twelve-round fights, yet repeatedly found Munguía with effective southpaw power shots. The Mexican’s volume and combinations helped him collect rounds, but they did not conceal the damage coming back. This was supposed to be a favorable title defense; instead, Munguía spent portions of it fighting to keep the challenger from taking over.

The sixth round brought the clearest danger. Zon hurt Munguía badly and pressed an attack that threatened to turn a difficult evening into another stoppage defeat. Munguía deserves credit for surviving and responding, but the crisis came against an opponent taking an enormous jump in competition.

His recovery mattered. Munguía resumed throwing combinations and used his activity to rebuild his case over the later rounds. Zon could land the more troubling punches without consistently matching the champion’s output, giving Munguía a route to winning rounds even when his defensive mistakes were the most memorable feature.

That distinction helps explain the decision without making the wide margins persuasive. Munguía’s busy spells counted, but Zon’s successes were too significant for this to resemble a routine defense. The challenger was dangerous enough to punish openings that Munguía should have been closing well before the championship rounds.

The officiating also deserved scrutiny. Two sequences in which Munguía appeared to go down were not ruled knockdowns, allowing him to avoid counts and the potential scoring consequences. Those were important moments in a contest where the official margins already seemed generous to the champion.

Munguía also escaped a point deduction for a clear rabbit punch. That foul warranted stronger action, particularly in a physical fight where the challenger was already having to overcome a substantial experience disadvantage. Taken together, the missed potential knockdowns and unpunished foul made the referee’s performance part of the story.

Zon did not need to win every round to expose the shortcomings in Munguía’s work. He found opportunities to land hard while the champion was attacking, showing the cost of throwing combinations without adequately protecting the return. Munguía could produce more punches and still emerge from a sequence looking like the more vulnerable fighter.

The concern carries added weight because Munguía has already suffered a knockout loss to Bruno Surace. Surviving Zon’s best attack prevented a repeat result, but it did not demonstrate that the underlying defensive weaknesses have been corrected. An inexperienced challenger was still able to bring him close to disaster.

For Zon, the defeat supplied evidence that his power could trouble a world champion over a distance he had never previously attempted. He fell short on the cards, but made a much stronger case for himself than the pre-fight expectations suggested.

Munguía kept his belt through persistence, offensive volume and the ability to recover when badly hurt. Those qualities earned him something on a poor night, but they cannot keep substituting for reliable defense. Against a more accomplished finisher, the openings Zon found could carry a much heavier price.

Sports.title: Rafael Espinoza Stops Ricardo Blandon on Cuts in Riyadh Under Three Rounds
Sports.content:
Rafael Espinoza (29-0, 25 KOs) retained his WBO featherweight title with a third-round TKO over Ricardo Blandón (21-7, 14 KOs), but a severe cut ended the fight before it could become much of a contest. The champion was comfortably ahead when the ringside doctor intervened on Saturday’s Canelo Alvarez–Christian Mbilli undercard in Riyadh.

Blandón accepted the opportunity on roughly a week’s notice after mandatory challenger Lorenzo Parra was ruled out. He faced a difficult task against Espinoza, and the opening rounds offered little indication that he could overcome the difference in technique. The Mexican established his jab, applied pressure, and made the replacement challenger work to get within punching distance.

Espinoza’s length gave him control of the approach. Blandón needed to get past the jab before he could make his own power useful, but he struggled to do that consistently. The champion could initiate the action from farther out, leaving the Nicaraguan trying to close ground while dealing with incoming punches.

That combination of reach and pressure made Espinoza difficult to dislodge. He did not have to surrender the initiative to use his physical advantages, and Blandón never established enough offense to make him reconsider his approach. For the brief time they fought, the champion dictated the terms.

The cut became the decisive factor in the third round. Its severity prompted the doctor to stop the contest, producing a TKO rather than allowing the scheduled twelve-round bout to continue. This was a medical ending, with the condition of Blandón’s eye determining the finish rather than a knockdown or a referee intervention during an unanswered attack.

That distinction matters when judging the performance. Espinoza was winning clearly, but the fight ended before he could demonstrate how thoroughly he might break down the challenger. The result rewarded his early control without providing the more complete finish that his pressure appeared capable of producing.

For Blandón, the short preparation and sudden ending made this a frustrating world-title opportunity. He arrived with four consecutive victories and respectable punching power, but neither translated into sustained success against the champion. Once the cut became too serious, there was no opportunity to attempt a recovery over the remaining rounds.

Espinoza had been out of action since stopping Arnold Khegai in November 2025. Returning with a successful defense keeps his championship run moving, although fewer than three completed rounds offered limited work after that absence. Blandón could not extend him enough to reveal much about his longer-distance sharpness.

The original opponent change also reduced what Espinoza could gain from the night. Beating a replacement challenger was necessary to protect his position, but it was unlikely to carry the significance of a successful mandatory defense against Parra. The abrupt medical stoppage narrowed that opportunity further.

Espinoza remains a difficult proposition at featherweight because his unusual height comes with an attacking style that prevents opponents from simply waiting outside. Blandón experienced that difficulty immediately. The champion kept his belt with little trouble, but a stronger opponent and a fuller contest are needed to give his next defense greater substance.

Having a world champion like Espinoza share the ring with a replacement drafted on seven days notice made for grim viewing. You could tell within ninety seconds Blandon had neither the footwork nor the size to deal with a six foot one featherweight, let alone mount meaningful offense.

Blandon was essentially a sacrifice brought in to salvage television time once Lorenzo Parra fell out. When the doctor stepped in to halt it over that eye cut, it almost felt like an act of mercy rather than a dramatic championship conclusion. Nobody gained anything from it. Espinoza gets a three round workout that told us nothing new, Blandon collects a paycheck after taking punishment, and the audience gets robbed of a genuine title contest.

Sports.title: Reito Tsutsumi Blasts Raymundo Rojas in Two Fast Rounds
Sports.content:
Reito Tsutsumi (6-0, 5 KOs) overwhelmed Raymundo Rojas García (16-3, 11 KOs) with speed and clean combinations, forcing a second-round TKO in a super featherweight bout on Saturday’s Canelo Alvarez–Christian Mbilli undercard. The Japanese southpaw took control early and gave Rojas little opportunity to turn his experience into anything useful.

Scheduled for ten rounds, the fight barely got going before the difference in technique became decisive. Tsutsumi pressed the action without sacrificing accuracy, putting punches together against an opponent who struggled to keep up. Rojas needed something to interrupt that attack, but he could not establish enough offense to make Tsutsumi hesitate.

The 24-year-old’s hand speed was the most obvious advantage. Rojas was repeatedly dealing with combinations rather than single shots, leaving him occupied with defending when he needed to be answering. Tsutsumi kept the initiative and prevented the Mexican from settling into a more competitive contest.

There was purpose behind the pressure. Coming forward alone would have given Rojas opportunities to use his own power, but Tsutsumi’s cleaner delivery made the aggression effective. He was able to attack quickly enough that the veteran had little room to build a response.

By the second round, Rojas had been unable to change the direction of the fight. Tsutsumi continued landing and brought matters to an early end, completing his fifth consecutive stoppage victory. It was another short night for a prospect whose opponents have struggled to make him work through the later rounds.

Rojas entered with eleven knockouts and more professional bouts behind him, giving him at least the possibility of making Tsutsumi respect his punching power. That possibility never became a sustained threat. The gap in speed and technique left Rojas trying to cope with the attack rather than impose his own fight.

For Tsutsumi, the encouraging part was how quickly he made those advantages count. A heavy favorite can win without revealing much, particularly against an opponent unable to offer a serious challenge. Here, the Japanese fighter at least avoided wasting time or letting the contest become untidy: he took charge and finished.

His strong amateur background, which included World Youth Championships gold, helps explain the polish he already brings to these early professional appearances. Saturday’s performance showed a fighter comfortable taking the lead on a major card, rather than one who needed several rounds to find his confidence.

The limitation is that another early finish leaves his longer-distance work largely unexplored. This was booked for ten rounds, but Rojas could not provide the sustained test that distance was intended to allow. Tsutsumi’s ability to adjust against someone who can match his speed or withstand his combinations remains a task for future opposition.

He has earned a more demanding opponent. Rojas could offer neither enough offense to slow him nor enough defensive success to extend him, and the result became one-sided quickly. Tsutsumi delivered what was expected of him, with the accuracy behind the stoppage offering more encouragement than the unbeaten record alone.

Sports.title: Carl Jammes Martin Stuns David Picasso in Ten Round Featherweight Upset
Sports.content:
Carl Jammes Martin pulled off a major upset against David Picasso, claiming the WBC Silver featherweight title by split decision after ten hard rounds. The unbeaten Filipino gave up noticeable height and reach, yet he neutralized those deficits through relentless tempo, explosive entries, and sharper power punching while Picasso struggled to enforce his natural advantages.

Picasso surrendered the center of the ring immediately. Instead of posting a long jab to halt the shorter challenger, the Mexican drifted backward and yielded control. Martin dictated every exchange, leaving Picasso hunting for single counter shots while mounting zero sustained offense.

The scores were 96-93 Martin, 95-94 Picasso, and 95-95 Martin.

Martin jumped on him immediately. Fast combinations carried the southpaw inside where his cleaner power punches caught the judges in tight rounds. Picasso fired back in spurts, but sporadic work never derailed the challenger.

The bout featured stretches of sharp technical exchanges, but Martin maintained a higher operational gear. Whenever Picasso tapped the brakes, Martin surged into the void, obliging the favorite to trade instead of resetting safely behind his guard.

That hesitation proved fatal for Picasso. A long reach functions as a defense only if it fires continuously. Because Picasso neglected to post a reliable perimeter, Martin stepped inside repeatedly without facing heavy incoming fire.

Martin handled tight spots well, staying composed whenever Picasso rallied. Securing the cards did not require total domination; Martin simply stayed busier and landed the more damaging shots across ten rounds to win over two of the ringside officials.

The split scorecards showed how tight several rounds were, yet Martin undeniably carved out the win through pure labor. He outworked the favorite during quiet sequences and scored whenever Picasso settled for single, isolated attacks.

The setback hits Picasso hard, coming shortly after his stoppage of Maicol Rincon and his resilient twelve round showing against Naoya Inoue last December. Toughness alone could not rescue this fight against a challenger setting an urgent pace.

Stepping up in weight elevated the magnitude of Martin’s triumph. The top ranked WBO super bantamweight proved he can outbox premier competition over the distance without relying on a knockout punch.

Martin walks away with a defining scalp and a clearer path to world title opportunities. Picasso departs carrying severe regret after failing to deploy the length, seasoning, and command needed to hold off a determined fighter.

Ghana News.title: 2026 Luv FM-Republic Bank Habitat mini-clinic records huge success in Kumasi
Ghana News.content:
The mini-clinic of the 2026 edition of the Luv FM-Republic Bank Habitat has recorded a successful outing in Kumasi, bringing together key players in Ghana’s housing and construction industry to promote affordable and accessible homeownership.

The event, held on October 29, 2026, at the Opoku Trading Arena in Adum, offered prospective homeowners, property developers and industry professionals an opportunity to engage institutions providing housing services, construction materials, financing and interior decoration solutions.

Now in its eighth year, the Habitat Fair seeks to address some of the challenges associated with land acquisition, building and homeownership, particularly in the Ashanti Region.

Organised in partnership with Republic Bank, the mini-clinic brought together stakeholders across the housing and construction value chain. Visitors had the opportunity to access professional guidance, explore products and services, and consider solutions suited to their housing needs and budgets.

Institutions offer guidance on homeownership

The Lands Commission and the Asantehene’s Lands Secretariat were among the participating institutions, providing visitors with information and guidance on land-related matters and other aspects of homeownership.

The event also showcased construction materials, home improvement products and interior decoration solutions.

JetSky Roofing Systems engaged patrons on its fire-resistant roofing systems and window products, while Prestodea Ghana showcased glass windows, balustrades and doors.

A representative of the Asantehene’s Lands Secretariat highlighted the importance of the initiative in helping members of the public navigate their homeownership aspirations.

Republic Bank highlights mortgage support

Head of Mortgage Banking at Republic Bank, Dan Adjetey Mohenu, reaffirmed the bank’s commitment to supporting individuals at different stages of their homeownership journey.

He explained that the bank’s mortgage and housing finance solutions were not limited to purchasing completed properties but also catered for individuals who prefer to construct their homes in phases.

The financing options, he said, could support different stages of construction, from foundation works to interior decoration, subject to the bank’s assessment criteria and requirements.

Main Habitat Fair scheduled for November

The partnership between Luv FM and Republic Bank is expected to continue offering prospective homeowners access to financial guidance and other essential services as they work towards owning homes.

The mini-clinic serves as a lead-up to the main 2026 Habitat Fair, scheduled to take place from November 25 to 29 in Kumasi.

The initiative comes amid growing demand for housing driven by population growth and urbanisation, with organisers positioning the fair as a platform for connecting prospective homeowners with institutions and services across the housing sector.

Ghana News.title: Stable on paper. What about your pocket?
Ghana News.content:
Dr Mahamudu Bawumia and Hon.Kojo Oppong Nkrumah have raised critical questions about Ghana’s economy. However, the Government is confident in its recovery from the cost-of-living crisis whilst forging a new economic policy initiative worth US$10bn over five years (about GH¢23bn a year).

Ghanaians must understand the context when looking at the macroeconomic indicators. Be well informed about the political equalisation in these conversations and ask the critical questions about the outcome, which, ultimately, is: JOBS, GROWTH, UNEMPLOYMENT. This article does exactly 3 things:

Peg the macroeconomic data side by side with the statements made

Examine the prospects of the Government’s New baby “New Economy”

And most importantly, whether the policies and promised 24hr economy have achieved the intended purpose of reducing the unemployment rate

And finally, what the state of unemployment looks like, which was the main issue at hand for which this government was voted into power: a promised 3-shift job system that will create employment and expand economic growth in key sectors.

Publicly available data show stability: inflation down from 23.8% to 5.2%; debt-to-GDP down from 61.8% to 44.7%; growth at 6%; multidimensional poverty improved by 3 percentage points (21.9%); and the bank lending rate halved (15.6%). One might argue that the current inflation print is somewhat detached from market reality; however, a lower inflation rate does not necessarily mean lower costs of goods and services.

According to the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS), the Consumer Price Index as at September 2026,

housing, water and energy inflation (10.3%) poses a huge financial burden on the ordinary Ghanaian. The double-digit inflation (10.3%) simply means the rent, electricity and water bills are hurting the pockets of consumers the most amongst other items in the consumer basket.

Government’s Growth figures, as reported in the 2026 Mid-Year Budget review, show Ghana’s Growth stands at 6%; farm growth has halved, from 7.1% to 3.9%, while services grew by 8% in 2026, down from 8.1% in 2025. The positives extend to a poverty reduction of 3 percentage points and the cost of borrowing.

However, the Growth figures do not reflect majorly in job creation, as youth unemployment currently stands at 32.4%, most precise, 1 out of 3 young job seekers have no work.

This begs the question: of roughly GH¢650bn budgeted over 2 years, and the GH¢1.6bn investment in flagship jobs and social schemes in 2026. Are they yielding the necessary outcomes? Could this be the possible concern fundamental to Dr Bawumia’s assertion of a Paper Economy to Hon. Oppong Nkrumah’s quest for accountability on policy outcomes estimated at GH¢650bn?



One could mention that Policy lags, under-execution and release lags are fundamental constraints to the transmission effect of these investments; however, the macroeconomic data.

In response to the growth figures and the major concern on jobs, now comes the government’s big bet, "The New Economy": moving from stability to increasing growth in the economy, mainly to create jobs. The President says US$10bn over five years (about GH¢23bn a year), with an ambitious statement: "We are not going to borrow money for the New Economy Policy... this is our own money."

However, this year alone, reports from the 2026 budgets and the Mid-review indicate that wages, interest and earmarked funds already take 79% of 2026 revenue (GH¢212bn). That leaves GH¢56bn for goods, services and all projects, and in 2026 the prospective New Economy of 2027 would have equalled 41% of it.

In perspective, what would funding it mean? New taxes, a tightened revenue mobilisation strategy, or domestic borrowing (bonds)? The 2026 budget already plans GH¢72bn of borrowing at home. But would that be what the President’s statement on “No borrowing for New Economy” means: domestic borrowing and not external borrowing?

A masterstroke for funding the New Economy will be a strong revenue mobilisation exercise to meet revenue targets. The lazy approach could be a hike in taxes.

As already noted, revenue was GH¢1.4bn short in the first half, with oil revenue 31% below target. One can only be optimistic about revenue performance for 2027.

The other downside risk remains the volatility of international commodity prices, especially for Ghana’s exports such as gold, which accounts for 68% of exports and how a projected fall can offset Ghana’s foreign earnings. From March to August 2026, Gold prices fell by 9.1%; the World Bank projects lower prices in 2027, and this risk weighs on Ghana’s fiscal position, as GH¢58bn of bonds fall due in 2027, the same year the New Economy starts.

In the world of political equalisation, whataboutism and ‘JANDAMism’, many conversations will arise. For you as a young person, a parent and a business owner, there are 4 key data points to watch:

|JOBS| 32.4% Youth unemployment

Unemployment has reduced by only 0.1 percentage point and currently stands at 13.0% (end of year 2024 to Q3 2025): 13.1% to 13.0% end of year. Youth unemployment for young persons within the ages of 15-24 remains relatively high at 32.4%.

This indicator is a critical outcome of job creation and expansion.

|CREDIT| 15.6% lending rate

According to the September 2026 press release by the Bank of Ghana, the cost of borrowing has reduced to 15.6%, a 14.6 percentage point reduction in previous rate of 30.2% in 2025.

Availability of funds from the banks to the customers including businesses and private citizens, has increased from 1.7% in 2025 to 29% in 2026.

|FARMS AND FACTORIES| 3.9% farm growth

Sector growth in agriculture has not seen improved growth as it grew at 3.9% compared to a 6.8% growth the previous turn. Agriculture remains a key sector of development , jobs and livelihood for the rural communities. It remains the engine sector to boost job creation and enhance development in rural areas.

Its inconsistent underinvestment and lagging growth figures point to the fundamental structural defects in our economy and job creation.



|GOLD AND CEDI| GH¢11.55 per US$

Gold prices under various transformations of the Gold for Reserve Program to the Ghana Accelerated National Reserve Accumulation Programme (GANRAP) and Operationalization of the then Precious Minerals Marketing Company (PMMC) to now, GOLDBod. It remains a major export earner to reduce pressure on foreign currencies and to build the reserves to absorb external pressure on the domestic currency. However, its impact relies on an optimal exchange rate and a positive trade balance: A position that improves export earnings without aggressively affecting local businesses through a relatively increased penchant for imports.

The reality check is YOU. Is money moving out of your pocket quickly? Money dey pocket?

Ghana News.title: From stability to transformation: 5 tests for Ghana’s 2027 Budget
Ghana News.content:
Ghana is preparing a budget with a different promise. After years of debt restructuring and spending restraint, the government wants to turn economic stability into jobs, investment and higher production. But the repayments coming due in 2027 will compete for the same public money.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) completed the final review of Ghana’s US$3 billion Extended Credit Facility in July. Its successor, the Policy Coordination Instrument, provides monitoring without new financing. The coming budget must show how Ghana intends to sustain its recovery while paying for its next phase of development.

There are gains to protect. September inflation was 5.2%, while provisional public debt stood at 45% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in June. But these figures cannot tell us whether new investments will deliver or how comfortably government can meet its repayments. Judge the budget by how convincingly it links its promises to financing and results. Five tests matter.

1. Show how the New Economy will be financed

The published Fiscal Strategy Document proposes investment equivalent to 1.5% of GDP annually for four years, approximately US$10 billion. It identifies two sources of financing: an additional 0.5% of GDP in revenue and room created by reducing the primary surplus.

The budget must now show what the money will be used for. Which projects are ready to begin? Who will implement them, and when should the public expect results? A programme intended to create jobs needs measurable employment and production targets alongside its costs. Any private investment expected to follow should be distinguished from money government has actually committed, with public guarantees disclosed.

2. Explain the safeguards behind the lower surplus

The government proposes lowering the primary surplus on a commitment basis from 1.5% to 0.5% of GDP from 2027. A primary surplus is the excess of revenue over spending before interest payments. Reducing it leaves more room for expenditure, but also means a smaller contribution towards containing debt, other things being equal. Productive projects can justify greater investment. The harder task is selecting those projects and protecting the budget if expected revenue fails to arrive. Government should explain how the proposed target fits the applicable fiscal rules, what safeguards accompany it, and which spending would be reconsidered if conditions deteriorate. Independent scrutiny by the Fiscal Council would help establish confidence in those choices.

3. Prepare for the repayments coming due

The repayment calendar is demanding. Government has announced GH¢58 billion of Domestic Debt Exchange Programme bond maturities in 2027 and another GH¢53 billion in 2028. A reassuring debt ratio does not remove the need to find money when bondholders are owed it. Building a Sinking Fund is therefore reasonable. Government reported GH¢15.6 billion accumulated by 22 July, while the Institute for Fiscal Studies questioned its treatment in the approved budget. The next budget should reconcile the fund’s opening balance, inflows, withdrawals and planned repayments. It should distinguish money saved from money borrowed to build a buffer. Borrowing ahead of maturity can ease immediate pressure, but it brings interest costs and another repayment date.

4. Show whether spending restraint is delaying delivery

Preparing for repayments must also leave room to deliver today’s budget. The Ministry of Finance reports a first-half primary surplus of 0.9% of GDP on a commitment basis. Yet capital spending was 39.3% below plan, while net arrears clearance reached only 38.2% of the programmed amount. The improved balance deserves recognition; the shortfalls deserve explanation. Delayed payment of old arrears does not itself explain a commitment-basis surplus. Nevertheless, unfinished projects and overdue bills have consequences beyond the fiscal tables. Contractors waiting for payment may struggle to pay suppliers and workers. Communities waiting for infrastructure continue to bear the cost of its absence. Government should show what it committed to spend, what it paid and what remains overdue. Where spending fell below plan, the explanation should distinguish genuine savings, rejected claims and delays in delivery. Spending less is not automatically evidence of failure, neither is it sufficient evidence of efficiency.

5. Show what public liabilities could cost taxpayers

Even a well-executed budget can be disrupted by obligations elsewhere in the public sector. The Fiscal Strategy Document already includes a Fiscal Risk Statement. The budget should build on it by showing how much major exposures could cost taxpayers, when support might be required and who is responsible. Energy-sector obligations, guarantees, gold-purchase operations and central-bank recapitalisation need clear treatment. The IMF’s July review recorded a waiver linked to cost-sharing under the domestic gold purchase programme and reaffirmed the commitment to recapitalise the Bank of Ghana by 2032. These issues need an explanation of their cost and financing. Liabilities already included in public debt should be distinguished from claims that might become government obligations, so that disclosure neither hides exposures nor counts them twice.

Before election pressures intensify

The 2028 election-year budget will be presented in late 2027. The coming budget is therefore an opportunity to establish safeguards before political spending pressures intensify. Its credibility will depend on what happens after the speech: whether projects progress, payments arrive and emerging risks are reported promptly.

None of these asks for less ambition. It asks government to cost its promises, explain its fiscal choices, prepare for repayments and account for delivery. Ghana’s next phase of development needs a budget that connects ambition to evidence. It should survive an audit.

Daniel is a PhD student in Accounting at the Muma College of Business, University of South Florida, a qualified Chartered Accountant (ICAG) and Chartered Management Accountant (CIMA). He previously worked as a financial analyst at Deloitte.

Ghana News.title: Ghana courts Qatari investors into key sectors of economy
Ghana News.content:
The Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority (GIPA), Simon Madjie, has called for increased investment from Qatar into strategic sectors of Ghana’s economy to strengthen bilateral economic relations and promote sustainable growth.

According to him, Ghana was seeking to deepen investment cooperation with Qatar by creating opportunities for partnerships across sectors, including agriculture, manufacturing, energy, infrastructure, financial services, tourism and the creative arts.

In an interview with Doha News in Qatar, Mr Madjie said improved air connectivity between the two countries would facilitate business engagements, promote trade and boost investment flows.

He was speaking on the sidelines of the ninth edition of the World Investment Forum 2026, hosted by the State of Qatar in partnership with UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) under the theme, “Investing in the Future.”

Mr Madjie said Ghana is keen on attracting Qatari investment into manufacturing, agro-processing, financial services, fintech, digital services, oil and gas, power generation, mining and tourism.

He also highlighted opportunities for cooperation in culture and the creative arts, adding that Ghana was interested in leveraging Qatar’s expertise to support the development of industries and strengthen business partnerships.

On the investment climate, Mr Madjie said Ghana was working to improve the business environment and create favourable conditions for capital inflows.

He pointed out thst the country offered incentives for investors seeking to operate in free zones, as well as incentives relating to factories, equipment and machinery.

Mr Madjie said Ghana’s participation in the forum was aimed at showcasing the country’s investment potential and encouraging Qatari businesses to explore commercially viable opportunities.

He called for stronger cooperation between the public and private sectors of both countries to establish sustainable partnerships that would serve their mutual interests.

Ghana News.title: MIIF leads 50-hectare forest restoration project in Sekyere Krobo
Ghana News.content:
The Minerals Income Investment Fund (MIIF), in partnership with the Forestry Commission and supported by Zijin Golden Ridge Ghana and other partners has commissioned a five-year project to restore 50 hectares of degraded forest at the Subri River Forest Reserve in Sekyere Krobo, Western Region.

The project, commissioned on October 29, 2026, forms part of MIIF’s Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Biodiversity Reforestation Project, which seeks to promote environmental sustainability and strengthen biodiversity conservation in Ghana’s mining regions.

Protecting Ghana’s natural heritage

Speaking at the commissioning ceremony, MIIF Chief Executive Officer, Justina Nelson, said the initiative reflects the Fund’s commitment to ensuring that the economic benefits of mineral resources are matched by responsible environmental stewardship.

“The true value of our nation's mineral wealth lies not only in what we extract today, but also in the natural heritage we preserve for generations to come,” she said.

She emphasised that the success of the project would not be measured simply by the number of trees planted, but by the extent to which the forest is restored and protected over time. This, she noted, would require sustained care, effective monitoring and the collective commitment of all stakeholders.

The Forestry Commission is providing technical expertise and implementation support to guide the rehabilitation process and promote the long-term survival of the restored forest.

The Executive Director of the Forest Services Division of the Forestry Commission, Dr Sarfo Adu, highlighted the importance of sustained collaboration and effective forest management in achieving successful restoration.

He said the Commission would provide technical guidance and implementation support to ensure the restoration work was effectively managed and that the trees planted survived to support the forest’s long-term recovery.

He also urged other corporate organisations to draw inspiration from MIIF’s initiative and partner with the Forestry Commission to help restore Ghana’s degraded forest landscape.

He said such partnerships would support the government’s Tree for Life Restoration Initiative, launched by President John Dramani Mahama on 21 March 2025.

Community participation key to sustainability

The Paramount Chief of Sekyere Krobo, Nana Kwao Badu II, commended MIIF and its partners for the initiative and welcomed the participation of farmers in the restoration exercise.

He called on the Forestry Commission to work closely with the farmers to ensure that they also benefit from their efforts to nurture and protect the trees.

He noted that recognising the role and livelihoods of local communities would encourage a stronger sense of ownership and responsibility for the forest.

Nana Kwao Badu II also expressed appreciation to MIIF for providing farm tools to support participating farmers and appealed for additional support for forest guards to strengthen the protection of the reserve.

His remarks highlighted the importance of combining environmental restoration with community livelihoods and effective forest protection.

A collective commitment to environmental sustainability

The five-year initiative brings together MIIF, the Forestry Commission and Corporate Ghana in a shared effort to address forest degradation, protect biodiversity and promote sustainable environmental practices.

MIIF acknowledged the support of the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, the Forestry Commission, Corporate Ghana, traditional authorities, the District Assembly and the people of Sekyere Krobo.

Through the restoration of 50 hectares of degraded forest, the Fund is reinforcing its commitment to responsible mineral wealth management and ensuring that environmental protection remains an important part of Ghana’s sustainable development agenda.

Ghana News.title: GAYO partners with MMDAs and schools to promote waste segregation in Greater Accra
Ghana News.content:
The Green Africa Youth Organization (GAYO) has partnered with metropolitan, municipal, and district assemblies and schools across Greater Accra to promote waste segregation among students.

The initiative, under GAYO’s Zero Waste portfolio, covers schools in seven municipalities, including La Dade Kotopon, Ledzokuku, Accra Metropolitan and Ablekuma West. It aims to help schools separate their waste at source, turn organic waste into compost, and recycle plastics.

Betty Adjei, Operations and Programs Director at GAYO, said the initiative comes ahead of a government directive requiring all households to start separating their waste from next year.

“When is the important time to support with infrastructure, to support this kind of policy?” she said. “It’s very important to catch them young.”

As part of the initiative, GAYO is distributing 200 bins, 300 books, pens and educational flyers to schools across the seven municipalities. Each school receives two bins to help students separate their waste. Ms Adjei said the initiative will later extend to markets and wider municipalities.

Antonio Yayrator Korkuvi, a Project Coordinator on GAYO’s Zero Waste portfolio, said about 60 percent of the financial resources given to assemblies go into managing waste. A waste analysis by GAYO found that about 60 percent of the waste generated in schools is organic.

“And so we are helping these schools to be able to separate their waste,” he said. “The organic waste is turned into what is called compost.”

He said the compost is used in school gardens to grow vegetables free of the chemicals found in synthetic fertilisers. GAYO is also training students to make compost themselves, while plastics will go to its material recovery facility to be processed into pellets.

The partnership also tackles a problem that has frustrated schools. Madam Habiba Kotomah, Education Director for the La Dade Kotopon Municipality, said schools that sorted their waste in the past saw it mixed back together by collection trucks.

She welcomed GAYO’s plan to collect the separated waste directly and pay schools a token in return. “So they will come around and pick the organic ones and pick the plastic ones,” she said. “I’m so happy my schools are going to be able to generate some form of IGF from this activity.”

Ms Adjei said the approach builds on work already underway. The La Dade Kotopon Municipal Assembly’s material recovery facility diverts more than 50 tonnes of waste a month.

At Forces Senior High School, Assistant Headmistress (Domestic) Rosina Lawal said the school has already placed bins within reach of students, and wants more.

“Imagine we have bins like one student, one bin. The school, and not only the school, the whole of Ghana will also look very beautiful,” she said. She urged GAYO to keep going: “They should add more, like Oliver Twist, we want more.”

Reducing organic waste in landfills also helps cut methane, a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide. More than half of the waste Accra produces is organic. In October 2026, officials of the Accra Metropolitan Assembly warned that Ghana risks missing its target of cutting methane emissions from the waste sector by 30 percent by 2030.

Ghana News.title: GAYO, some Accra schools turn to composting and recycling to beat the waste problem with fresh bins
Ghana News.content:
Schools in Accra that separate their waste say their efforts are being wasted because collection trucks mix the sorted rubbish back together when they pick it up.

Education officials in the La Dade Kotopon Municipality say the problem has led many schools to give up sorting altogether. Now, the Green Africa Youth Organization (GAYO) wants to change that. Under its Zero Waste initiative, it plans to collect separated organic and plastic waste directly from schools in seven municipalities across Greater Accra.

Madam Habiba Kotomah, Education Director for the La Dade Kotopon Municipality, said some schools were part of an earlier pilot that provided bins for sorting, but the effort collapsed at the point of collection.

“We do the sorting in the schools. But when the truck comes around, they put everything back together and it’s frustrating,” she said. “So at a point, most of them stopped the sorting.”

She said schools also lack enough bins, despite repeated requests to the assembly.

Waste is a heavy burden on local government. Antonio Yayrator Korkuvi, a Project Coordinator on GAYO’s Zero Waste portfolio, said about 60 percent of the financial resources given to assemblies go into managing waste, mostly organic waste and plastics.

Schools are a major source. “Per the waste analysis that we’ve done, we found out that about 60 percent of the waste that is generated in the school is organic waste, followed by papers and then plastics,” he said.

When organic waste is dumped and left to rot, it produces methane, a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide. More than half of all the waste Accra produces is organic, and most of it ends up in landfills. In October 2026, officials of the Accra Metropolitan Assembly warned that Ghana risks missing its target of cutting methane emissions from the waste sector by 30 percent by 2030.

Poorly managed waste also has more visible costs. Betty Adjei, Operations and Programs Director at GAYO, pointed to the floods in June and July. “We saw what happened during the June-July flooding, where a lot of waste were within our communities,” she said.

She said the push for schools comes ahead of a government directive requiring all households to start separating their waste from next year. “It’s very important to catch them young,” she said.

Under the initiative, GAYO is working with schools in the La Dade Kotopon, Ledzokuku, Accra Metropolitan and Ablekuma West municipalities, among others, to set up sorting systems and train students.

Separated organic waste is turned into compost for school gardens. Mr Antonio Yayrator Korkuvi said vegetables grown with the compost are free of the chemicals found in synthetic fertilisers. Plastics will go to GAYO’s material recovery facility to be processed into pellets.

Madam Kotomah said GAYO has agreed to collect the sorted waste from schools and pay them a token in return. “So they will come around and pick the organic ones and pick the plastic ones,” she said. “I’m so happy my schools are going to be able to generate some form of IGF from this activity.”

Ms Adjei said the model is already working at municipal level. The La Dade Kotopon Municipal Assembly’s material recovery facility diverts more than 50 tonnes of waste a month, from organics to plastics. She said the initiative will later extend to markets.

At Forces Senior High School, Assistant Headmistress (Domestic) Rosina Lawal has built a culture of keeping bins within reach of every student. She said her goal is one bin for every student.

“Imagine we have bins like one student, one bin. The school, and even not only the school, the whole Ghana will look very beautiful,” she said.

She admitted that enforcing cleanliness has not made her popular. “Parents may talk, the students may hate you, but the fact is, me, I want to make a name,” she said. “You could see the whole school is looking nice.”

She urged GAYO and other partners to keep going. “They should add more, like Oliver Twist, we want more,” she said. “They shouldn’t relax.”

Ghana News.title: Why Financing Government is more rewarding in Africa than financing enterprise and the threat to economic integration
Ghana News.content:
The gradual implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area has brought greater focus on the advantages of significantly increasing intra-African trade from the current 16%–17%. It is recognised that Africa’s economic integration will make it more rewarding to produce, invest and trade, boosting growth, jobs and shared prosperity across Africa and her 1.5 billion-strong population.

The campaign now, and rightly so, is about getting African governments to enable two low-hanging key drivers of intra-African trade: visa-free travel and connected payment systems that allow Africans to move freely, buy and sell across borders using simply their mobile money wallets. This is because, according to the research desk of the Africa Prosperity Network (APN), these two moves alone can increase intra-African trade to more than 25% within the first five years of implementation.

Once a tailor or seamstress in Bamako can promote his or her clothes on Instagram, a customer in Maputo can buy instantly online using her mobile money wallet in Mozambican meticais, her local currency, and the seller can receive payment right then in West African CFA francs, opening that commercial highway will create the incentive for investors and financiers to put money into the transport and logistics that will ensure that goods sold across borders in Africa get to buyers in no time.

It is through this lens that I welcome the statement from Ghana’s President, John Dramani Mahama, in Moscow on 29 October 2026. His call for local-currency trade settlements and integrated digital payments, alongside greater local processing of Africa’s mineral and agricultural resources, brings together two priorities too often discussed separately: producing more value in Africa and making it easier to trade that value across Africa.

But, fundamentally, Africa’s single market must make it more rewarding to produce, invest and trade. Removing visa restrictions and connecting payment systems are essential: Africans should be able to travel across the continent and buy and sell across borders using their mobile money wallets. But easier movement and payments will achieve far more if the businesses expected to serve that market can also access affordable finance.

This brings us to a damaging incentive in many African economies, which is that financing government can be more rewarding than financing enterprise. When governments borrow heavily at high interest rates, banks and investors can earn attractive returns from Treasury bills and bonds, with fewer operational demands than investing in production, the real economy.

Manufacturers need machinery, reliable electricity and skilled workers; agribusinesses face weather risks and seasonal cash flows. These enterprises create jobs, yet they struggle to attract capital or even borrow from the banks when government securities offer compelling returns.

High nominal yields do not necessarily mean high real returns: inflation and currency depreciation can erode them. Government bonds can also finance infrastructure that enables enterprise. The problem arises when persistent deficits absorb scarce savings and push up borrowing costs for businesses.

America offers a warning from a different stage of development. Its relative decline in manufacturing dominance, particularly against China, is often attributed partly to financialization, which is the growing influence of financial returns and shareholder valuations over business decisions. Critics argue that maximising share prices and short-term payouts can take precedence over expanding productive capacity.

In Africa, the danger is that financing government becomes more rewarding than financing enterprise. In America, it is that maximising financial valuations becomes more important than expanding productive capacity. The mechanisms differ, but the common danger is finance becoming detached from the production that sustains prosperity. America built a formidable industrial base before these concerns emerged. Africa, however, has yet to industrialise at the scale our population demands. We cannot afford to starve production of capital before building that foundation.

This is why affordable finance belongs at the heart of Africa’s integration agenda. A functioning single market serving some 1.5 billion people would strengthen the commercial case for factories, agricultural processing and regional supply chains. But market access alone cannot finance machinery or fulfil an order. Without stronger African production, we risk integrating markets largely for goods made elsewhere.

This is also why we at the Africa Prosperity Network welcome the Africa Credit Rating Agency. Its inaugural CEO, Dr Sifiso Falala, brings experience from challenging established rating practices through his work at Plus 94. AfCRA will help institutionalise and tackle the issue of how African risks are assessed and, ultimately, how productive investment can secure affordable finance.

Integration and sound economic management must therefore advance together. Low, stable inflation makes long-term investment easier to plan. Credible public finances and sustainable government borrowing reduce competition for scarce savings. Reliable electricity, predictable taxation and enforceable contracts improve the prospects of productive enterprise. Simply ordering interest rates down cannot substitute for these foundations.

The objective for our continent is a connected economic system: a larger market makes investment more attractive; affordable, patient capital makes production possible; and efficient transport and payments help businesses reach customers and get paid. Our focus now at APN, with the support of our partners, is to go for these two quick wins of cross-border digital payments interoperability and visa-free travel.

Local processing requires investment. Investment needs viable markets. Those markets need practical ways to move people, goods and money. President Mahama’s call at the Russia-Africa Summit thus speaks directly to the challenge of making African enterprise more competitive and rewarding. Its promise will be fully realised when national economic policies support the producers whom continental integration is intended to empower.

His reaffirmation of Nkrumah’s vision of African unity is encouraging. His anticipated African Union chairmanship in 2027, coinciding with Ghana’s 70th independence anniversary, would offer an opportunity to rally fellow leaders behind this practical economic Pan-Africanism.

Africa Prosperity Dialogues 2027 provides a timely platform to translate that ambition into proposals for action. Its theme, “The Borderless Africa We Want: Move Freely. Pay Seamlessly. Trade More,” captures the connections between mobility, payments and commerce. The financing argument gives that agenda its productive foundation, which is that African businesses must be able to make what this larger market needs.

Hosted by President Mahama in Ghana on 13–15 January 2027, with strategic partners including AfDB, Afreximbank, BADEA, AUDA-NEPAD and major African multinational companies, the Dialogues, fifth in the annual series, will bring private sector and civil society perspectives into the deliberations preceding the 40th AU Summit.

More so because its focus connects directly with the AU’s 2027 theme, “AU at the Dawn of its 25th Anniversary: Leveraging the Full Potential of SAATM and New Technologies for Continental Integration.” The Single African Air Transport Market and new technologies can help connect businesses and consumers across our fragmented continent. Alongside freer movement and interoperable payments, they can make the single market more accessible to those expected to build it.

APD 2027 must help turn these connections into a coherent agenda for our leaders: remove barriers to trade while improving the conditions for production. The experiences of those who invest, employ and trade should inform the policies intended to serve them.

The measure of success will be more African savings financing African enterprises, more resources processed locally and more young people finding worthwhile work. Our single market will, thus, fulfil its promise when it makes it pay to produce right here in Africa.

The author is the Founder and Executive Chairman of the Africa Prosperity Network, organisers of Africa Prosperity Dialogues 2027. To register, visit www.apd2027.africaprosperitynetwork.com or email gabby@africaprosperity.network.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
