World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Polish president holds crisis talks in court standoff
World.content:
A dispute over the politicisation of Poland’s constitutional court is deepening, with no side appearing to back down.

The Polish president has held crisis talks with political leaders as a dispute over the independence of the country’s top constitutional court deepens.

Representatives of nationalist, far-right, and some governing coalition parties attended President Karol Nawrocki’s talks at the presidential palace on Saturday, while Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s governing centrist party, Civic Coalition, stayed away.

Nawrocki said in a statement that he convened the “urgent” consultations “due to the threat to Poland’s internal security” presented by the sudden suspension on Friday of the Constitutional Tribunal’s chief judge, Bogdan Swieczkowski.

No breakthrough had emerged by Saturday afternoon.

Meanwhile, in a Saturday evening speech addressing the ongoing crisis, Tusk accused conservative nationalist opposition leaders of wanting to “destroy democracy and rule of law”.

“Let’s call things by their name,” he said. “For years in Poland there exist organisations and politicians who wish to destroy democracy and rule of law.”

Followers of the opposition right-wing Law and Justice party (PiS) gathered outside the court on Saturday, extending protests that have been running for weeks in support of PiS-friendly judges.

Constitutional crisis

The Constitutional Tribunal is Poland’s top court for deciding constitutional matters. It has been at the centre of a years-long political saga related to the politicisation of Polish courts, which Tusk says began under the right-wing PiS government.

Swieczkowski, whom the PiS appointed during its 2015-2023 government, was accused of using his powers as head of the court to block parliament from electing new judges.



Tusk argued that the court’s judges were not politically neutral and that Swieczkowski’s removal was a “painful” but necessary decision to restore the rule of law in Poland after years of erosion under PiS rule.

The court’s official X account on Friday described the government’s move as a “coup d’etat”.

Nawrocki, himself a right-wing figure, has also blocked nominations to the court under his administration.

A key complaint brought by Tusk and his pro-European party was that the court’s PiS-aligned judges frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over EU law.

The European Commission on Saturday urged Nawrocki to accept the nomination of new judges at the centre of the country’s constitutional crisis, the AFP news agency reported.

US Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose called for calm on all sides.

“The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse,” Rose wrote in a post on X.

World.title: Dutch authorities rescue 38 people adrift in rubber boat
World.content:
Refugee and migrant boats are rarely found in Dutch waters, and authorities are still trying to establish where this one came from.

Authorities in the Netherlands have rescued 38 people found adrift in a rubber boat off the Dutch coast, in one of the first such interceptions for the country.

Two of the people on board the dinghy when it was rescued are thought to be smugglers, while the rest are migrants, military police spokesperson Doron Wallin told The Associated Press news agency on Saturday.

“We don’t know where they came from – France, the Netherlands or Belgium – and we don’t know where the boat was heading,” Wallin said.

The boat was discovered drifting with no motor off the coast of the Netherlands’ Zeeland province, far southwest of Amsterdam. No one was wearing a life vest.

All 38 on the boat were men, 36 of whom were from Afghanistan, and two – the suspected smugglers – were from Sudan, according to the AFP news agency. The two Sudanese men have been arrested on suspicion of people smuggling.

It is not known where the boat was headed, but refugee and migrant crossings in small boats from France to the United Kingdom have become commonplace in recent years. It is unusual for boats to be discovered in Dutch waters, however.

“These are things you usually see in France and Belgium. We rarely see it here in the Netherlands before today,” Wallin said.

Dutch authorities will open an investigation into the case on Sunday.

World.title: Trump loses legal battle over Epstein-linked Wall Street Journal case
World.content:
Judge permanently drops Trump’s $10bn WSJ lawsuit, ruling the president failed to prove actual malice in the newspaper’s reporting.

A federal judge has permanently dismissed United States President Donald Trump’s multibillion-dollar defamation lawsuit against media mogul Rupert Murdoch and The Wall Street Journal.

On Saturday, US District Judge Darrin Gayles concluded that the president had failed to establish the standard of “actual malice” required for defamation suits.

Under US law, a successful complaint must show that the defendant released a defamatory statement knowing it was false or with “reckless disregard” for its accuracy.

Gayles, however, said that Trump was “grasping at straws” with his $10bn case against The Wall Street Journal.

“The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice,” Gayles wrote.

“Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false.”

The judge went so far as to suggest that Trump’s legal team had attempted “to manufacture flaws with the investigation” published in The Wall Street Journal.

The case stemmed from coverage that linked Trump to the late disgraced financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

On July 17, 2025, The Wall Street Journal published an exclusive describing a sexually suggestive birthday note gifted to Epstein for his 50th birthday in 2003, as part of a book of congratulatory letters.

The letters were reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell, who is serving a 20-year prison sentence for her involvement in Epstein’s sex-trafficking scheme.



The note attributed to Trump includes typed text framed by a hand-drawn outline of what appears to be a curvaceous woman. At the bottom, where her pelvic region might be, is Trump’s signature.

Trump vehemently denied responsibility for the text, the signature and the artwork. A copy of the birthday letter was later released through the House Oversight Committee.

The Wall Street Journal’s article came at a time when Trump’s second administration was facing intense scrutiny over whether it had withheld documents about Epstein’s alleged sex crimes, despite promises of transparency.

Critics had also raised questions about the nature of Trump and Epstein’s relationship. The two men appear to have socialised together, and Epstein was known to have surrounded himself with powerful figures from politics, academia and the business world.

In 2025, Trump said he ended his relationship with Epstein after the financier “stole” female employees from his Mar-a-Lago resort.

Epstein was convicted of soliciting a minor for sex in Florida in 2008, for which he served 13 months in jail. In 2019, he faced federal charges related to sex trafficking, but he was found dead in his New York City jail cell before he could be brought to trial. His death was later ruled a suicide.

Legal advocates say Epstein’s victims are estimated to number in the hundreds.

After the release of The Wall Street Journal report, Trump branded the newspaper’s coverage “false, malicious, and defamatory”.

His lawsuit, filed in the federal court in Miami on July 18, 2025, accused the paper and its reporters of having “knowingly and recklessly” published “numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements”.

The result, it alleged, was “overwhelming financial and reputational harm” to the president. Two journalists associated with The Wall Street Journal article were named among the defendants.

In April, Judge Gayles dismissed the defamation lawsuit, ruling that Trump had failed to prove the reporting was borne of “actual malice”.

But that initial ruling gave Trump the opportunity to refile his complaint, which he did in May.

The updated lawsuit claimed The Wall Street Journal had been reckless in not showing how reporters had received and verified the letter.

Saturday’s Miami ruling deals a final blow to Trump’s attempt to sue over the issue. Gayles’s decision dismisses the case “with prejudice”, which effectively blocks any future litigation on the matter.

Trump has other ongoing defamation cases against other media outlets, including the BBC and The New York Times.

World.title: French officials eye social media’s role in promoting unrest.
World.content:
Pinned

Hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets in cities across France again on Saturday, the latest expression of national grievance that has led to clashes between protesters and the police and kept the country on edge.

As dusk fell and official rallies wound down, unauthorized marches splintered off in Paris, stoking fresh fears of chaos as night approached.

Adding to those fears: Halloween, which falls on Saturday. The French authorities, citing calls on social media for people to revolt that encouraged them to wear masks and costumes, warned that the risk of a new outbreak of violence was high.

In Paris, tensions began flaring between protesters and the police in the late afternoon, as officers fired tear gas at people who refused to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration, compared with 110,000 last Saturday. After the main demonstration ended, hundreds of protesters, many masked and clad in black, formed an unauthorized procession in eastern Paris.

The interior ministry estimated that nationwide, 320,000 people demonstrated, compared with 410,000 last week. Protesters and the police also clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes.

Corentin Schnell, a 19-year-old engineering student, took part in the unauthorized march in Paris because, he said, he was angered by accounts of the police using tear gas and stun grenades against protesters in past weeks. “I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on,” he said.

Earlier in the week, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, promised to deploy 70,000 police officers, matching the numbers on Oct. 24. That operation helped keep a lid on outbreaks of arson and looting, although then, too, there were clashes as the police tried to disperse the crowds in the evening.

There was ample fuel for a repeat of those combustible scenes. Students, who are returning to school on Monday after a two-week break, were not mollified by the government’s initial response to their demands. The Education Ministry agreed to cap some class sizes, offer low-interest loans to rebuild school buildings and phase out an unpopular online college admissions platform.

The students vowed to go on protesting. Their two-month-old movement has grown to include university students, public workers and veterans of the “yellow vest” movement that convulsed France from 2018 to 2020.

The authorities have said they are most worried about trouble breaking out after nightfall.

“We are seeing numerous calls to gather coming from the far left, the radicalized extreme left, and from certain radicalized ‘yellow vests’ websites, which are urging people to attend rallies or public gatherings starting at 8 p.m. in many cities across France,” Mr. Nuñez said at a news conference.

Some of the messages were violent, Mr. Nuñez said, calling for “revolution” and “insurrection.” Those gatherings will be forbidden, and any attempt to gather despite the ban will lead to arrests, he said.

Demonstrators have been encouraged on social media to turn up wearing Halloween costumes. Mr. Nuñez warned that it was a criminal offense to conceal one’s face during a demonstration that disrupted public order.

Here’s what else to know.

Social media: French officials are increasingly concerned about social media’s role in attracting people and inciting violent behavior. Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself. Read more ›

Far-right activists: While the government has blamed far-left activists for much of the mayhem, officials confirmed that bands of young men with links to the far right have also infiltrated the demonstrations. They use the pretext of protecting shop owners but often clash with far-left groups.

Widening movement: The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month. Read more ›

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

World.title: 'We came back from hell', say Ukrainians after years in Russia-occupied front-line city
World.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic content.

Olha has one word to describe what life has been like in the front-line city of Oleshky over the past few years: "Horror".

Disembarking alongside her from a coach in the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv with their immediate family and dog, her husband Viacheslav put it this way: "We came back from hell."

The couple were among hundreds of residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city who crossed into northern Ukraine via Belarus on Saturday, many reuniting with loved ones they had not seen for years.

Oleshky, seized by Russia during the first few days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River and on the other side by Russian forces.

Olha and Viacheslav had lived there with their son and daughter, both in their 30s. Even as the shelling around them intensified, they feared that trying to escape could be even more dangerous, with routes mined and subject to drone attack.

As supplies dwindled, the couple said they made an attempt to find food by crossing through minefields earlier this month. "People were stepping on mines, dying and being maimed, all just to survive," Olha told the BBC.

Those who were too afraid to go out in the city had resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive.

"We saw that the situation wasn't getting any better, so we realised we had to get out," Olha said.

World.title: Ukrainian evacuees reunite with family after years trapped in Russia-occupied city
World.content:
There were raw emotional scenes as people evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky crossed from Belarus into the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv.

Families cried as they reunited with relatives they had not seen for years, with two sisters running and crying out as they embraced their father.

Some elderly residents were so weak they were carried on stretchers. They had been trapped in the frontline city without food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked US First Lady Melania Trump for her efforts in brokering a local ceasefire that paved the way for their evacuation on Friday.

Upon their arrival, Dasha and Anya Palii sprinted across the tarmac screaming towards the bus carrying their father Mykhailo.

Their cries and their tears captured the sheer relief of three years of desperate worry, fearing they would never see him again.

Their mother Zhanna clasped Mykhailo's face and stroked his forehead again and again, as if checking he was the same man she had left behind. He promised her, finally, they will now get married.

Tetiana and Volodymyr, an older couple carrying their cat, told the BBC they no longer have a home, after it was burned down in the first year of the war. They have been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour.

They said they instantly took the decision to leave but feared their journey could be disrupted. Now they have to work out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.

World.title: Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across Europe
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of protesters demonstrated across France as the country prepares for a general strike in the coming days.

In Paris, police fired tear gas and clashed with protesters in a third weekend of nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living and poor public services.

More than 320,000 people took to the streets around the country and at least 290 protesters were arrested, according to France's interior ministry. Police say about 70,000 demonstrated in Paris.

The authorities prepared extensively to avoid a repeat of the violence, rioting and looting that happened two weeks ago.

Protests also took place in Albania, Germany and Italy as youth take to the streets across Europe, the BBC's correspondent James Waterhouse reports.

World.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
World.content:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.

The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.

Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.

"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the hack.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.

Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.

All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.

The company said its next goal is resuming withdrawal services for users, saying it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday 1 November and would provide a further update once details were confirmed.

The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.

North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.

World.title: India's opposition set to hold mega rally seeking election chief's resignation
World.content:
Tens of thousands of people are expected to gather in the Indian capital, Delhi, for a mega opposition rally, seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner and electoral reforms.

The rally, called by the main opposition Congress party, will begin around noon at the famous Ramlila Maidan grounds, with leaders claiming a million people could attend.

Several top leaders of the Congress-led INDIA alliance have said they would attend and the influential Gen Z-led pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has also pledged support.

The rally comes amid growing criticism of a voter-list revision exercise that has removed 130 million names from the draft rolls across India.

The Election Commission of India (ECI) says the exercise is aimed at updating the voters' list by purging names of people who have died or moved away from their registered addresses.

But opposition parties allege that the exercise - known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) - could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) by removing eligible voters from the rolls. They accuse the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the BJP of "vote chori (theft)". Both the BJP and the ECI have denied the allegations.

The controversy intensified in September when The Indian Express newspaper in its investigation, external reported that the CEC, Gyanesh Kumar, made key decisions related to the exercise without the agreement of the two other election commissioners, who had raised objections on more than a dozen occasions.

World.title: How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán
World.content:
Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.

Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina.

During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students.

A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used.

"From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - VuÄiÄ supporters - gathering near voting stations," PÃ©ter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything."

Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.

OrbÃ¡n in Hungary, VuÄiÄ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.

Orban chose cheese, VuÄiÄ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.

They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of Serbia's Nis oil refinery. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs.

A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.

World.title: Ethiopian PM puts ministers through military training
World.content:
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country's development.

Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre.

The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training.

Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba.

It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last.

In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable.

He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership.

"Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both.

Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives.

The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia.

It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries.

Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

World.title: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak
World.content:
More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows.

Eight of 26 provinces are now affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases.

The outbreak, which started in May, became the country's deadliest in its history in August, public health officials said. The current case fatality rate is 48.6%.

In its latest update, the health ministry said the epicentre of the epidemic remains in the Ituri province, in the north-east of the country, which is a conflict zone, making it harder to contain the virus.

Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.

This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations (UN), and the second largest in history.

The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak.

Testing and treatment are under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added.

The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is not yet any treatment or vaccine for this strain.

DR Congo's previous deadliest outbreak saw 2,299 deaths recorded between 2018-2020, the UN said.

The deadliest in history occurred in West Africa between 2014 and 2016, killing more than 11,325 people and spread across several countries, including Italy, the UK and United States, according to the WHO.

The UN warns that the current outbreak is "taking lives at a much faster rate".

Ebola is a rare, deadly disease caused by a virus, and symptoms come on suddenly.

As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.

The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

Adding to the challenge of treating the disease, some health workers and a politician have been attacked while responding to the outbreak.

Earlier this week, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack when responding to an Ebola alert. Local youths had accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi.

Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents in the outbreak's first 100 days.

In Uganda, two people died and 20 cases were recorded shortly after the outbreak started, but no cases have been reported since August. Travel restrictions remain in place for those crossing into the country from neighbouring DR Congo.

In Kenya, there have been nine confirmed cases and two recorded deaths.

Two suspected cases were identified in Nigeria on Saturday, its disease control centre said, adding that the individuals have been isolated and they are undergoing testing.

Earlier in October, one woman was confirmed to have the disease in the country but was flown to Switzerland for further treatment.

The likelihood of infection for people in the Europe area is "very low," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said.

World.title: Ebola: No new cases in Nigeria as two suspected cases in North-east test negative
World.content:
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has said two suspected Ebola cases identified in Adamawa State have tested negative for the virus.

The development came hours after the agency announced that two suspected Ebola cases had been identified in Nigeria’s North-east, without disclosing the state where they were found.

In a statement signed by its Director-General, Jide Idris, on Saturday evening, the NCDC said the samples collected from the two individuals tested negative for Ebola virus after two rounds of testing.

The agency said the suspected cases were reported in Yola, Adamawa State, on 30 October after the two individuals presented with symptoms suggestive of Ebola.

“Fortunately, the samples turned out negative for EVD after two rounds of testing,” Mr Idris said.

Mr Idris said there is currently no laboratory-confirmed Ebola case in Adamawa State.

He added that the index case previously confirmed in the Federal Capital Territory remains the only confirmed Ebola case reported in Nigeria to date.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Ebola outbreak

The development comes 11 days after Nigeria confirmed its first case of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus.

Nigeria is one of five countries that have detected Bundibugyo virus disease during the current outbreak, which began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in May.

The outbreak has remained concentrated in the DRC but has spread beyond the country.

Nigeria’s first confirmed case of Ebola in 2026 was a woman who travelled from Uganda to Abuja and tested positive on 20 October. She was subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland for continued treatment.

The NCDC’s latest situation report said 62 contacts linked to Nigeria’s confirmed case had been identified and were being monitored.

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, had said genomic analysis showed that the virus detected in the Nigerian patient was closely related to the strain identified in Kenya’s first imported case. He, however, said the finding did not establish that the Nigerian patient was infected in Kenya.

WHO’s latest update reported 10,274 confirmed cases and 4,992 deaths in the DRC as of 28 October. Kenya has recorded nine confirmed cases and two deaths, while Nigeria has one confirmed case at the time of the update.

World.title: Ebola: Saudi Arabia suspends travel to Kenya, halts visa issuance
World.content:
Saudi Arabia has suspended travel by its citizens to Kenya and halted the issuance of visas to travellers arriving from the East African country as concerns grow over the spread of the Ebola virus across parts of Africa.

The restrictions also prohibit entry into the Kingdom for travellers arriving directly from Kenya or through third countries if they have stayed in Kenya or any other country experiencing an active Ebola outbreak within the 21 days preceding their arrival.

The Saudi Press Agency (SPA) announced the measures in a statement published on its official X account, saying they followed epidemiological assessments by the country’s health authorities.

According to the agency, the measures are intended to mitigate the risks associated with the Ebola outbreak and protect the health of citizens, residents and visitors.

The restrictions build on preventive protocols introduced by the Kingdom in July 2019 and strengthened in May 2026 for travellers arriving from countries considered at risk of Ebola outbreaks.

In June, Saudi Arabia also suspended travel to and arrivals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Uganda and South Sudan, while strengthening surveillance and screening at its entry points for travellers arriving from neighbouring countries.

The Kingdom’s Public Health Authority, known as Weqaya, said the health situation within Saudi Arabia remained reassuring and under constant surveillance.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It added that it was monitoring regional and international epidemiological developments in coordination with relevant health agencies and would implement additional preventive measures as necessary.

Spread across Africa

The restrictions come amid the ongoing Ebola outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which was first declared in the DRC in May 2026.

The outbreak has since spread beyond the DRC, with imported cases reported in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria, as well as France.

According to the United States Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), as of 28 October, the DRC had recorded 10,274 confirmed cases and 4,992 deaths.

Kenya had reported nine confirmed cases, including two deaths, while Uganda recorded 20 cases and two deaths. Nigeria had one confirmed case, with no deaths recorded.

The spread of the virus beyond the DRC has heightened concerns among health authorities about cross-border transmission and the need to strengthen surveillance and early detection.

Ebola in Nigeria

Nigeria’s Ebola response has also entered a new phase following the identification of two suspected cases in the North-east.

On Saturday, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) announced that the two individuals had been isolated, while contact identification and listing were ongoing.

The agency said laboratory tests were being conducted to determine whether they had contracted the virus.

However, it cautioned that being classified as suspected cases does not mean the individuals had tested positive for Ebola, stressing that confirmation would depend on laboratory results.

The NCDC did not disclose the states where the suspected cases were identified.

World.title: Group seeks end to health workers’ absenteeism in PHCs
World.content:
The Health Policy Research Group from the University of Nigeria, Nsukka has appealed to the Enugu State Government to intensify action to address health workers’ absenteeism in Primary Healthcare Centres (PHCs) in Enugu State.

The Coordinator of the group, Obinna Onwujekwe, made the appeal on Thursday during a programme, Stakeholders’ Policy Dialogue on addressing health workers’ absenteeism and strengthening accountability in PHC facilities in Enugu.

Mr Onwujekwe, a professor, also urged the government to strengthen accountability in PHCs across the state.

He said the dialogue provided an opportunity for the representatives of the Enugu State Ministry of Health, Primary Healthcare Agency, National Health Insurance Authority, community leaders and media professionals to brainstorm on addressing health workers’ absenteeism at PHCs.

The coordinator said the dialogue was organised to present research findings and engage policymakers and other stakeholders on practical measures to reduce absenteeism among health workers.

He stressed that the research identified transportation challenges, inadequate workplace support and limited community involvement as some of the issues contributing to absenteeism in PHC facilities.

Mr Onwujekwe explained that the group prioritised three interventions capable of improving health workers’ attendance and service delivery.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He explained that the decision to prioritise the interventions followed extensive consultations with relevant individuals and bodies.

“One of the findings is that providing transportation support to health workers, especially those serving in remote communities, will encourage them to report to work regularly.

“We also discovered that providing support systems within health facilities, where colleagues support one another, can improve attendance.

“Community involvement is equally important because when communities participate in monitoring healthcare services, it helps to strengthen accountability,” he said.

The coordinator said the research demonstrated that combining the three interventions could significantly reduce absenteeism and improve healthcare delivery.

He explained that the policy dialogue was intended to translate research evidence into practical government policies and programmes.

“We have conducted a study and generated evidence. What we are doing today is bringing stakeholders together to discuss how this evidence can be translated into policies and practice.

“We are talking about evidence-based policymaking, where decisions are guided by research findings rather than assumptions.

“Our expectation is that the government and other policymakers will take renewed action to ensure that these interventions are implemented across the state,” he said.

The coordinator expressed optimism that implementing the recommendations would ensure that residents seeking medical attention at PHC facilities would meet health workers on duty.

He acknowledged that although Governor Peter Mbah of Enugu State had invested heavily in building of PHCs, the research and policy dialogue would help ensure that health workers were constantly on duty at the facilities.

“Our research is complementary to the efforts of the state government because we want to ensure that the health centres being constructed are not left without health workers.

“We expect the government to utilise this evidence to strengthen its interventions against absenteeism,” he said.

Clock-in system

Mr Onwujekwe praised the state government’s introduction of a clock-in system to monitor health workers’ attendance at PHCs.

The coordinator argued that the introduction of the clock-in system was a recognition of the challenges posed by absenteeism.

He said addressing the problem requires multiple strategies beyond attendance monitoring.

“The evidence we have produced will further help the governor and the state primary health care development agency to reduce absenteeism in PHCs,” he said.

Pamela Ogbozor, a research associate, presented the research findings, explaining that the intervention ran from August 2025 to January 2026 in four PHC facilities in Nsukka, Igbo-Etiti, Enugu North and Nkanu West Local Government Areas.

Ms Ogbozor stressed that eight other facilities served as control locations, where the researchers did not introduce the interventions.

She said 100 per cent of health workers in intervention facilities regularly completed attendance registers, compared with 90 per cent in control facilities.

The research associate said the study also recorded that 15.4 per cent of workers in intervention facilities left before their shifts ended, compared with 48 per cent in control facilities.

ALSO READ: Delta extends retirement age for clinical health workers

She listed types of absenteeism to include workers failing to report for duty, arriving late or leaving before the end of their shifts.

The researcher warned that absenteeism could expose patients to complications, death and workload with few on duty.

A representative of the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission in the dialogue, Stephen Obi, said absenteeism and ghost workers were serious challenges to healthcare delivery.

“Absenteeism and ghost workers go together and to the commission, it is a serious challenge,” he said.

Mr Obi said the dialogue had provided valuable information which he would be taken back to the commission.

One of the participants in the dialogue, Alex Ugwu, lauded the programme.

Mr Ugwu, who is the chairman of the Ward Development Committee at Hilltop PHC Ngwo, told reporters after the programme that the initiative had broadened their knowledge about ways of tackling absenteeism at PHCs.

“This programme has helped us to know the places to improve on to address absenteeism in the health sector across Enugu State and beyond,” he said.

He hailed the research group, explaining that the outcome of previous research had resulted in government policies that improved healthcare service delivery in his community’s PHC.

World.title: Catholic diocese, CAN reject inclusion of clerics in APC campaign list
World.content:
The Catholic Diocese of Enugu has rejected the inclusion of the Auxiliary Bishop of Enugu Diocese, Ernest Obodo, in the Enugu State All Progressives Congress (APC) Faith-Based Campaign Group.

PREMIUM TIMES reports that the APC in the state had included Mr Obodo and many other Christian clerics in the party’s governorship campaign group.

But in a statement on Friday, the Secretary of the diocese, Wilfred Agubuchi, described the inclusion of the clerics as unauthorised, misleading and unacceptable.

Mr Agubuchi, also a Catholic priest, said Mr Obodo was listed as the director of the Faith-Based campaign council without his knowledge or consent.

The secretary argued that the unauthorised inclusion of the bishop’s name created a false impression of his political disposition and constituted a serious misrepresentation capable of undermining his integrity and “ecclesiastical reputation.”

“We reiterate that the Catholic Church does not engage in partisan politics, participate in political campaigns or endorse political parties.

“The church remains politically neutral and steadfastly committed to her spiritual mission and the promotion of peace, justice and the common good,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Agubuchi stressed that while individuals have the right to engage in partisan politics, the church must not be associated with such activity.

“While individual Christians are free to exercise their civic and democratic rights, no individual or group should exploit the name, office or identity of the church or its ministers for partisan political interests,” he said.

Demand for withdrawal

Mr Agubuchi said the diocese has demanded the withdrawal of the bishop’s name and other clerics from the campaign council.

“We therefore demand the immediate removal of Bishop Ernest Obodo’s name, as well as the names of all other Catholic priests included without their knowledge and consent, from the said campaign list and any related publications,” he stated.

“Furthermore, any continued or subsequent unauthorised use of the Bishop’s name, title, image or ecclesiastical office for partisan political purposes will attract appropriate legal action.”

CAN kicks

Meanwhile, the Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN) Enugu State Chapter has earlier opposed the inclusion of Mr Obodo in the campaign council.

The bishop is the chairman of the Enugu State chapter of CAN.

In a statement on Thursday, the Secretary of CAN in Enugu State, Innocent Offor, also stated that the bishop’s name and those of other members of the association were added to the campaign council without approval.

“CAN Enugu did not authorise, endorse, or consent to the inclusion of its leadership in the campaign council.

“Consequently, the publication must not be construed as an indication of the association’s political affiliation, endorsement of any political party, or participation in partisan political activities,” Mr Offor, also a cleric, said.

The secretary stressed that it was improper for the APC to present Christian leaders as members of a partisan political campaign structure without their prior knowledge, and consent.

“Any attempt to associate them with a particular political party risks creating unnecessary division within the church and undermining the unity and impartiality expected of religious leadership.

“CAN Enugu therefore dissociates itself from the said publication and urges the public, particularly members of the Christian community, to disregard any suggestion that the inclusion of these names represents the endorsement or participation of CAN Enugu or the affected Church leaders in the APC campaign council,” he said.

“We call on the publishers and relevant authorities to acknowledge this clarification and take the necessary steps to correct the impression created by the unauthorised publication.”

World.title: Tinubu hails EFCC after FBI praises role in sextortion arrests
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has commended the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) for its role in the extradition of two Nigerians accused of sexually exploiting and extorting teenage boys in the United States.

The commendation followed a letter from FBI Director Kash Patel to EFCC Chairman Ola Olukoyede, praising the commission’s assistance in an investigation into criminal networks involved in financially motivated sextortion.

The investigation, known as Operation Artemis, led to the extradition of Mudasiru Afeez Olawale and Adebola Festus Adekunle to the US in August.

In his letter, Mr Patel said the cooperation of the Nigerian agency was crucial to the outcome of the cases.

“The successful outcome of these cases would not have been possible without your assistance and dedication to international law enforcement collaboration,” he wrote.

In a statement shared on Saturday by his Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, Mr Tinubu praised the EFCC chairman and his team for their work.

“This is the kind of institutional performance we are determined to build across our country. I commend the EFCC Chairman and his team for their professionalism and dedication,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The president noted that his administration would support law enforcement agencies in pursuing offenders, regardless of where their crimes were committed.

“Nigeria must never become a haven for criminals who exploit innocent people, whether at home or abroad. Our law enforcement and anti-corruption institutions have my full support to pursue offenders and bring them to justice in accordance with the law,” he stated.

How the investigation unfolded

The EFCC said its Lagos Zonal Directorate 2 facilitated the extradition of both suspects on 26 August following separate FBI investigations into sextortion schemes targeting teenage boys.

According to the commission, the schemes targeted male minors, particularly those aged between 13 and 17. The suspects allegedly used intimate photographs to threaten victims and demand money through money transfer services, gift cards and cryptocurrency.

The FBI linked the investigations to two separate cases involving American teenagers who died by suicide after being subjected to online sexual exploitation and extortion.

In one case, a 13-year-old boy allegedly received a message on Instagram from someone who proposed an exchange of nude photographs. The individual later threatened to share the boy’s photographs with his Instagram contacts unless he paid money.

The commission noted that the threats reportedly continued even after the boy indicated that he intended to take his own life.

The FBI subsequently identified individuals allegedly involved in the scheme and requested the EFCC’s assistance in investigating them for possible prosecution under Nigerian law.

Extradition proceedings

The EFCC said the FBI sought Mr Olawale’s extradition to face a seven-count indictment, including charges relating to the sexual exploitation of a minor resulting in death, enticing a minor to engage in sexual activity, threatening communications and distributing child sexual abuse material.

The commission initiated extradition proceedings at the Federal High Court in Lagos in suit number FHC/L/CS/353/2024.

Trial judge Ambrose Lewis-Allagoa rejected the application on 10 June 2024, but the Office of the Attorney-General of the Federation appealed the decision.

But EFCC stated that on 7 July, the Court of Appeal in Lagos set aside the ruling, paving the way for Mr Olawale’s extradition.

The US Department of Justice noted that Mr Olawale, 24, was indicted in August 2023 and extradited on 27 August. He appeared before a federal court in Greensboro, North Carolina, the following day.

The department credited Nigerian authorities, including the Attorney-General of the Federation, the Federal Ministry of Justice and the EFCC, with assisting in the extradition.

It said Operation Artemis involved FBI agents, analysts and forensic experts working with Nigerian and other international law enforcement agencies to tackle sextortion networks operating from Nigeria.

ALSO READ: Nigerian extradited to US for fatal sextortion of minor

The department noted that the schemes had been linked to dozens of deaths by suicide among American teenagers.

Mr Olawale’s charges remain allegations. The US Department of Justice said he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in court.

Nigeria’s financial crime record

Mr Tinubu’s commendation comes after Nigeria was removed from the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) grey list in October 2025 and the European Union’s list of high-risk third countries in January.

The president said the developments reflected his administration’s efforts to strengthen the country’s financial system and restore international confidence.

“Our fight against corruption is not measured by publicity but by results. Stronger institutions, effective law enforcement and international cooperation are essential to building a Nigeria where honest enterprise can thrive, and criminals are held accountable,” he noted.

He urged the EFCC and other law enforcement agencies to sustain their efforts, assuring them of his administration’s continued support in tackling financial crimes and protecting Nigerians.

World.title: Governor Lawal presents staff of office and official vehicles to 19 Zamfara emirs
World.content:
Governor Dauda Lawal has presented staff of office and official vehicles to 19 emirs in Zamfara State. The coronation and presentation ceremony took place at the Trade Fair Complex in Gusau, the state capital.

Among the dignitaries in attendance were His Eminence the Sultan of Sokoto, the Etsu Nupe and the Emir of Gwandu.

Following their oaths of office, Governor Lawal presented staff of office to 11 first class emirs and eight second class emirs.

Governor Lawal (L) chatting with the Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Sa’ad Abubakar during the ceremony in Gusau



Each newly coronated emir also received a GAC ULTRA SUV (2025/2026 model), a MIKANO ZNA HILUX vehicle and an EV ANTIQUE MODEL car (DDP). The vehicles are intended to support their travels and help them engage more closely with their communities.

In his remarks, Governor Lawal said the ceremony reflected his administration’s recognition of the traditional institution as an enduring part of society and an important partner in promoting peace, stability and development.

He noted that the ceremony also reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to giving traditional rulers the recognition and institutional support they need to carry out their responsibilities effectively.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said, “The staff of office being presented today signifies the authority entrusted to you by the State,” he said.

“It also represents a responsibility to govern your respective domains with fairness, wisdom, integrity, and compassion.

“I expect every emir to carry out their responsibilities without discrimination, uphold justice, and ensure that the traditional institution remains accessible to all members of the community.

“Our people must find guidance, fairness, and reassurance in their traditional rulers.

“Recognising the importance of royal palaces as centres of traditional authority and community engagement, I reaffirm our commitment to completing the reconstruction and rehabilitation of the remaining royal palaces.

“This is part of our broader effort to strengthen these institutions and improve the conditions in which traditional rulers carry out their responsibilities.

“We are also providing official vehicles to the 19 emirs. These include GAC ULTRA SUVs (2025/2026 models), MIKANO ZNA HILUX vehicles, and EV ANTIQUE MODEL cars (DDP).

“This provision is intended to facilitate travel across your respective emirates, encourage closer engagement with your communities, and improve coordination with government institutions.

“I expect these vehicles to be properly maintained and used responsibly in support of your official duties.”

The governor also urged the royal fathers to build a productive partnership between their emirates and the State Government.



Earlier, the Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Sa’ad Abubakar, urged the newly coronated emirs to remain fully loyal to the authority. He also encouraged them to respect and uphold the dignity of the traditional institution as they discharge their duties.

World.title: A tale of two emergencies: Why Nigeria does not need new science, By Adewale Adeyemo
World.content:
Nigeria trains excellent doctors and exports many of them. What it lacks is the chain that carries a collapsing person to one of them in time… That chain can be built. Stabilise first and bill later, through a funded federal scheme that reimburses hospitals that comply. Enforce Section 20, so that refusal carries real consequences. Build urgent care centres along the major expressways and in the cities where the crashes and collapses actually happen. Give NEHA the mandate to run them. Set up coordination that knows, in real time, which emergency unit has a bed, a scanner and a team. Staff and stock those units round the clock.

TWO EMERGENCIES. ONE MONTH APART. TWO WORLDS.

On 15 September 2025, in Park City, Utah, a police dog called Bruno went over the edge of a highway overpass. He broke two legs and fractured his jaw. An officer knelt on the road and held him still. A helicopter flew him to a specialist hospital in Salt Lake City. Surgeons operated the next day. Soon after, he limped out past staff who lined the corridor and clapped as he passed.

On 14 October 2025, in Ibadan, the gospel singer, Olayemi Bayonile Bolaji, known to his many fans as Toluwanisings, slumped in the early hours. His media aide, Babadunni Gbolabo said that eight hospitals turned him away. His family confirmed his death that same morning.

Eight doors. Eight refusals. Somewhere between them, the time he had left ran out.

A dog met a system. A man met a corridor of closed doors.

TOLUWANISINGS WAS NOT THE FIRST THIS YEAR. HE WILL NOT BE THE LAST.

On 29 December 2025, Anthony Joshua, the two-time world heavyweight champion, was in a crash on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway at Makun, Ogun State. His close friends, Sina Ghami and Kevin “Latif” Ayodele, died at the scene. Joshua survived with minor injuries. The world watched images of a global sportsman being pulled from the wreckage by bystanders. Not paramedics. Not a trained first-response crew. Bystanders.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

There was no air ambulance. No roadside stabilisation unit. No equipped centre within reach of that stretch of road at that hour. President Bola Tinubu called Joshua personally. The world’s attention came and went. The infrastructure gap stays.

Nigeria recorded 5,421 road traffic deaths in 2024 alone. The Joshua crash was not an outlier. It was a famous version of what happens quietly, somewhere on a Nigerian road, every single day.

ONE COUNTRY. THREE FUNERALS. THE SAME MISSING CHAIN.

Over 11,000 kilometres separate Salt Lake City from Ibadan. The real distance is measured in minutes, in money, and in who answers when you knock.

This is not a quarrel with Bruno. He deserved every hand that reached for him. What moves me is what was already in place before he fell. A trained responder. An evacuation plan. A hospital ready to receive him. An institution ready to pay the bill.

Toluwanisings had a car, people who loved him, and hope.

Sina Ghami and Latif Ayodele had a famous friend, a working mobile phone, and the attention of a Nigerian president. None of that bought them a stabilising clinician on the hard shoulder of the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway.

We like to believe that illness alone decides who lives. Often, the system does. In emergency medicine, the clock is part of the disease. In a major stroke, the brain loses an estimated 1.9 million neurons for every minute without treatment. In major trauma, the first hour decides outcomes. The same injury can be survivable in one city and fatal in another. Human physiology does not change at the border. The road to care does.

AND YET THE SKILL IS AT HOME. I HAVE WATCHED IT SAVE SOMEONE CLOSE TO ME.

On 16 July 2025, I sat thousands of miles away, gripping my phone. A relative had arrived at University College Hospital, Ibadan, at 11 a.m. Moribund. A blocked artery was starving the brain.

The messages came one at a time.

“…in the CT room now.”

“The neurologist is there. It is 6 hrs post ictus.”

My heart sank. Every clinician knows what that number means. The standard window for clot-dissolving treatment closes at four-and-a-half hours. After that, the risk of bleeding into the brain rises sharply and the tissue that can still be saved shrinks.

The neurologist did not take the easy refusal. He read the scan carefully. He weighed what could still be saved against what could be lost. He spoke with us. Then he went ahead.

The country already has pieces of the puzzle… What is missing sits in the middle. A dedicated tier of Urgent and Emergency Care Centres, physically positioned on the expressways and in the major cities where people actually collapse. Walk-in. Specialist-led. Twenty-four hours. Rapid diagnostics on site. Air stabilisation capability. The facility that the NEMSAS ambulance drives the patient to. The place the bystanders on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway could have reached in time.

Then one word.

“Thrombolysed.”

It was 1:53 p.m. Two hours and fifty-three minutes after arrival. About seven-and-a-half hours after the first symptoms.

Today, my relative walks, runs, talks and drives, with no deficit you would notice.

That was textbook hyperacute stroke care. Delivered in Ibadan. By Nigerian hands.

So the skill was never the problem. Access was.

Our access came through people. Medical school classmates and a senior mentor who are like family picked up the phone, made the calls and stayed with us until it was done. I will carry that debt for the rest of my life.

But I must be honest about what that means. It means privilege. Our network carried us past the cash deposits, the delays and the gridlock that kill ordinary Nigerians at the gate. And behind the right team on duty, a working scanner and the drug in stock, I believe, sat the grace of God.

Grace should not have to stand in for a system. No Nigerian should need the right phone numbers to survive.

THE LAW IS ALREADY ON THE PATIENT’S SIDE.

Section 20 of the National Health Act 2014 states that a health care provider, health worker or health establishment shall not refuse a person emergency medical treatment for any reason. The penalty is a fine of ₦100,000, up to six months in prison, or both.

On paper, the right exists. At a locked gate before dawn, it does not.

The reasons are known. Hospitals that treat first are often never paid. Emergency units run short of staff, beds and blood. No one tracks which hospital has space. Families are left to drive from gate to gate, guessing, while the clock runs. On expressways, there is no one to call at all.

WHAT NIGERIA ACTUALLY NEEDS. SPECIFICALLY.

The country already has pieces of the puzzle. The National Emergency Medical Service and Ambulance System (NEMSAS), launched in 2022 and now operational across 33 states and the FCT, dispatches ambulances and funds the first 48 hours of care through the Basic Health Care Provision Fund. The Federal Road Safety Corps patrols the expressways. The National Emergency Management Agency responds to disasters. The National Primary Health Care Development Agency runs primary care at the ward level.

What is missing sits in the middle. A dedicated tier of Urgent and Emergency Care Centres, physically positioned on the expressways and in the major cities where people actually collapse. Walk-in. Specialist-led. Twenty-four hours. Rapid diagnostics on site. Air stabilisation capability. The facility that the NEMSAS ambulance drives the patient to. The place the bystanders on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway could have reached in time.

Every advanced nation has this tier. The United Kingdom has 999 and Walk-in Urgent Treatment Centres. The United States and Canada has 911 as their national emergency number and Level 1 trauma centres. Rwanda has SAMU, co-funded by the WHO and the World Bank, with ambulances and air units covering the whole country. Nigeria has the ambulance but not the destination.

This gap needs an owner. The clean answer is a National Emergency Healthcare Authority (NEHA), a dedicated federal agency that establishes, regulates and operates urgent care infrastructure nationally. It would absorb NEMSAS as its dispatch arm, coordinate with the FRSC on expressway positioning, work alongside NEMA on mass casualties, and sit under the Federal Ministry of Health with independent funding. One agency. One mandate. One accountable name when a Nigerian dies at a gate.

The alternative is what we have now. Six overlapping bodies, no single owner, and a Toluwanisings every month that we do not read about because he was not a gospel singer.

A rotation model that offers diaspora consultants eight to twelve weeks a year in a well-run urgent care centre, with proper accommodation, family-friendly scheduling, and professional indemnity, would attract hundreds. Not because they are paid more. But because they are finally offered a way to serve home that fits their stage of life. The older cohort will anchor the specialist teaching. The younger ones, still mid-career abroad, would add shorter rotations when they come to see loved ones.

AND WHO WILL STAFF THEM. THE DIASPORA ANSWER.

A federal agency is only as good as the clinicians who stand inside its buildings at 3 a.m. This is where Nigeria has a quiet advantage it has never used properly.

Nigerian-trained physicians fill senior consultant posts across the NHS, the Mayo Clinic, Johns Hopkins, Toronto General, Mount Sinai. Thousands of them. Many are now in their late 50s and 60s. In the Western systems where they practise, the pattern at that age is well known. Full clinical rotas are swapped for teaching, mentorship, governance, and part-time consulting. Children are grown. Mortgages are paid. Personal needs are smaller. What rises is the desire to give back something that lasts.

Most of them already return home for two or three weeks each year. Family visits, funerals, weddings. Almost none of that time is converted into structured clinical work at home. If the state built the right platform, that calculus can change.

A rotation model that offers diaspora consultants eight to twelve weeks a year in a well-run urgent care centre, with proper accommodation, family-friendly scheduling, and professional indemnity, would attract hundreds. Not because they are paid more. But because they are finally offered a way to serve home that fits their stage of life. The older cohort will anchor the specialist teaching. The younger ones, still mid-career abroad, would add shorter rotations when they come to see loved ones. A working holiday with purpose rather than guilt.

This is how the brain drain begins to reverse. Not by begging physicians to come back permanently, which few will, but by letting them come back regularly, meaningfully, in formats that respect the lives they have built. Over a generation, the clinical teaching, the governance culture, and the standard of care seeded by returning diaspora consultants build the lasting institutions Nigeria needs.

Until those institutions stand on their own, the diaspora is the bridge.

None of this works without those who stayed. The Nigerian consultants, registrars, nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, laboratory scientists, radiographers and allied health professionals who have carried the system through every power cut, every strike, every unpaid month, are the backbone of any future. The diaspora is the bridge. The home workforce is the ground the bridge stands on.

A model that threatens their livelihoods will fail, and deserves to. A model that strengthens them will succeed. The pay structures, the training opportunities, the promotion pathways, and the clinical leadership roles must be designed to lift Nigerian clinicians first. Diaspora rotations should supplement, teach, mentor and share, never displace. Every returning consultant should see herself as a visitor in the house of colleagues who kept the lights on, not as the owner of a new wing. The welcome goes both ways. Those at home must open the door. Those abroad must know they are coming into someone’s workplace, not building their own.

Get this balance right and both sides win. Get it wrong and the diaspora becomes just one more imposition on a workforce that has already carried too much.

PRIVILEGE IS QUIET. THOSE WHO HAVE IT RARELY SEE IT.

It looks like an ambulance that comes when you call. A hospital that stabilises first and asks for money later. A law that is enforced. A trained paramedic on a stretch of expressway where strangers currently kneel over the dying.

Talent is spread evenly across the world. Safety nets are not.

Nigeria trains excellent doctors and exports many of them. What it lacks is the chain that carries a collapsing person to one of them in time.

That chain can be built. Stabilise first and bill later, through a funded federal scheme that reimburses hospitals that comply. Enforce Section 20, so that refusal carries real consequences. Build urgent care centres along the major expressways and in the cities where the crashes and collapses actually happen. Give NEHA the mandate to run them. Set up coordination that knows, in real time, which emergency unit has a bed, a scanner and a team. Staff and stock those units round the clock.

None of this needs new science. It needs will, money and follow-through.

Until then, survival in Nigeria will remain a lottery of luck, location and who you know.

No one should die at a hospital gate. No one should die on the hard shoulder of a Nigerian expressway, while bystanders do what paramedics should.

Rest in peace Toluwanisings.

You sang of hope. May we build a country that keeps it.

Adewale Adeyemo, a London-trained consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist with a special interest in clinical risk management and patient safety, writes from Canada.

World.title: CIBN urges banks to increase lending to MSMEs, honours 755 professionals
World.content:
The President Chartered Institute of Bankers of Nigeria (CIBN), Dele Alabi, has urged Nigerian banks to increase lending to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), in order to generate higher returns for banks after the industry recapitalisation.
