Meanwhile, the Alaska Democratic Party has sued state elections officials, alleging absentee in-person voting sites did not open as advertised in some rural communities. The director of the Division of Elections in a letter dated Monday said the agency signs agreements with local or tribal offices to operate the sites and that most of the 18 highlighted had opened. A message seeking comment from the state Department of Law was not immediately returned.

World.title: Perspective: Forget the ballroom, we're headed to Cheesecake Factory!
World.content:
Perspective: Forget the ballroom, we're headed to Cheesecake Factory!

toggle caption i Timothy Hiatt/Getty Images North America

Food fight!

This week, the Cheesecake Factory restaurant chain unexpectedly found itself in the political discourse.

During a campaign event in Ohio, former President Obama criticized President Trump's affection for gold decor, saying, "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory."

Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent retaliated by having a French Dip Cheeseburger for lunch at a Cheesecake Factory near the White House, telling reporters, "I had a great meal, always have a great meal. I would tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try."

But this latest partisan debate made me wonder. Why spend $600 million or more to build a new White House ballroom to host state dinners? Why not just host those esteemed events instead at the Cheesecake Factory?

Sponsor Message

Come to a state dinner, I've been told, and you kind of have to gulp down whatever yellow squash velouté or fricassée of fava beans a server slides under your chin.

But isn't America all about freedom, choice and options galore?

Cheesecake Factory restaurants have more than 250 items on their menus. Now that's America! Chicken and Waffle Skewers! Tex-Mex Eggrolls! Pickle Fries!

What says America more? The Dover Sole Meunière, served with Potato Pavé, Spring Ramps, Snow Peas, and Parsley Oil served to King Charles III at a state dinner this spring? Or the Cheesecake Factory's Buffalo Blasts: chicken, cheese and hot sauce stuffed into a spicy wrapper, deep-fried, and served with celery sticks and blue cheese dressing?

"I'm absolutely stuffed," I imagine His Majesty saying. "British troops in 1814 would never have burned down a Cheesecake Factory!"

When French President Emmanuel Macron received a state dinner at the White House in 2018, it opened with a Goat Cheese Gateau. I'd bet that wherever French officials travel, hosts push a Goat Cheese Gateau in front of them, saying, "You'll love it! So French!"

So I can imagine a French president saying, "Forget the gateau! I want Asian Chicken Nachos! Wonton chips, peanut sauce and fromage fondu? Le yum!"

Sponsor Message

Move state dinners to a Cheesecake Factory, and foreign heads of state might even say, "Give me that plate of Fried Macaroni and Cheese balls, and I'll sign any tariff agreement you want!"

World.title: Drone photo award winners: Far-out landscapes. Ship recycling. Rugs, rugs rugs!
World.content:
Drone photo award winners: Far-out landscapes. Ship recycling. Rugs, rugs rugs!

toggle caption i George Steinmetz

It looks like a spacecraft that settled gently onto a golden beach.

Off the coast of Bangladesh, an enormous vessel lies stranded on the mudflats, its steel hull partially dismantled as workers mill around it. This unusual aerial view of a tanker, specially designed to transport liquified natural gas used for cooking, electricity and transport, won photographer George Steinmetz the top prize — overall winner of the 2026 Siena Drone Photo Awards.

Each year, the Siena Drone Photo Awards highlight bird's-eye views of our planet, revealing landscapes, livelihoods and human stories often invisible from the ground. Here, we've selected some of this year's winning and highly commended photographs, focusing on the countries of the Global South.

Sponsor Message

In an interview with NPR, Steinmetz says he's been long fascinated by Bangladesh's shipbreaking industry, where enormous vessels from around the globe, nearing the end of their working lives, are dismantled and their materials recovered for reuse. The photograph is titled "Shipbreaking on the mudflats, Bay of Bengal." Steinmetz sent up his drone north of Chattogram (Chittagong), along this 13-mile coastal strip, offering a stark glimpse into what this industry is like.

He was exploring the relationship between human populations and the environment for a book project and saw the industry as an extraordinary example of recycling on a vast scale.

Photographing it proved surprisingly difficult. The ship breaking industry has faced criticism from environmental organizations, human rights groups, labor unions and non-governmental organizations for its unchecked pollution, the leeching of chemicals into the sea and dangerous working conditions . Shipyard owners are wary of journalists and photographers. Local photographers initially warned Steinmetz that securing access might be nearly impossible.

Undeterred, he surveyed and photographed the entire coastline north of Chattogram with his drone, searching for a vessel that would make an especially striking photograph. He eventually settled on the liquid natural gas tanker. "The trick for me was to find the right ship, that was in a really interesting state of disassembly. And these tankers are very unusual boats. It just looked weird, like some kind of a spaceship. It takes workers a long time to break it down. And then they have to wait for the tide to be right so they can pull the pieces ashore. They have big winches and boats that they use to get the stuff ashore."

Sponsor Message

He was able to convince the owner of the tanker to allow him to photograph it. The timing of the drone photo was crucial. Steinmetz wanted to capture the vessel at low tide, when the surrounding mudflats were exposed and workers could be seen moving around its enormous hull. Their tiny figures would look like ants, giving viewers a sense of the ship's mammoth scale. He spent several days photographing the vessel, returning as the tides shifted and the workers continued to take the ship apart for scrap metal.

After graduating from Stanford with a degree in geophysics in 1979, Steinmetz had first dreamed of photographing landscapes from above while hitchhiking across Africa, often traveling on the roofs of trucks.

In 1996, National Geographic agreed to finance an aerial photography project around the Sahara, for which Steinmetz learned to fly a motorized paraglider. "It was like being in a flying lawn chair or [sitting on] the front of a spoon," he says. Drones have now completely transformed aerial photography, allowing photographers to capture the world from perspectives that were once difficult, expensive or impossible to achieve, Steinmetz says.

Today, armed with a drone rather than a paraglider, he continues to explore how a view from the sky can reveal stories that remain invisible from the ground.

Southern Turkey: Carpet Fields

toggle caption i F. Dilek Yurdakul

Why would anyone spread hundreds of beautiful carpets across open fields, leaving them exposed to a blazing Mediterranean sun for weeks or even months?

In southern Türkiye, this is part of a traditional process that gives handmade rugs their immensely sought-after, softly faded colors. Under the intense sunlight, the vibrant reds, blues and other hues gradually mellow into glowing, muted tones.

For Ankara-based documentary photographer and lawyer Dilek Yurdakul, the drone was not simply a technical choice. It was an essential storytelling tool. "I wanted to create an image that first attracts the viewer through its beauty but then invites them to look deeper, to discover the people, traditions and cultural memory behind it," she says. The photograph won first place in the contest's People section.

Sponsor Message

Yurdakul traveled six hours in blistering heat from Ankara to the Döşemealtı district of Antalya to capture this spectacle. "The first sight was astonishing. The fields were far larger than I had imagined. Thousands of carpets and kilims in different colors, sizes and patterns stretched across an enormous landscape," she says. From above, the carpets resemble a giant patchwork quilt, almost as if melded together, but her photograph captures the shadows between these slices of color.

The aerial perspective allowed her to bring together several layers of the story in a single frame, she says: the artistic richness of Anatolian craftsmanship, the scale of the landscape and the human labor that connects them.

"For me, this was a visual metaphor for the invisibility of labor. In many societies, the people whose work sustains everyday life remain largely unseen and unrecognized."

East Java, Indonesia: Tumpak Sewu's Majestic Waterfall

toggle caption i Colas Decloitre

In this photo, highly commended in the Nature category, an imposing horseshoe-shaped waterfall spills over the cliffs of East Java, Indonesia, at sunrise. Boston-based, French-British drone photographer Colas Decloitre had hoped to capture the interesting shape of the waterfall with Mount Semeru rising behind it. What he hadn't anticipated was catching the active volcano behind the waterfall, glowing red and writhed with ash, in the middle of an eruption.

"The only way to get the right alignment of the waterfall and the volcano is with a drone, as you can only be on the side of the waterfall yourself," he says. Using his drone, he could position the waterfall against the volcano, revealing an intriguing landscape that could only be viewed from the air.

Argentine Puna: The Last Ember

toggle caption i Isabella Tabacchi

It looks like the glowing eye of a fiery monster.

It's actually a volcanic cone, the pile of rock, ash and hardened lava that builds up around the mouth of the volcano over time.

Sponsor Message

The Last Ember, by Italy-based photographer Isabella Tabacchi , is an example of how a drone photo has the power to transform landscapes into a dream-like quality. It was a commended entry in the Nature category.

The photo was taken in the Argentine Puna, a vast, remote, high-altitude plateau in the Andes of northwestern Argentina: a landscape of volcanoes, ancient lava fields, salt flats and desert mountains. The cone's reddish color comes from iron-bearing minerals in the volcanic rock, while the surrounding dark terrain consists of lava that cooled and hardened long ago.

Exploring these volcanic landscapes requires careful planning, long journeys across remote terrain and constant attention to the conditions. "At high elevations, the thin air and rapidly changing weather can also make drone operations more demanding," Tabacchi says.

Her winning photo was a case of serendipity.

"I captured it during an exploratory flight, while studying the volcanic landscape and experimenting with different compositions," she says. "It wasn't even photographed during the golden hour [shortly after sunrise or before sunset] which is usually the time I prefer for landscape photography."

"When I reviewed my photographs, I found myself much more attracted to this earlier composition. There was something about the geometry of the lava field, the small red cone and the immense volcanic wilderness surrounding it that felt far more powerful to me than the warmer, more traditionally dramatic light of the other photograph."

It reminded Tabacchi of an important lesson she learned throughout her photographic career: Extraordinary landscapes don't always need extraordinary light to create a compelling image.

"Sometimes the strength of a photograph comes from the subject itself, its shapes, its geological history and the unexpected perspective from which we discover it," she says.

Lake Natron: What Lies Beneath

toggle caption i Holly Kirkland

Another commended entry in the Nature category is Holly Kirkland's "What Lies Beneath."' At first glance, it looks like someone splashed ink over a canvas. But what seem like tiny specks of ink are actually lesser flamingos flying over Lake Natron, near the Tanzania–Kenya border. A former kindergarten teacher from Delaware, Kirkland is a self-taught photographer and plans to relocate to Kenya in the year ahead to build a larger body of aerial work.

Sponsor Message

This photo wasn't taken with a drone. (Siena does accept other aerial photography entries in the drone category). Kirkland took the shot on a Sony A1 Mark II with a 70-200mm f/2.8 lens while hovering over the landscape in a helicopter, strapped into her seat with the door flung open.

The photograph reflects the ecosystem of the Rift Valley soda lakes — highly alkaline environments where these birds thrive as the dominant species. They are called soda lakes because they contain exceptionally high concentrations of dissolved sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate, the same chemical compounds found in household baking soda and washing soda.

These caustic waters would burn the skin of most other animals, but flamingos have evolved specific adaptations to turn this harsh landscape into a sanctuary. For instance, they have extra leathery, scaly skin on their legs to withstand chemical burns and specialized salt glands in their nasal cavity to filter out the excessive salt. It's an important breeding ground for these birds, Kirkland says, with an unusual landscape, like an entirely different world, with "painterly looking plumes of sediment under the surface of the lake."

"I've never seen anything like it," she says.

"I think that when you're looking down, there's just so many different layers of beauty that you see from above that you could never see from the ground," she says.

Kazakhstan: Alien Land

toggle caption i Isabella Tabacchi

Another highly commended photo in the Nature category by Italy-based photographer Isabella Tabacchi , the Alien Land depicts the layers and patterns of deposited sediments, tectonic movements and erosion over millions of years — natural geological formations in Mangystau, Kazakhstan.

"My fascination with Kazakhstan began in a rather unexpected way," says Tabacchi. "I was flying from Tokyo to Rome when our plane encountered considerable turbulence while crossing Kazakhstan. I remember becoming curious about the vast country beneath us. In my imagination, it seemed like a land of remote, mysterious places, still waiting to be explored."

Sponsor Message

In 2024, she traveled there for the first time. The formation featured in Alien Land, which she nicknamed Jellyfish (their branching patterns reminded her of a jellyfish swimming through water), was the result of extensive research rather than a chance encounter.

"I spent countless hours studying satellite imagery, searching for unusual geological shapes and patterns in the Mangystau desert," she says. "Together with my guide and best friend Sav, I then explored the region in a Toyota Land Cruiser 4x4, trying to locate these formations on the ground. It was an extraordinary experience, turning shapes I'd discovered on a screen into real landscapes that I could finally photograph."

Mangystau is one of the strangest, wildest, and most mysterious places Tabacchi has ever visited. "There's something about its immense, almost empty landscapes that makes me feel completely isolated from the rest of the world, as though I'm standing at the edge of infinity," she says. "It's a feeling I find difficult to experience anywhere else: a mixture of solitude, freedom and wonder."

Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh: Rohingya Life Between Aid and Uncertainty

toggle caption i Shahedul Islam Sadik

More than 1 million Rohingya refugees currently live in Bangladesh, primarily concentrated in congested camps around Cox's Bazar. Shahedul Islam Sadik , a student at the Faculty of Fine Arts, University of Rajshahi in Bangladesh, says he has always wanted to tell their stories.

His drone shot of the settlements was commended in the Urban category . "I wanted to document how a humanitarian crisis had reshaped not only the lives of displaced people, but also [show] the natural and geographical landscape of their place of refuge. The photograph is therefore about more than population density; it also captures the visible consequences of a prolonged crisis," he says.

Sadik was struck by how densely populated and congested the settlements are. "What stayed with me most, however, was the sense that receiving assistance does not necessarily mean having the life one wants," he says. "Life in the settlements can feel confined, without the freedom they once had in their homeland."

Sponsor Message

He wanted viewers to notice not only the lack of physical space but also what it represents in the refugees' lives. "For me, the drone photograph captures more than overcrowding; it reflects a lack of personal space, freedom and room to breathe, both literally and figuratively," he says.

Bangladesh: Ferry boats, Dhaka

toggle caption i George Steinmetz

A burst of color and celebration fills the waterways of Dhaka, Bangladesh, as thousands of people make their way home for Eid, one of the most important festivals in the Islamic calendar.

Every year, the holiday triggers a massive exodus from the capital, as migrant workers and other residents travel to their hometowns to reunite with family. Ferries, packed with passengers and their belongings, become a vital means of transport.

For photographer George Steinmetz, the scene offered a striking contrast to his photograph of Bangladesh's shipbreaking industry. This photo was commended in the Urban category. From above, the crowded boats, their brightly colored decks and passengers' festive clothing create a vibrant patchwork against the river.

"I've never seen a ferry terminal like that," he says. Dhaka's Sadarghat Launch Terminal is widely recognized as one of the largest and busiest river ports in the world , frequented by 50,000 people every day.

"It's such a joyous scene," he says. "They have shopping bags full of gifts of food to bring to their families. When it's packed with people, I knew would be really epic. And again, it's like they look like ants."

Steinmetz captured the scene using a drone launched from the rooftop of a building overlooking the waterfront. But he almost missed the opportunity. The skies were overcast, and rain began falling shortly after his drone made the photograph. Had the rain started any earlier, he might have been unable to fly his drone.

For Steinmetz, drones offer the freedom to explore a scene from different angles, searching for the perfect composition rather than settling for the first striking view.

Sponsor Message

"I don't just want to get a picture. I want to get the best possible picture," he says.

Kamala Thiagarajan is a freelance journalist based in Madurai, South India. She reports on global health, science and development and has been published in The New York Times , The British Medical Journal , the BBC, The Guardian and other outlets. You can find her on X: @Kamal_t.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: Canada is in the U.S. midterm spotlight. Will the results be a blessing or a curse?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In most U.S. elections, Canada never comes up. But not this time.

From ads in Michigan and New Hampshire , to stump speeches and debates in New York and Iowa — plus interviews in Nevada and Alaska — the word "Canada" is coming up repeatedly as affordability takes centre stage.

Democrats are seizing on Trump's Canadian tariffs to prosecute a larger argument about his care for Americans' cost of living, while Republicans are either defending the tariffs for the sake of protecting the U.S. economy — or distancing themselves.

In recent days, Trump himself has been especially fixated on Canadian affairs. He and other U.S. officials teased a potential trade deal earlier this week, though sources told CBC News that despite intensified talks, it does not mean an imminent agreement.

But what does it mean for Canada to be in the U.S. midterm spotlight, and will the results on Tuesday be a blessing or a curse for Canadians? CBC's The House spoke to experts and former officials about Canada's significance — and the risk that Trump could blame Canada if he loses.

LISTEN | Experts and former U.S. officials discuss Canada's significance in midterm elections: The House 21:09 Will the U.S. midterm results be a blessing or curse for Canada? American voters head to the polls on Tuesday for pivotal midterm elections — and Canadian tariffs have become a key issue in battleground states. But is the spotlight good for Canada? Guest host J.P. Tasker speaks to experts and former U.S. officials about how big a role Canada is playing in these races, and the risk of Canada incurring Trump's wrath if he loses.

How much does Canada matter?

Polls show Trump's dispute with Canada is deeply unpopular among American voters in both major parties.

And for U.S. states close to the Canadian border or which do a lot of trade, Canada has "become a bread-and-butter kitchen table issue," said Scotty Greenwood, a Canada-U.S. relations specialist and founder of Ottawa Street Strategy.

"The tariffs, particularly on Canada, but tariff policy in general, makes the cost of living way higher for Americans. And so that's how it's come to pass that Canada is a ballot question in a bunch of U.S. races," Greenwood said.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: How will the US midterm elections affect you? Leave your comment here and our team may get in touch or read your comment on air.

The challenge for Republicans, and opportunity for Democrats, is that many races in those states — like Michigan, Maine, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Nevada — will decide whether the Democrats retake the House of Representatives and Senate.

Republican candidates in those states are certainly cognizant of Canada. In Maine, for example, incumbent Republican senator Susan Collins said during a debate earlier this month that she has been "the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs with Canada."

Over the last two months, Trump has shifted around his Canadian tariffs to give Maine residents relief, and Collins has claimed credit. Trump lifted tariffs on Canadian cement and road salt in September, then scrapped duties on another array of products in October.

Troy Jackson, right, is challenging Maine Sen. Susan Collins for her seat, and has attacked Collins for her response to Trump's trade war with Canada. (Gregory A. Rec/The Associated Press)

But Collins's Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, has seized on the issue and dismissed her approach, arguing Maine residents "can't eat road salt." Polls suggest Jackson is in the lead by a few points.

Emily Cain, a former Maine state senator and Democrat, says she doesn't think anyone expected Canada to feature so prominently in the Senate race. And while Collins has persevered before, Cain added that she is now facing her biggest challenge.

"Donald Trump should be bracing for a bad night on Tuesday night," Cain said.

Another example is Michigan, where Republican senate candidate Mike Rogers is squaring off against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. Rogers has worked to distance himself from Trump's tariffs, noting, like Collins, that Canada is not an enemy.

Dennis Lennox, a Republican political strategist in Michigan, told The House that Canada is "not coming up every day" in discussions, but is a key figure in the larger debate about Trump's trade agenda.

Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers, left, listens to a supporter during a campaign event Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, in Muskegon, Michigan. (Paul Sancya/The Associated Press)

Lennox also said he thinks there are many Americans who are still willing to give Trump leeway on his tariffs to see if they will achieve their stated purpose of bringing manufacturing jobs back to the United States.

"If you don't start seeing more concrete results from the Trump trade policy, you're going to see the pushback amongst Americans grow and it's gonna be louder," Lennox said.

Could Trump punish Canada if he loses?

In the leadup to Tuesday, Trump and his representatives have regularly attacked Canada. Last week, the U.S. president said during a campaign rally that he'd let Canada keep ice hockey and its national anthem if it joined the United States.

Also last week, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released what it described as examples of Canadian officials trying to influence the midterm elections. The list included statements from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and others.

When asked about the possibility of retaliation if Trump loses the midterms, John Bolton, a former adviser, told The House that nothing can be ruled out.

Former Trump adviser John Bolton, right, speaks beside moderator Prof. Jeff Frankel during an appearance at Harvard University on Sept. 29, 2025, in Cambridge, Mass. (Michael Dwyer/The Associated Press)

"In Trump's world, there are only two kinds of people. There are winners and losers. Trump is a winner; therefore, he will not lose on Tuesday. Other people will be responsible. It will be their fault because it's never his fault," Bolton said.

Greenwood said that the Trump administration will be looking for a "pre-buttle" if the Republicans lose the midterms, but she isn't sure if that blame will fall on Canada.

"I don't think that will pass the smell test, to be honest," Greenwood said.

As for the prospect of a trade deal, Greenwood said even if Democrats retake the two chambers of Congress, Trump still has "an awful lot of time left and executive authority left, particularly with respect to foreign policy and trade policy."

"So it's not like everything is going to change for Canada/U.S., the day after election day or the day after the new Congress is sworn in in January. It's going to be a long, tough road."

Will the attacks stick after Trump?

Lennox said he worries about the long-term consequences of Trump's attacks, and there could be a risk that "Canada is going to become a partisan issue…. Obviously the Democrats will be in support of Canada, and the Republicans will be against it."

Most Americans, "according to the polls, disagree with the president's stance vis a vis Canada, but there's still a large segment of Republican-based voters who are going to side with President Trump on whatever he says."

According to polling from YouGov that was released last month, 38 per cent of Republican respondents said they consider Canada to be an "unfriendly" or an "enemy" of the United States — in contrast to just eight per cent of Democratic respondents.

WATCH | A key issue in the midterms: Canada-U.S. trade war emerges as key issue ahead of U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:18 The Canada-U.S. trade war is solidifying itself as a major ballot-box issue in pivotal states ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

A separate poll from Pew Research also last month found American views of Canada have cooled slightly, mostly among older Republicans.

Still, Bolton said it would be a "big mistake" to overstate Trump's long-term consequences, as many of his policies do not have majority support among Americans, nor within the Republican Party.

“I think people who say, 'Well, he acts this way all the time, this represents a permanent change in the American attitude toward Canada' are just over-reading the consequences of Trump," Bolton said.

"He is an aberration. There's never been a person like him in the American presidency, hopefully never will be again."

World.title: More Canadian provinces are ditching the time change. But did they pick the wrong option?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Millions of Canadians will turn their clocks back one hour this weekend, while millions of others will not. This divide is putting Canadians under different time systems — with potentially different consequences for their health.

Most of British Columbia, as well as Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories are no longer changing their clocks twice a year, joining Yukon and Saskatchewan. Most of Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces will still turn their clocks back on Nov. 1 for the end of daylight saving time.

For Quebec, this could be the last time. Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon announced Wednesday that his government is moving to end the twice-yearly clock change, but it has not yet decided which time the province will keep. He said that decision will be made after consulting experts.

Research suggests permanent standard time — the time we return to in the fall — is more closely aligned with the body's internal clock than permanent daylight time, which several provinces have chosen.

Here's what winter time would look like across Canada under proposed time-zone changes

Joseph De Koninck, an emeritus professor of psychology at the University of Ottawa, has studied sleep for decades. He said the springtime change is the most problematic because people lose an hour of sleep when they set their clocks forward, creating a mismatch between the body's internal biological clock and solar time.

De Koninck explained that our biological clock uses light to synchronize itself. As daylight changes with the seasons, our circadian rhythms adjust gradually. Making a one-hour adjustment all at once, however, is much more difficult.

"We are able to adapt, but it's not optimal for our health."

The Edmonton skyline at dawn. As one of Canada's northernmost major cities, Edmonton will see winter sunrises as late as 10 a.m. under Alberta's new permanent daylight time. (John Robertson/CBC)

Why morning light matters

Michael Antle, head of the University of Calgary's psychology department and a professor who studies circadian rhythms, said permanent standard time would have been better for Alberta.

Because of the province's northern latitude and position within its time zone, it already has late winter sunrises, Antle said. Permanent daylight time will push them forward another hour.

"It's not the choice I would have made," he said of the province's decision.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: What questions do you have about getting a good night's sleep? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show

Antle said daylight time essentially means society has agreed to get up and go to work or school an hour earlier.

Most people's circadian clocks run slightly slow, making them somewhat "night owlish," he said. Morning light helps speed up that clock.

Michael Antle, a University of Calgary psychology professor, says permanent standard time is healthier because it better aligns with people's body clocks. (Submitted by Michael Antle)

When morning light arrives later, there can be a mismatch between what the body wants to do and what work or school requires.

Antle described this effect as "social jetlag."

Antle pointed to population studies that found people exposed to later sunsets slept less and had higher rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease. He also cited Russian research that found winter depression among young people increased while Russia observed permanent daylight time.

WATCH | B.C. scientists warn permanent daylight time could do more harm than good: Why some scientists don't support B.C.'s switch to permanent daylight time | Duration closed caption 2:17

Why researchers say permanent daylight time is a bad idea

Both researchers distinguish between the disruption caused by changing the clocks and the effects of living on daylight time year-round.

Antle said the spring change creates a sudden shift that can leave people feeling as though they're living on the wrong time for several weeks. Permanent daylight time would extend that mismatch through the darkest months of the year.

He would prefer permanent standard time. Continuing to spring forward and fall back would be a compromise, he said, preserving later summer evenings without the longer-term winter mismatch.

Night owls who work regular daytime jobs may struggle the most because they already find it difficult to wake up early, Antle said.

Those darker mornings are also having a real-world impact. Ski hills in Alberta's Bow Valley, for example, are delaying their opening times this winter to give staff more daylight to prepare the slopes before skiers arrive.

But most schools and workplaces have less flexibility to change their hours based on when the sun is up.

WATCH | Why Atlantic Canada should consider permanent standard time: Changing clocks twice a year a question of public health: prof | Duration closed caption 6:43 Rébecca Robillard, an associate professor at the University of Ottawa and co-chair of the Canadian Sleep Research Consortium, explains why Atlantic provinces should consider ditching the time change.

Canada becomes a natural experiment

Canada's emerging patchwork could give researchers an opportunity to study neighbouring populations living under different time systems.

Antle said he would have preferred a year's notice to collect baseline data before Alberta made the change.

He said researchers should examine mental health, vehicle and pedestrian collisions, school performance and attendance, and workplace attendance and tardiness.

De Koninck noted that researchers now have tools to document sleep habits over time and compare how people adapt in different provinces.

But he expects Western Canadians may make their feelings known before researchers have years of data to analyze. People may not fully understand what permanent daylight time means, he said, until they've experienced a winter with much later sunrises.

"Those who've tried it haven't liked it," he said.

For De Koninck, the larger concern is what prolonged sleep disruption can mean for people's health.

"If you feel sleep deprived, then you have a host of issues, psychological and physical," he said.

"You can't play with your sleep."

World.title: Alberta woman accused of sex with 15-year-old guilty of sexual assault
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Sundre, Alta. woman accused of having sex with a 15-year-old boy at a New Year's Eve party has been convicted of sexual assault and sexual interference.

Alexa Suitor, 35, did not outwardly react when the jury foreperson read the verdict Saturday afternoon after 24 hours of deliberating.

The jury began deliberations Friday afternoon after hearing closing arguments prepared by prosecutors James Molloy and Laura Somers and defence lawyer Patrick Fagan.

Justice Douglas Mah will hear sentencing arguments at a later date.

Fagan indicated to the court he will be asking for a discharge for his client, which would mean she would not serve any time in jail.

Over the week-long trial, the jury heard that on Dec. 31, 2023, a number of teens and adults attended a New Year's Eve party at a home in the Sundre area.

The teens and Suitor spent most of the night drinking in a cabin on the property while the other adults hung out in the main house.

'We took it too far'

At the end of the night, Suitor and several of the teens worked out sleeping arrangements. Some were to spend the night on cots in the living room; others would be in the bedrooms.

The victim — who CBC News is calling C.D. to comply with a publication ban — testified that he fell asleep on a cot and woke up to Suitor touching his penis. He said this led to sexual intercourse on the cot.

C.B. said the next day, he received a Snapchat message from Suitor saying “we took it too far last night.”

Two friends of C.B.’s also testified.

Suitor denied sexual touching

One friend said that she saw the pair having sex when she went into the kitchen to get a glass of water.

The other friend said that he saw the next-day Snapchat message from Suitor.

Suitor testified in her own defence, telling jurors that the sex and sexual touching never happened.

World.title: NASA telescope predicted to plunge back to Earth after failed rescue mission
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An aging NASA telescope is barely clinging to space after a failed rescue effort left it tottering lower and lower.

The U.S. Space Force predicts the Swift Observatory will come crashing down on or around Friday.

Most of the 1.5-ton telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere. But a handful of pieces made of denser-than-lead tungsten and some mirror parts could survive re-entry, according to NASA's Brad Cenko, the mission's chief scientist.

Any surviving wreckage will most likely plunge into the ocean. But swaths of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America are within the re-entry zone. The Space Force is tracking the telescope's dwindling path.

Its cosmic cremation has the Swift team mourning yet full of gratitude for the observations the telescope made during its 22 years in orbit. Swift blasted off on Nov. 20, 2004, to search for some of the biggest explosions in the universe: gamma ray bursts and supernovas.

Workers look at the final pieces of protective cover on the Swift spacecraft that must be removed at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in September 2002. (NASA/The Associated Press)

"We've known this day would come since before Swift was launched. At least in low-Earth orbit, what goes up must come down. And that end is catastrophic," said Pennsylvania State University's John Nousek, an astronomer who led the control team.

Intense solar activity over the past few years dragged Swift down faster than usual. NASA hired Katalyst Space a year ago to mount a rush rescue. But the company's three-armed robot named Link ran into trouble after launching in July and got no closer than 12 to 15 kilometres to the telescope. Link plunged back to Earth in September.

Swift resumed observations once the rescue attempt was called off, discovering even more gamma ray bursts and other ultra high-energy events. But by late October, the telescope was too low to remain steady for observations, and its systems were shut down.

Its final tally: more than 2,000 gamma ray bursts and 1,400 exploding stars, not to mention a slew of comets, asteroids and star-shredding black holes. The telescope's superpower was its ability to swivel swiftly — thus its name — toward erupting celestial events.

NASA considered Swift a first responder for the Hubble and Webb space telescopes and others that would follow its alerts and provide deeper investigations. Scientists are still figuring out how to fill the gap.

"Our fervent hope is that the lessons learned by the successes of Swift can be applied to new generations of space missions to accelerate our discoveries about the universe," Nousek said in an email.

World.title: Judge throws out Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saying the president was "grasping at straws," a U.S. federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump's $10-billion lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to wealthy financier Jeffrey Epstein.

U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law.

The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the Journal's investigative reporting.

When a case is thrown out "with prejudice," it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.

The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term.

In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September.

Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them "fake news" and insults their journalists.

Trump called reporting 'malicious'

The lawsuit was over a story the Journal published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter that the paper said bore Trump's name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday.

The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump.

The letter bearing Trump's name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, "Happy Birthday - and may every day be another wonderful secret," according to the newspaper.

Trump denied writing it and called the story "false, malicious, and defamatory."

WATCH | Trump's lawsuit over Epstein birthday letter: Trump sues over Wall Street Journal report linking him to Epstein | Duration closed caption 2:36 U.S. President Donald Trump is suing over a Wall Street Journal article linking him to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Trump is also ordering his Department of Justice to produce ‘pertinent’ grand jury testimony in the Epstein case.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having "knowingly and recklessly" published "numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements," which, it alleged, caused "overwhelming financial and reputational harm" to the president.

Suit previously dismissed, then refiled

Gayles previously dismissed the suit in April, saying Trump had failed to make the argument that the article was published with the intent to be malicious. But he gave the president a chance to file an amended complaint, which he did in May.

In Saturday's ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court's landmark 1964 ruling in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. That decision made it harder for public figures to win libel lawsuits because it requires proof that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth.

"The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice," Gayles wrote.

"Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false."

The judge also noted that the Journal's story did not ignore or minimize Trump's denial, "Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it."

Gayles also said several other allegations in the lawsuit did not have merit.

World.title: Suspect identified in Toronto home invasion where residents were shot, attacked with hammer
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Toronto police named Daijohn Richards, 23, of Toronto as a suspect wanted in connection with a home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood in which a businessman's family members were shot and attacked with a hammer. Daijohn walked into a Toronto hospital with a gunshot wound on Thursday, after it's believed he was accidentally shot by an accomplice during the home invasion. He was discharged from the hospital on Friday and is now missing.

Toronto police have named a suspect in a home invasion in the Bridle Path neighbourhood in which a businessman's family members were shot and attacked with a hammer.

Daijohn Richards, 23, of Toronto has been identified as a suspect wanted in connection with the investigation, Insp. Kristy Smith said at a Saturday news conference.

Richards walked into a Toronto hospital with a gunshot wound on Thursday, after it's believed he was accidently shot by an accomplice during the home invasion, she said.

"Richards was shot in the right shoulder and as such he may be experiencing pain or discomfort in that area and people may look to see him favouring that side of his body," she said.

Smith said investigators are also looking for two other suspects in the case, but don't have any other details other than they were wearing dark clothes and might be in their 20s. Anyone with details about the perpetrators are urged to contact police, she said.

"All three suspects are considered armed and dangerous and we are asking members of the public to not approach them," she said.

Toronto police identified Daijohn Richards, 23, as a suspect in a home invasion investigation after a residence in the Bridle Path neighbourhood was broken into and a family was attacked on Oct. 29, 2026. (Toronto Police Service)

Speaking directly to Richards, Smith said police are actively looking for him and that his "world just got smaller."

"I strongly urge you to contact a lawyer and turn yourself in," she said, adding police would not share any details on potential prior arrests or charges for Richards, to avoid jeopardizing any court processes.

Police are typically called to the hospital when someone appears with a gunshot wound, however they are not able to arrest anyone without reasonable grounds linking them to a crime, Smith said.

She said police did interact with Richards on Thursday, but that they did not have information at the time to arrest him before he was released from the hospital Friday afternoon.

"We need to make sure we ironclad a conviction and don't just go off of suspicion," she said.

There's no evidence to suggest the incident was targeted and the motive is believed to be profiting from crime in an affluent area "where there are things that are sought after," Smith said.

Family traumatized, recovering from attack: father

On Thursday morning, Toronto police responded to reports of a violent home invasion at a residence near Hyde Park Circle and Post Road.

WATCH | Toronto police identify suspect in Bridle Path home invasion: Toronto police identify suspect in Bridle Path home invasion | Duration closed caption 2:10 Toronto police have identified one of three suspects wanted in connection with a home invasion near Hyde Park Circle and Post Road in the Bridle Path neighbourhood. Police say four family members were injured in the incident. CBC's Dana Roberts has the details.

They said three suspects, armed with handguns and a hammer, forced their way into the home, made demands for valuables and attacked four adults in the home — a 75-year-old father, 64-year-old mother and their 26- and 28-year-old daughters.

"The family asleep in their homes were awakened by three masked suspects entering their bedrooms," Smith said, adding some have been released from hospital and some remain.

"What I can say is that through the grace of god, [the family members in hospital right now] are in life-altering condition, and not life-threatening condition," she said.

David Morton, CEO of real estate services company MAC Group, said three members of his family are recovering in hospital after they were shot during the home invasion. All four members of the family were also attacked with a hammer, he said in an emailed statement issued Friday.

"No family should ever have to experience this," he said, adding the family is traumatized and recovering after the attack on Thursday.

Smith said the Canada's criminal code gives people the right to protect their home in a dangerous situation, but that police do not recommend using force yourself if possible.

David Morton, CEO of MAC Group, a real estate group, said his family is 'traumatized' after they suffered a violent and 'horrific' home invasion in their Bridle Path home Thursday. (macsuites.ca)

"You are responsible for that use of force," she said, adding people should call police instead where possible.

"You are justified by law, but that's a case-by-case situation."

World.title: Youth-led protests sweep across France, Europe for a 3rd weekend
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.

About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.

France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout.

Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween.

Police clash with protesters in Marseille, France, on Saturday. About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country. (Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty Images)

Authorities in France reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Saturday night.

Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred marches the previous two Saturdays.

Diverse grievances

At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labour unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.

The marchers' grievances are diverse.

Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.

WATCH | France is broke. Can the protests change anything?: France is broke. Can student protests change anything? | Duration closed caption 5:10 For weeks, high school students in France have forced a chaotic confrontation about the government’s priorities, but as CBC’s Chris Brown explains, their demands for more funding come as the country faces a precarious debt crisis.

A few Halloween costumes stood out in the crowd, including a zombie Michael Jackson from Thriller, a pirate and a Spider-Man. Protesters waited calmly, chanting and singing through megaphones.

Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats."

He said that he hoped Saturday's protest would be festive in honour of Halloween, to counter the image of violence that has attached itself to France's protests.

Police impose curfew, other measures

The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labour unions and others angry at French President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.

While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.

A protester ignites a firework in Paris on Saturday. France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday. (Pedro Nunes/Reuters)

Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centres to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la République and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. local time on Saturday and Sunday.

Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.

Germany, Italy and Spain

In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly translated as "Gen Z's got this" or "Gen Z takes charge" — rallied in many cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that more than 180,000 people had signed up online, but as of Saturday afternoon only several thousand marched in various cities across the country.

Young protesters also gathered at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.

PHOTOS | Costume-clad protesters demonstrate in Europe:

"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.

Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.

"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

Some shops on the Kurfüerstendamm boulevard had boarded up their windows on Friday, although authorities said they were unaware of specific threats of violence. An additional 1,500 police officers were deployed to the German capital to quell possible riots.

A person walks near storefront with boarded up windows on Berlin's Kurfüerstendamm boulevard on Saturday. (Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters)

In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Saturday afternoon after online appeals for protests, and fears of rioting and looting. However, there was little sign of protests and no major disturbances by midafternoon. Police frisked some groups of black-clad youngsters, and checked their identities, local media reported.

Many stores in the city were also boarded up as a precaution.

In Barcelona regional police planned to activate their highest-level alert after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings. Rioting there on Oct. 24 led to about 130 arrests, mostly of minors.

Italian police were on alert after clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna, and calls to protest circulated on TikTok in Belgium, the Netherlands, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal.

World.title: 'No one is safe' as Ebola outbreak surges to more than 10,000 cases, Africa's top doctor warns Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the world's fastest-growing outbreak of Ebola hit more than 10,000 confirmed cases this week, Africa's top doctor warned there could be "massive" spread into additional countries — and even other continents — unless countries such as Canada offer more support.

"No one is safe today," said Dr. Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), in an interview with CBC News from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on Friday.

"We are calling on all African countries to increase the level of preparedness. But we're also calling our Western countries, especially Canada, because Canada is where my heart is."

Kaseya is from Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, and has led Africa CDC for the past three years. But he has called Canada home since 2013. He told CBC News he has been living apart from his family — his three children attend university in Toronto, and his wife remains in Laval, Que. — as he works to end an unprecedented crisis that began in his home country.

He singled out Canada as an ally to African health officials, though he said more can still be done.

"This is my message to Canadians: No fear, no panic, but take it seriously, and even talk to your parliamentarians, talk to other people you know, if they can provide more support for this outbreak," he told CBC News.

"I really want to be back home to celebrate with my family, but we need to stop this outbreak before doing that."

Death toll surpasses 5,000

Kaseya's comments follow a grim new milestone in this year's Ebola outbreak. Confirmed cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo have surpassed 10,000, while the latest report from the country's public health institute shows the death toll has surpassed 5,000.

The outbreak was first declared in mid-May, but scientists suspect the Bundibugyo strain of the virus had been spreading undetected for months in some of Congo's most remote regions.

Ongoing conflict, public distrust and the lack of an approved treatment or vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain have further complicated efforts to contain the outbreak.

It is now the country's largest-ever outbreak and the fastest-growing and second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded — behind only the West Africa Ebola crisis, which infected more than 28,000 people, mainly across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, from 2014 to 2016.

"If this outbreak [continues] like that, with the same magnitude, in one year we'll have more than what West Africa had in two years and a half," Kaseya said.

"But it won't be just a few countries. It will be more countries. It can also affect some other continents."

A much smaller number of infections have already appeared in neighbouring countries, including Uganda, Kenya, and most recently in Nigeria, which reported its first Ebola infection in a decade.

That patient, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat, was flown to Switzerland for treatment on Monday , the latest in a series of patients evacuated to European countries since the outbreak began.

Kaseya said imported infections could continue as teams on the ground struggle to slow community transmission in new areas of Congo.

The risk to Canada remains low, he added, though he implored Canadian officials to "move from low to zero by supporting [Africa] to stop the outbreak where it is currently."

WATCH | Ebola outbreak now deadliest in Congo's history: Ebola outbreak now deadliest in Congo’s history | Duration closed caption 2:05 The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo is officially the deadliest in the country’s history, and health officials worry the crisis will only get worse when children return to school.

Canada offered $8M to Ebola fight

Canada committed $8 million to the Ebola response in May, including $2 million for Africa CDC to accelerate surveillance and strengthen biosecurity measures. In late July, Health Canada also authorized Moderna to launch a clinical trial of its vaccine targeting the Bundibugyo virus.

The federal government also introduced temporary border measures aimed at reducing the risk of Ebola entering and spreading in Canada, including outbreak alerts issued for Kenya and Nigeria in October.

"The Government of Canada will continue to monitor the situation closely and may adjust these measures, as appropriate, based on evolving evidence and the epidemiological situation both in Canada and internationally," the Public Health Agency of Canada told CBC News in a statement this week.

Alongside those official efforts, Canadian research teams are also working behind the scenes to study this once-rare form of Ebola.

University of Winnipeg microbiologist Jason Kindrachuk said Canadian and Congolese scientists have sequenced more than 1,000 genomes to date, offering insights into how the virus is behaving and whether existing vaccines may offer cross-protection for the Bundibugyo strain.

But he stressed there are "finite resources" for that collaborative, cross-border work.

WATCH | Congolese students separated from loved ones due to travel restrictions: Congolese students in Montreal separated from loved ones due to Canada travel restrictions | Duration closed caption 1:45 In May, Canada implemented temporary measures restricting entry into the country for foreign nationals arriving from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda or South Sudan due to Ebola risks. As a result, many Congolese students in Montreal face a difficult dilemma: they want to visit their families, but fear the restrictions will prevent them from re-entering Canada for their studies.

Canadian scientists 'scramble' for research funding

"We're trying to scramble with funds from whatever sources we have to be able to keep things like genome sequencing alive, to keep testing alive … so I think at some point we need to see bigger investment, and certainly sustained investment, from the high-income areas of the world," Kindrachuk said.

"I think there's a real need for Canada and other countries to step up."

Kaseya praised Canada's efforts to date, including the close collaboration between African and Canadian health officials, but agreed that the threat of Ebola could persist for months without broader support to end the crisis.

"We'll continue to work hard to keep Canada safe — we'll do our best to keep all other countries in the world safe — but … if we do not provide support, we cannot guarantee that all of us will be safe," he said.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella
