World.title: Spain observes third day of mourning as unions demand urgent action following deadly train collision
World.content:
Spain is observing a third day of national mourning on Saturday following a deadly train collision in Urda, Toledo, that claimed the lives of at least 69 people earlier this week.

 

Residents and local officials gathered on Saturday in a Spanish village near the site of the collision for a memorial Mass honouring the victims.

The pews inside the San Juan Bautista church were packed, while dozens more people gathered outside to listen to the service, some wiping away tears.

Meanwhile, distraught relatives of the victims endured growing anguish on Friday as authorities worked to identify bodies. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said Spain was working "tirelessly" to complete the identification process.

Castilla-La Mancha's leader Emiliano Garcia-Page warned they "do not rule out more dead," saying the emergency services had collected "31 bags of partial remains" that complicated the identification work.

The legal authorities in charge of the process have said 67 reports for missing people remain active, including 14 for foreign nationals.

They concern citizens from the United States, Canada, Australia, France, Japan, Mexico, Argentina, Venezuela, Tunisia and the Czech Republic.

A Portuguese citizen who worked on one of the trains is among the dead, Portugal's government said on Friday. Another 39 injured people remained in hospital in Castilla-La Mancha, per authorities.

Wednesday's crash was the country's second such disaster this year and one of Europe's deadliest rail accidents this century.

LZB system failure under investigation

Train drivers are demanding urgent measures to strengthen rail safety in Spain.

The Spanish Union of Train Drivers and Railway Assistants (Semaf) has requested a review of regulations governing how trains should operate when their automatic protection systems fail.

In a statement, Semaf has urged the State Railway Safety Agency (AESF) to act "urgently" to "clarify and amend the regulations governing the rail protection system, LZB," as well as the procedures related to the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS).

According to preliminary information from the Independent Authority for the Technical Investigation of Accidents and Incidents (AITAT), the LZB system stopped functioning at 8:31 am on Wednesday, prior to the collision. However, it has not yet been determined whether the LZB failure was the direct cause of the accident.

Semaf aims to prevent trains from resuming normal operations if there is a risk that two trains could end up on the same section of track.

The Minister of Transport Óscar Puente, who ruled out resigning on Friday, announced new measures aimed at reducing technical risks and "restoring public confidence" in the railway system, though he has not yet specified what those measures will be.

The concerns raised by the train drivers are not new. In January 2026, Semaf reported that hundreds of train drivers had long been reporting incidents on the railway network, without receiving any response or seeing any corrective measures taken.

Following an accident in Adamuz (Córdoba), Semaf reached an agreement with the government to strengthen railway safety; however, the union has since reported further delays in implementing the agreed-upon measures.

Sánchez acknowledges 'shattered confidence'

The Urda train accident has put further pressure on Sánchez ahead of elections in November.

Sánchez said on Friday that trust in the high-speed network was "shattered" but pledged "solutions" to prevent further accidents.

The incident happened on a key line linking Madrid to the southern city of Seville, which was also the scene of a collision in January that killed 46 people in the region of Andalusia.

Train driver union Semaf has called two fresh strikes at state operator Renfe for November 10 and 12, demanding "structural measures" for rail safety, after maintaining a stoppage on Thursday that had been organised before the accident.

The head of the main conservative opposition Popular Party, which leads most polls, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, accused the government of "not replacing an obsolete security system when it should have done so".

"Who's going to get on a train now? Now you're scared when you do," Cecilio, a relative of a victim, told the AFP news agency.

"Lots of lives have been lost in nine months. I think this should make everyone reflect - the whole of society, the politicians - about why this is happening in the 21st century," he added.

"I am not blaming one side or the other, but something is going wrong here."

World.title: 'A lot of lies': Kaja Kallas criticises Russian FM Lavrov following G20 meetings
World.content:
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accused Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov of telling "a lot of lies" on topics such as the Ukraine war during talks with G20 ministers in Atlanta on Friday.

 

"We were talking about the big geopolitical crisis, including Ukraine, and we were able to address Sergey Lavrov head on with this," she told the AFP news agency.

"Of course, he put forward a lot of lies, a lot of false narratives" that Europeans challenged, Kallas added.

European officials also reportedly used the opportunity to put further pressure on Moscow as they sought to secure a ceasefire in the Black Sea - prompting pushback from Lavrov, a diplomatic source told AFP.

British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband said he had also told Lavrov in the plenary that "he should have the courage to tell Putin that Russia will not win this war."

The UK minister is also said to have confronted Lavrov over a recent attack on a Dnipro railway that killed 15 people as he stressed Moscow was the "aggressor" in the conflict, which began in February 2022 when Russian forces launched their full-scale invasion.

In a press conference on Friday, Lavrov "welcomed" the US' willingness to engage in dialogue with Moscow while hitting out at what he called Europe's "arrogant boycott."

"This is a good lesson for our European colleagues," he said of Washington's approach.

Several officials at the meetings also reportedly refused to stand for a "family photo" with Lavrov, leading US organisers to cancel the picture.

The G20 meetings come just days before the US' key midterm elections, which will determine the balance of power in Congress for President Donald Trump's final two years in office.

US approves Patriots package for Ukraine

On Friday, the US State Department announced that Washington had green-lit a package of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion for Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has continued to plead with US and European allies for more interceptors for its forces as Ukraine continues to weather Russian missile and drone attacks.

And while he welcomed the new package and thanked the US for its "strong decision," he warned that delivery could take years.

"Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.

"However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he added. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Lavrov on the sidelines of the G20 in Atlanta.

World.title: 'Northern women and esotericism': Life after death explored at Finnish National Gallery
World.content:
The Latin words arcana and borealis mean "hidden knowledge" and "the north", two elements at the heart of the Finnish National Gallery's latest exhibition.

 

"Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism" is the first large-scale museum show to examine how female artists from across the Nordic region and Sápmi have engaged with esotericism, spirituality and alternative systems of knowledge from the 19th century to the present day.

The exhibition brings together more than 200 works by 50 artists and features both well-known and overlooked artists, including Hilma af Klint, Tyra Kleen and Tove Jansson.

Tyra Kleen, Forbidden Fruit, 1909, gouache on paper, Riddarhuset, Tyra Kleen Collection. Photo: © Bobo Lindblad, Lindblad Studio

Previously the connection between modern art and esotericism, occultism and magic has been explored mainly through famous male artists, according to Dr Marja Lahelma, Chief Curator at Ateneum Art Museum and co-curator of the exhibition.

"For quite a long time art history has been dominated by narratives focusing on male artists and on this notion of the individual genius. Our focus is on women and we also draw attention to this idea of communality and working together," Dr Lahelma explained to Euronews Culture.

Tove Jansson, Mysterious Landscape (c.1930–1939). Finnish National Gallery. Collection / Ateneum Art Museum. Photo: Finnish National Gallery / Hannu Pakarinen

Art, spirituality and handicraft

"Arcana Borealis shows how the boundaries between art and spirituality, fine art and craft, object and process, individual authorship and collective making begin to blur when viewed through the lens of artist women and esotericism" added Dr Nina Kokkinen from University of Turku, co-curator of "Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism" .

Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism. Installation view, Ateneum Art Museum, 2026. Photo: Finnish National Gallery / Aleks Talve

The range of materials featured in the exhibition is exceptionally wide, including textiles, ceramics, metal engravings, and traditional media from sacral art, such as stained glass and mosaics.

Handicraft involves matrilineal transmission of tradition, that is, passing down knowledge and skills from one woman to the next. Sámi duodji, the traditional Sámi craft tradition, brings together spirituality, the tacit knowledge passed on from one generation to another, and values related to nature.

Hilma af Klint, The Dove no 1, Group IX, Series UW, 1915, oil on canvas, By Courtesy of The Hilma af Klint Foundation. Photo: Moderna Museet

Some of the artists gathered on the exhibition were saying that they were guided by some kind of non human agency whether it was angels or guiding spirits, or in some cases a source of nature.

Halloween or Kekri

"This is a perfect exhibition to visit for Halloween, or Kekri as we say in Finnish. Esotericism is about light and darkness. We can explore themes such as death in art through this esoteric theme and sometimes the hidden knowledge, the secret knowledge that esotericism is all about, can be found through exploring darkness rather than light," explained Dr Marja Lahelm.

Anna Cassel, Untitled II, No. 33, 1915, oil and metallic paint on canvas, Private collection. Photo: By Courtesy of The Hilma af Klint Foundation / Anders Fredriksén

Arcana Borealis – Northern Women and Esotericism at Ateneum Art Museum, Finnish National Gallery is on open until 28 February 2027.

World.title: Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean
World.content:
The ratification of a maritime agreement between Libya and Turkey is stoking tensions across the eastern Mediterranean. Athens has condemned the deal as illegal, amid wider regional concern over Turkey’s growing influence.

Advertising

On Thursday, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis criticised the deal, which Libya’s eastern-based parliament ratified on 20 October, calling it “blatantly illegal, null and void”. The agreement sets out an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) between Libya and Turkey that encompasses the Greek island of Crete.

Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli signed the agreement in 2019, but the rival administration in eastern Libya had refused to ratify it until October.

“I don’t think it’s possible to overestimate its political and symbolic importance. The whole world knows that Turkey has been pursuing this parliamentary ratification,” said Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui of the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank.

“People thought that eastern Libya was a reliable friend of the enemies of Turkey, and that the process was going to drag on for several years,” he added.

According to Harchaoui, the ratification is a bold step in Ankara’s broader strategy to assert its influence across the region, known as the Blue Homeland doctrine.

Turkey courts Libya's rival factions in bid to further Mediterranean ambitions

“We should never forget that the exclusive economic zone is a corollary of the Blue Homeland doctrine,” he said. “And the Blue Homeland doctrine is really about nationalism, commitment to projecting Turkish influence across all of Africa, across the sea.”

Divided country

Libya has been divided since Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a Nato-backed uprising in 2011. The Government of National Unity rules the west from Tripoli, while the Government of National Stability holds sway in the east from Benghazi.

Ankara has long backed the Tripoli-based government, but it has recently set out to win over the Benghazi administration, hoping to bridge Libya’s deep divide. Benghazi’s approval of the maritime deal is seen as a direct result of these diplomatic efforts.

“It’s one of the most critical diplomatic achievements recently in the Mediterranean,” said Elem Eyrice Tepeciklioglu, professor of African studies at the Social Sciences University of Ankara. “This agreement is also a reflection of Turkey’s efforts to engage with both parts of the country.”

Tepeciklioglu expects the EEZ to bring economic rewards. “The region covered by the deal has significant energy resources. So it’s important for energy exploration as well,” she said.

Regional resistance

Ankara now faces strong opposition in the region. Greece, Cyprus and Egypt have all condemned the agreement, arguing that it encroaches on their territorial waters, while the European Union and the United States have also voiced concerns.

With vast energy reserves believed to lie beneath the disputed waters, Federico Donelli, professor of international relations at the University of Trieste in Italy, warns that tensions could rise.

Turkey and Egypt turn page on decade of friction with show of friendship

“The more immediate risk is an increase in diplomatic tension and especially competing activities in disputed maritime areas,” he said. “So exploration licences, seismic surveys, naval deployment and even some naval drills could be used to reinforce competing claims, and the possibility of incidents could increase.”

Donelli suggests that Italy, which has close ties to both Turkey and Libya, could play a key role in easing tensions with its fellow EU members Greece and Cyprus. Meanwhile, Ankara is reaching out to Cairo and has invited Egypt to join the maritime pact.

Libya expert Aya Burweila of the Athens-based Center for Hellenic and Mediterranean Studies says the ratification caught Greece off guard.

“For Athens, symbolically, it’s a huge blow. I don’t think they expected it,” she said. “If you see the map, you know, it basically cuts across Crete’s maritime waters.”

Despite Greece’s tough rhetoric, Burweila believes diplomacy can prevail. “It’s [the agreement] more symbolic than anything else, because I don’t see how it can be enforced,” she said. “So I think this is an opening for negotiations with Egypt and Greece and other countries. And I think these talks are already happening between Libya and Egypt.”

France hosts global push to promote stability in Libya, keep elections on track

Israeli concern

The agreement also risks inflaming tensions between Israel and Turkey, which have already been sharpened by Ankara’s support for Hamas and the war in Gaza. Israel is increasingly worried about Turkey’s regional ambitions. In September, Israeli Navy commander Vice Admiral Eyal Harel warned of Turkey’s growing assertiveness in the Eastern Mediterranean.

Harchaoui believes Israel’s concerns are likely to grow. “Turkey was able to pull off an extraordinary win. If you look at just the area of influence, it has almost won eastern Libya. Turkey is going to just sell more weapons; it’s going to build more airstrips, so it’s literally expanding… So they [Israel] have to decide: are they going to remain in the rhetorical space or do something about it?”

World.title: US judge narrows Macrons' defamation lawsuit against American podcaster
World.content:
A judge in the United States has ruled that French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte ​could continue their defamation lawsuit against the companies of the American podcaster Candace Owens, but not against Owens herself.

Advertising Read more

Editor’s note: This story was updated at 13:25 on 30 October 2026 to include a statement from lawyers for Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron, sent to us by counsel for Macron's legal team. It responds to the court’s ruling on Candace Owens’ motion to dismiss the case against her.

In the statement, lawyers for the Macrons said: “We are pleased that the Court rejected Mrs. Owens’ attempt to remove the case from Delaware, where her companies continue to publish and monetize her defamatory falsehoods. As for Mrs. Owens personally, we are keeping all options open to ensure that, in addition to the liability she still faces through her companies, she is held accountable personally.”

***

The Macrons had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 against Owens and two companies, accusing her of helping fan online rumours about whether Brigitte is a transgender woman.

Owens, 37, an influencer with a large following on social media platforms, has claimed that Brigitte was a man.

Delaware Superior Court Judge Sheldon Rennie said in a ruling on Tuesday that Owens could not be held personally liable in the case.

But Rennie allowed the suit against two companies associated with her – Candace Owens LLC and GeorgeTom Inc – to continue.

Question of jurisdiction

Rennie said the Delaware court did not hold jurisdiction over Owens because her residence was in another state, Tennessee.

The ruling means that if the French first couple were to eventually win the case, Owens' personal assets would be shielded.

In their lawsuit, the Macrons said Owens ⁠touted ​false claims and conspiracy theories ​against them "to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money".

Rennie deferred judgment on Owens' motion to dismiss ‌the ⁠Macrons' litigation until he was briefed on how French defamation law and statutes of limitation intersect with US law.

"I am in the absolute best mood over this Macron dismissal," Owens said on X on Wednesday.

'Centuries of patriarchal history': why trans rumours are wielded against women

Damages to Brigitte Macron

Brigitte Macron, 73, has taken to the courts in France to combat claims she was born a man.

Two French YouTubers, Natacha Rey and Amandine Roy, were convicted in September 2024 of spreading false claims after they posted a video in December 2021 alleging that Brigitte Macron had once been a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her brother.

Rey and Roy were ordered to pay €8,000 in damages to Brigitte Macron and €5,000 to Jean-Michel Trogneux.

The defendants were also given a suspended fine of €500.

Did French media silence enable Brigitte Macron fake news story to go viral?

Brigitte Macron had filed a libel complaint against the two women after their claim went viral, triggering conspiracy theories notably among the far right.

Roy, an online fortune-teller, interviewed Rey, a self-described independent journalist, for four hours on her YouTube channel in December 2021.

The women discussed the unsubstantiated rumour that Brigitte Macron had undergone gender reassignment, with Rey claiming to have uncovered a “state lie” and “scam”.

The claim went viral just weeks before France's 2022 presidential election, spreading even to the US where Owen derided the first lady in a now deleted YouTube video.

World.title: Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience
World.content:
After the Student List's election victory, Aleksandar Vucic's power apparatus is disintegrating. People want justice as soon as possible. But the losers still hold sway in the judiciary and administration.

Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.

Vucic complained at a press conference, before fewer microphones than usual, that the winners were practising "revolutionary terror." He threatened: "If they continue to terrorize those who think differently – beatings, destruction and all the rest – and the state authorities do nothing, we will be forced to organize ourselves."

Vucic regards the immediate resignation of the general director of the Serbian state broadcaster RTS as an example of this "terror." Senior RTS editors have also been dismissed.

On Monday, a small group of protesters invaded the Informer TV station. Thousands of complaints have been lodged against Informer over the years for its demonization of Vucic critics. Now, journalists' associations are calling for its license to be revoked.

Tabloid media outlets loyal to Vucic have already changed their tone. Unlike Informer, they no longer refer to the Student List as "terrorists" and "mercenaries."

Old accusations against Vucic

The List, which emerged from the student revolt, is made up of professors, activists and artists. In the election on October 25, it won 53% of the vote, leaving Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) trailing with just 39%.

Aleksandar Vucic concedes defeat in the parliamentary elections on October 25 Image: Zorana Jevtic/REUTERS

Since then, things have moved fast. In many cities, citizens peacefully removed portraits of Vucic from municipal buildings. The public prosecutor's office for organized crime has launched investigations, including into electoral fraud. A special commission is examining the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, which critics say did Vucic's bidding, and persecuted his opponents.

The accusations against him are old ones: that he and his system kept the media under tight control; that state contracts were only awarded to companies loyal to the regime; and that Vucic, his party, and the Serbian state had links to organized crime.

The catalyst for the revolt was the collapse, two years ago, of the concrete canopy on the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad. Sixteen people died. The accident is believed to have happened as a result of poor workmanship and corruption in the awarding and execution of the renovation contract.

Those who were celebrating in the streets a few days ago are already growing impatient. The new parliament has not yet been convened, and the SNS still controls many levers of power.

"A society that was oppressed for so long by a party that acted like a feudal lord now, understandably, expects justice," Dejan Bursac from the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory at Belgrade University told DW. "In this power vacuum, people are getting impatient."

Vucic and leading officials promise to be a strong opposition, and expect to make a quick comeback once "this lot" have ruined the country. But the majority of critics are calling for Vucic to be investigated and charged. "The SNS people are acting as if they had lost a local election somewhere in democratic Scandinavia, not as if they were part of a deeply corrupt and criminal regime," said Bursac.

How much damage can the old government do to the new one?

It's very common in Serbia for politicians to switch allegiance from one camp to another. They go where the power is. Even Vucic has admitted that many of his former comrades-in-arms are turning their backs on him. "We are going to see cases of people resigning or staying in the shadows, even putting themselves forward as informants for the next government," said Zlatko Minic from Transparency Serbia , an organization that monitors the work of governments.

The million-dollar question is: How much damage can the old government do to the new one? "There's still time for many officials to award contracts and create financial obligations for the agencies they run without necessarily committing a criminal offense," Minic warned.

However, those familiar with the situation said that for some time now the Student List has had contacts with officials in the police and administration opposed to Vucic's style of government. The winners of the election may now be able to prevent certain actions. On Wednesday, the List again demanded the resignations of leading officials in the police and judiciary. Whistleblowers were also asked to come forward if the outgoing government should try to "destroy documents."

Against all odds: How Serbia's students took on Vucic To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In a symbolic move, Student List representatives held their first press conference in Pioneers Park in front of the parliament building. Vucic's followers fenced off the park in 2025, turning it into a pro-government encampment. According to investigative journalists, it also became a base for thugs and criminals who attacked anti-government demonstrators. The morning after the Student List's election win, its supporters went out with binbags and cleaned up the park.

No change in foreign policy

The victorious Student List unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focussed on making changes in domestic politics, and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

"Our plan is to stabilize and develop the country, not to destabilize it with some abrupt change of course on foreign policy," Oliver Toskovic, a psychology professor and future member of parliament, told DW.

Toskovic said that, unlike under Vucic, the EU will not be misused as a "cover." Serbia's EU accession process recently stalled, with Vucic accusing "the West" of inciting a "color revolution" in Serbia.

"We are very dependent on Russia for energy. This is really a mistake of the previous government," Toskovic said. "But for that reason, sanctions right now would destabilize the country. And that would not be good for us or for the EU." How energy policy will develop under a Student List government is still unclear.

Where Vucic would frequently take aim at Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading representatives of the new List have promised better relationships with Serbia's neighbors and a reduction in tensions. On Kosovo, Ilija Srdanovic, the Student List's lead candidate, has said the party is open to dialog with the government in the Kosovar capital, Pristina. He has already spoken by phone with the prime minister of Croatia.

The electoral process is not yet over. On Sunday, November 1, the vote will be repeated in some 50 polling stations because there were irregularities first time around. Once these votes are counted, parliament can be convened. The formation of a government is expected to be quick, but for now the names of the prospective members have not been disclosed.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: More than 290 arrested in France as some weekend protests turn violent
World.content:
Protests continue across France as 320,000 people take to the streets over rising living costs and poor school conditions for a third consecutive weekend, with clashes reported in several cities.

A number of clashes have been reported between protesters and police in several French cities on Saturday as hundreds of thousands of people again took to the streets nationwide to protest the rising cost of living and conditions in schools.

France has seen weeks of widespread anger and weekend protests over the rising cost of living and growing inequality Image: Matthieu Rondel/AFP

'Radical elements' attempted to enter some city centers

The French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people had participated in demonstrations across the country, including 70,000 in Paris.

"The marches proceeded smoothly within the framework of the declared demonstrations," the ministry said, while noting that "radical elements" in several cities, including Bordeaux, Toulouse and Marseille, had attempted to enter city centres "with the aim of carrying out vandalism and looting."

In Marseille, footage showed fires burning in the streets as firefighters responded. Clashes with police were also reported in Rennes and Toulouse.

After a largely peaceful start to the day, police fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon in the late afternoon, according to French media reports and live broadcast footage. Tensions in the capital escalated as demonstrators reached the end of their march on the city's southern outskirts.

Footage aired by BFMTV showed fireworks exploding and incendiary devices being thrown at officers in riot gear, with several officers caught in the flames.

Around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were mobilized across the country Image: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP

Police arrest more than 290 people across France

Paris police carried out more than 1,200 checks at railway stations and nearby areas early on Saturday to identify potential troublemakers, the city's police prefecture said.

The checks aimed to prevent demonstrators from bringing fireworks, knives and other prohibited items to the marches.

Police also deployed "all available resources" in the air to monitor security throughout the day, the prefecture said. An official order authorized camera-equipped drones to capture and transmit live images of the situation across the capital.

More than 290 arrests were made on Saturday across France, according to police.

Authorities also feared that Halloween celebrations could give people an opportunity to conceal their identities Image: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP

Preparations ahead of the protests

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned earlier Saturday that the demonstrations posed a "very high risk," citing calls for looting and rioting.

Around 70,000 police officers and other security personnel were deployedacross the country to maintain order during the protests.

Authorities also feared that Halloween celebrations could give people an opportunity to conceal their identities while committing offenses.

Amid concerns over attacks on public buildings and looting, officials ordered protest routes in Paris and other cities to be moved away from city centers.

Many shops and businesses responded by boarding up their windows and taking other precautions. Curfews and other restrictions were also imposed in several cities, including measures targeting specific areas and minors.

A car burns during protests over living costs and education in Paris on Saturday, October 31 Image: Emma Da Silva/AP Photo/picture alliance

Third consecutive weekend of mass action

A similarly large security deployment last weekend largely prevented a repeat of the violence and destruction seen during the October 17 protests.

Young people have been taking to the streets for weeks to protest inadequate staffing and equipment in schools. Since mid-October, other groups have joined the demonstrations, mainly over the rising cost of living.

Trade unions, school and student organizations, and the grassroots Yellow Vest movement, which first rose to prominence in France in 2018, called for Saturday's protests.

World.title: Germany's Gen Z protests disrupted by violence on Saturday
World.content:
Skip next section What are the rules governing protests in Germany?

Germany guarantees its citizens the right to protest, as here in Berlin on August 8 against the far-right AfD Image: Michael Kuenne/PRESSCOV/ZUMA/picture alliance

People in Germany have the fundamental right, enshrined in the constitution or Basic Law, to assemble in public provided they remains peaceful and are unarmed.

However, several states have adopted their own assembly acts, which means some of them have additional restrictions, such as a ban on protesting on highways in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Notification generally necessary

Federal law itself imposes the obligation on organizers of protests to notify the local authority entrusted with approving public assemblies at least 48 hours before they invite people publicly to take part.

This aims to allow authorities to put in place security measures and to lessen the impact of any assembly on others by, for example, instigating traffic control measures.

Spontaneous assemblies are, however, also allowed in cases where a topical issue of urgent importance is at stake, and there is no notification requirement for indoor assemblies.

Protests or other assemblies can be banned beforehand or dispersed while they are underway, but this is considered a means of last resort.

Some locations are also subject to restrictions on protests, such as the area around the Reichstag building in Berlin where the German parliament sits, and around the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.

Demonstrations around the Reichstag are, for example, permitted only when the parliament is not in session.

Germany no stranger to big protests

Post-war Germany has seen several massive demonstrations, including one in 1983, when 250,000 people — according to police estimates — gathered in the then West German capital, Bonn, to protest against the decision by NATO to station American nuclear missiles on German territory.

That was, however, surpassed in size by a protest in Berlin in 2003 against the invasion of Iraq by US-led forces, which drew a crowd of around half a million people.

There is some more detail on the law regarding the right of assembly in this DW article.

World.title: Ukraine news: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reach Kyiv-controlled territory
World.content:
Skip next section Wadephul says Europe and US are 'on the same side' on Russia

"Speaking to the Russian Foreign Minister is not a concession we're making to Russia, but it is normal to speak," German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told DW when asked about normalizing relations with Russia. Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

At a news conference after the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, DW correspondent Benjamin Alvarez Gruber asked German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul whether Sergey Lavrov's presence and the possibility of Russian President Vladimir Putin attending the G20 summit in Doral, Florida, in December signaled a normalization of relations with Russia.

Wadephul said the US and European countries were "on the same side."

"Speaking to the Russian Foreign Minister is not a concession we're making to Russia, but it is normal to speak," he said, adding that foreign ministers must be prepared to engage even with adversaries.

"You don't have to negotiate with partners, but you have to negotiate with somebody who has a different position and who's somehow also an adversary to freedom and to security in Europe. So it is necessary that we speak, and for that reason I think it was useful," Wadephul added.

The G20 foreign ministers skipped their traditional family photo at a meeting in Atlanta on Friday, amid objections from several European countries, Australia and Canada to appearing alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

Wadephul said: "We are not in a position that it was necessary or useful or a good idea to have a family photo because in the very situation we are in, Russia does not really show an interest to share our values and to share our interests."

The US State Department removed the photo from the agenda to prevent it from becoming a distraction or a spectacle.

10/31/2026 October 31, 2026 Cologne's tiny crossing barrier has a bigger future

A railway crossing barrier just 46 centimeters (18 inches) long has become an unlikely selfie attraction in Cologne — but the city's transport operator says it serves a purpose.

The miniature arm stands beside tracks leading to a tram maintenance depot in the Weidenpesch district. It has even appeared on Google Maps as "Germany's smallest barrier."

Despite online mockery, it is no mistake. "It serves as a placeholder," said Cologne transport operator KVB spokesman Stephan Anemüller.

Installed in 2020, the barrier is to be extended once a planned cycle path is built alongside a nearby housing development. That avoids having to overhaul the crossing equipment later.

KVB is enjoying the attention. Anemüller called it "an amusing attraction" and said the operator would try to secure it a place in Cologne's city museum when it is eventually removed.

World.title: Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
World.content:
A wave of shootings and extortion threats has rattled India's film industry. This time, those claiming responsibility are very different from the Mumbai underworld that had Bollywood in its grip back in the 1990s.

"In the entire film industry, whoever works without aligning with us, or works with Salman Khan, will be killed."

This warning was delivered in an audio message by presumed attackers on Indian actor Tiger Shroff in Mumbai earlier this month, as they claimed responsibility for the shooting.

The apparent perpetrators said they were connected to Lawrence Bishnoi, a student-politician-turned-gangster who has been in prison since 2014. Notably, police have not confirmed the gang's involvement.

The shots fired at Shroff, which injured his driver, were only the latest in a string of attacks targeting prominent figures from the Mumbai-based film industry, popularly known as "Bollywood".

Since 2022, gunmen fired shots at actor Salman Khan's apartment and at the home of filmmaker Rohit Shetty in Mumbai, as well as actor Disha Patani's family home in northern India. Actor Ranveer Singh also reportedly received an extortion demand of nearly $1.1 million (around €980,000).

The attacks have spread to the other side of the globe, with a cafe owned by comedian Kapil Sharma in Surrey, Canada, also hit three times.

For an industry that once lived in the shadow of organized crime, the attacks have revived old fears, harking back to the crime bosses of the 1990s. But experts say the threat facing Bollywood today looks very different from the one it faced three decades ago.

When the underworld ruled Bollywood

In the 1990s, Mumbai's underworld was deeply entangled with the Hindi film industry.

"The mafia was always fascinated with the movie industry," said S. Hussain Zaidi, crime journalist and author of "Dongri to Dubai: Six Decades of the Mumbai Mafia," who has covered organized crime in the city for over three decades.

Gangsters like Dawood Ibrahim, Abu Salem and Chhota Shakeel "were totally obsessed" with Bollywood, he told DW, much like mafiosi who sought a foothold in Hollywood.

During his era, Dawood Ibrahim has been one of the most wanted men in India Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

To the gangsters, films offered glitz and glamor, but also a way to launder their profits. They invested in films "so that they could control the industry and have a legitimate way of making money," Zaidi added.

When producers didn't cooperate, the consequences could be fatal. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar, founder of the label T-Series, was shot dead. In 2000, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan, father of Bollywood star Hrithik Roshan, was shot and wounded.

Mumbai's streets were "made red with blood" in 1998, Zaidi said, describing the year as the pinnacle of gang killings.

D. Sivanandhan, the former Police Commissioner of Mumbai, who led the crackdown, says 101 businessmen were shot dead in 1998 alone, or one "every third day," mostly over unpaid extortion demands.

Police efforts were reinforced by a tough new organized crime law passed in 1999, which Sivanandhan calls the "ultimate weapon." Security forces used electronic surveillance and preventive detention, and seized some 2,500 illegal weapons.

"A few encounters also happened, but that is not a policy nor a strategy,” he told DW, referring to police shootouts.

By the early 2000s, the gangs' hold had been broken, and a new Mumbai seemed to be emerging.

A gang run from a prison cell

The man believed to be behind the latest wave of attacks is not from Mumbai.

Bishnoi, 33, comes from a landowning family in the northern state of Punjab and was studying in Chandigarh when he was drawn into violent student politics. Then, he was arrested, incarcerated and eventually turned to crime, says journalist Jupinderjit Singh, author of "Gangs of Punjab."

"He was introduced to the University of Crime through the jail," Singh told DW.

Lawrence Bishnoi was a student politician in the northern city of Chandigarh before gaining notoriety as a gangster Image: Sameer Sehgal/Hindustan Times/IMAGO

Bishnoi went on to build what Singh describes as one of the first criminal syndicates spanning several northern Indian states. Investigators say he still directs operations from prison using concealed phones and messaging apps.

Currently, Bishnoi is held in a jail in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's home state of Gujarat.

His network stretches beyond India's borders. In September 2025, Canada designated the Bishnoi gang a terrorist entity. Last month, the FBI added Satinderjeet Singh, popularly known as Goldy Brar, to its Ten Most Wanted list, offering up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest. US prosecutors described him as the alleged leader of Bishnoi's group in North America.

While Bishnoi comes from an affluent landowning family, his shooters are mostly poor. The gang usually recruits them online.

"There are so many youngsters who want to do something… they are just pulled by the lore attached to Lawrence Bishnoi," Singh explained. "Recruiting is no big issue… They offer money, protection, weapons."

Why target film stars?

For Bishnoi, it seems personal.

In 1998, Salman Khan was accused of killing a blackbuck, an antelope revered by Bishnoi's community. Bishnoi vowed revenge, and many of the attacks targeted people close to the actor, including the 2024 killing of politician Baba Siddique, which police have linked to the gang.

Singh sees the feud as a bid for respectability. Criminals "always try to find something that makes them a moral guardian," he says, and this case was Bishnoi's "chance to redeem himself."

Salman Khan was granted bail in 2018 as he appealed a conviction for killing two rare antelopes Image: AFP

But money and intimidation matter too.

"Bollywood has a lot of money," Singh added, pointing that the previous generation of gangsters was no longer in position to take advantage.

"With Dawood Ibrahim and his counterparts away, there was a vacuum, and Lawrence Bishnoi is trying to exploit that."

Sivanandhan explained the old Mumbai gangs ran a whole "basket" of illegal businesses, from smuggling to protection rackets and cricket match-fixing. Their members were "local boys," while the Bishnoi gang has “nothing to do with Mumbai,” he added. It targets Bollywood because the industry is "loaded with money" and a "soft underbelly."

"They are using Bollywood as an ATM," he told DW. "Insert a card and collect your money."

Meanwhile, Zaidi sees the attacks mainly as publicity. "It's a way to grab headlines," he told DW. Within hours of the recent attack on Shroff, someone claimed on social media that he was targeted for being close to Khan, a logic Zaidi called "absolutely illogical and absurd."

But publicity is useful to gangs that live off extortion. "The base material of extortion is: create fear," a security professional responsible for the protection of several Bollywood stars, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue, told DW.

Is Bollywood under siege?

Still, experts say its hard to argue that the ongoing violence is comparable to the 1990s crime wave.

"I won't say resurgence, because that would be a bit of an exaggeration," Zaidi said. In the 1990s, several rival gangs fought for control of Mumbai. Today, other than Bishnoi's faction, other gangs are not considered active in Mumbai.

The film industry is also not paying up the way it once did, because the shift to digital payments has made large cash transactions hard to hide, he added.

India's banned film 'Satluj' finds new audiences To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sivanandhan disagrees. The shootings at walls and gates, followed by quick claims on social media, are "all aimed at collecting… extortion money," he said. In his view, "cash-rich Bollywood would be coughing up so much, which is enough to run an army of people."

At any case, the fear remains real.

And even if violence is not as prevalent, hundreds of thousands of people rely on the Mumbai film industry for their livelihoods.

"If the fear of the underworld continues, leading names may be forced to leave Mumbai," the All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) President Suresh Shyamlal Gupta wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah.

"Mumbai will not be allowed to go back to the underworld days of the 1990s, and Bollywood will not be allowed to work in the shadow of fear," Gupta wrote.

With security forces seemingly on the back foot, gangsters are likely to continue their campaign.

Several Bollywood stars have already stepped up their security.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like
World.content:
What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection, as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

How names influence first impressions

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness.



For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.



What do Nigerians think of bullying? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why some names attract negative judgments

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

How humor helps people cope with embarrassing names

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

How an embarrassing name can also offer a sense of belonging

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

Tiny describes a similar ambivalence.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

Superpower laughter — how humor makes us strong , To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."



Edited by: Richard Connor

World.title: India news: Amit Shah challenges Rahul Gandhi to debate vote theft in parliament
World.content:
10/31/2026 October 31, 2026 Vote theft row: Shah challenges opposition as INDIA bloc prepares major protest

Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Friday challenged opposition leaders Rahul Gandhi and Akhilesh Yadav to discuss allegations of electoral irregularities in parliament, even as the opposition geared for a major rally against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar , according to media reports.

"I am ready to call a special session of Parliament to discuss vote theft allegations," Shah said, accusing the opposition of making baseless allegations against the Election Commission and staging protests while skirting parliamentary debate.

His remarks came as the opposition INDIA bloc prepared to hold a symbolic "public impeachment" of Kumar on Saturday, followed by a major rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan on November 1.

Around 30 speakers from 21 opposition parties are expected to participate.

The opposition is demanding Kumar's resignation over his role in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the scrapping of the SIR, alleging that the exercise could disenfranchise voters and benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

In a call for the November 1 rally, Rahul Gandhi said "anyone who cares about democracy must come."

"The vote is yours. The fight is also yours," the Congress leader wrote on X.

Earlier, the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) also threw their weight behind the rally saying the movement would lend its support to any organization fighting for free and fair elections in India, including the opposition alliance.

World.title: Renfe elevará sus condiciones de seguridad en la línea Madrid-Sevilla para evitar nuevos siniestros
World.content:
Primera reacción de calado en la operativa ferroviaria tras el suceso de Urda (Toledo), que el pasado miércoles costó la vida a 69 personas en la línea de alta velocidad Madrid-Sevilla. La operadora con mayor presencia en la red, Renfe, va a lanzar una consigna a sus maquinistas para que tengan claras nuevas prescripciones de circulación “aplicables ante una pérdida de transmisión de datos por fallo del sistema [de seguridad] LZB”. La operadora trabaja en coordinación con el operador de la infraestructura Adif en una versión definitiva que será aplicada lo antes posible. Lo que hará Renfe es elevar las condiciones de seguridad en caso de crisis ordenando una marcha lo más lenta posible, según el documento al que ha tenido acceso EL PAÍS, sometido aún a cambios, y que será distribuido entre el personal de la compañía pública.

Ante una situación degradada del LZB, que se produce de forma imprevista, como ocurrió en un segmento de 63 kilómetros del Corredor Sur a las 8.30 horas del día 28, Renfe recuerda en el texto a sus más de 6.000 conductores que “una gestión adecuada en el proceso de esta situación degradada es fundamental para evitar sucesos no deseados”. La pérdida de transmisión puede derivar en dos situaciones: bloqueo total (Meta40) y bloqueo parcial (Meta 000) de los trenes. En el primer escenario, “el maquinista deberá ser consciente en todo momento del punto de la infraestructura en el que se encuentra y observar la señalización lateral. Deberá reducir la velocidad por debajo de 80 o 60 kilómetros por hora según el porcentaje de frenado y volver a pulsar Liberar. Desde ese momento se considera circulando al amparo BSL (sistema de señalización basada en balizas situadas en el lateral de la vía), informando de esta situación al RC (responsable de circulación del centro de control de Adif)”.

Si el bloqueo es parcial, como sucedió en el caso del AVE accidentado en Urda, se demanda a los maquinistas “efectuar detención inmediata”. Una vez frenado el tren, prosigue la orden de Renfe a su personal, “no actuar sobre el pulsador Rebasar ni reanudar la marcha hasta haber recibido del RC el telefonema LZB3”. De esta última orden, Renfe asevera que es “el único telefonema válido para reiniciar la marcha en esta situación y siempre con prescripción marcha a la vista”. No queda espacio para que un maquinista acepte o respete un protocolo LBZ4, con el que el centro de control de Adif puede indicar el avance a marcha normal, como sucedió el miércoles. Esa fatídica mañana, el maquinista de Renfe preguntó al controlador de Adif en Madrid-Atocha si estaba seguro de que el protocolo correcto era el de la marcha normal que permite el LBZ4, recibiendo la confirmación como respuesta.

La compañía que opera los servicios de alta velocidad AVE y Avlo adoptará una garantía adicional para que sus convoyes circulen al mínimo ritmo posible cuando se quedan sin el amparo del LZB en la línea Madrid-Sevilla: “Durante la marcha a la vista prescrita, no se excederá en ningún caso la velocidad de 40 kilómetros por hora hasta rebasar la señal indicada en el telefonema LBZ3, independientemente del aspecto que presente alguna señal previa si la hubiera. De esta prescripción se informará al RC tras recibir el telefonema LZB3”. Es decir, ningún maquinista de Renfe rodará a más de 40 por hora y así se lo indicará a los operarios del gestor de la infraestructura Adif para la adaptación del tráfico en el corredor.

Otra acción que se demandará a los conductores, tal y como reza en una versión de la consigna aún moldeable, es que cuando se vean en la situación que vivió el AVE siniestrado en Urda soliciten al centro de control en Madrid “la conformación de que en el cantón [segmento de vía] de bloqueo BSL solo se encuentra su tren, antes de aceptar el telefonema LZB3”. Esta última consigna se traduce en que no se arrancará hasta tener plenas garantías de que el cantón que se va a ocupar está totalmente libre. En el caso de la tragedia de Urda, el AVE de Renfe recibió la orden de partir a 200 kilómetros por hora pese a que en su mismo cantón había un Iryo detenido y sin poder reanudar la marcha. De ahí la versión que parte del ministro de Transportes de que ese imperativo resulta “inexplicable”. La unidad de Renfe avanzó 25 kilómetros en 17 minutos, sin recibir indicación alguna de frenado ni por parte del centro de regulación del tráfico ni desde la propia vía, y colisionó con el convoy de Iryo que bloqueaba la vía en Urda a una velocidad de 160 a 200 kilómetros por hora.

El ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, señaló el viernes en una larga rueda de prensa que se iba a poner en revisión “todo el sistema ferroviario para modificar lo que sea necesario” en favor de garantizar la seguridad. El sindicato de maquinistas SEMAF ha demandado por carta a las operadoras y a la Agencia de Seguridad Ferroviaria que se imponga la marcha a la vista, como única opción, en caso de que el LZB quedara inhabilitado.

Se considera que un tramo está en situación degradada cuando deja de ser vigilado por el sistema de señalización, comunicaciones y seguridad LZB, en el caso de la Madrid-Sevilla, o por el ERTMS en el resto de corredores. Estas tecnologías actúan sobre el tren modulando las velocidades de circulación e incluso activando el frenado automático cuando la vía está bloqueada. Si esta primera capa de seguridad se cae, el tramo es considerado convencional y no de alta velocidad, entrando en juego un doble sistema de respaldo, el ASFA y el SBL. Una de las diferencias entre el LZB y el ASFA es que el primero sitúa a los trenes en pequeños cantones, evitando que los crucen cuando el posterior está ocupado. Con el ASFA se amplían esos segmentos de vía.

En el caso del grave accidente ocurrido en Urda, el maquinista del AVE de Renfe ocupó un cantón por el que circulaba un Iryo hasta su detención en puertas de una estación LZB que había registrado un fallo. La maquinista de este último comunicó su situación de parada en dos ocasiones al centro de control de Adif en Atocha, la última de ellas a las 8.48. El protocolo de su compañía le ordenaba tras dos intentos fallidos de reinicio del LZB comunicar con el equipo de mantenimiento para recibir asistencia. Pero el tren nunca llegó a retomar la marcha al ser embestido por el AVE, cuyo maquinista desconocía que se dirigía a un fatal desenlace. Incluso los cinco minutos que discurren entre la última llamada de la conductora del Iryo y el golpe recibido a las 8.53 horas hubieran sido suficientes, afirmó Puente, para evitar la tragedia.

La activación de medidas más estrictas de seguridad, en este caso por parte de Renfe, buscan evitar nuevos accidentes y recuperar la confianza de los viajeros. El ministro reveló el viernes ante la prensa que en lo que va de año el sistema LZB se ha caído en 170 ocasiones, un 75% por causas ajenas a la infraestructura (robos de cable y condiciones climatológicas adversas, principalmente).

En el caso de las líneas dotadas con el más moderno ERTMS, la actuación de la propia tecnología es distinta a la del LZB: también obliga a frenar a los trenes, pero genera una señal artificial en la parte delantera conocida como EOA (Fin de Autorización, por sus siglas en inglés). El rebase de un EOA siempre se produce con marcha a la vista (a baja velocidad). En el ERTMS de nivel 2, que es el instalado por ejemplo en la línea Madrid-León, la que va a Galicia o Alicante, el responsable de circulación tiene constancia en todo momento de si el maquinista está incumpliendo una autorización o el tren se mueve indebidamente. La información transmitida es más compleja que en el nivel 1 o allí donde aún se utiliza el referido LZB.

La línea Madrid-Sevilla tiene ya instalado el ERTMS en la totalidad del trazado, trabajo que se ha llevado desde 2021 hasta el pasado verano y que ha ejecutado Hitachi Rail, misma empresa encargada del mantenimiento del LZB. En estos meses el sistema está en fase de test en laboratorio, y se espera para el arranque de 2027 la transición desde el LZB con que se abrió el corredor Sur en 1992 al más moderno escudo de seguridad. El ERTMS es el actual estándar europeo, está operativo en el resto de la red española, y su generalización en toda Europa busca favorecer los tráficos transfronterizos.

World.title: Una cadena de fallos técnicos tumbó el sistema de seguridad ferroviaria LZB en Urda
World.content:
La ficha de la incidencia abierta por Adif a las 8.30 del miércoles, 23 minutos antes del siniestro, señala pérdidas de tensión, comunicaciones telefónicas caídas y “pérdida de información intermitente”. Posteriormente, la empresa pudo constatar que la comunicación con los maquinistas se mantuvo en pie

El sistema de registro de incidencias del gestor de la infraestructura ferroviaria Adif recoge una cadena de fallos técnicos en el área de Urda (Toledo) el miércoles día 28, a las 8.30 de la mañana, que desembocan en una serie de instrucciones inconexas a los maquinistas, por parte del centro de mando en Madrid-Atocha, y en el fatal accidente entre un AVE de Renfe y un tren de Iryo. La ficha abierta a esa hora por “avería en instalaciones de seguridad” entre las localidades toledanas de Mora y Orgaz toca al tramo que va del kilómetro 89,5 al 119,7 de la línea de alta velocidad Madrid-Sevilla. El siniestro ocurre en el 118. La descripción del fallo, según recoge el documento adelantado por ABC y al que ha tenido acceso este periódico, es “Caída central LZB Urda”, lo que resume una cadena fatal de incidencias tecnológicas.

Adif tiene en ese punto una central con equipos (tres ordenadores) que dan servicio al sistema de seguridad alemán LZB, que comunica trenes e infraestructura, modula la velocidad de circulación e impide que los convoyes entren en riesgo de colisión. Cuando las órdenes de al menos dos de esos ordenadores al tren no coinciden, el LZB se desactiva. Como es sabido, por el relato del ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, esa caída del sistema de señalización motivó la parada de seis trenes, entre ellos los dos siniestrados. Pese a quedar inhábil, el escudo cumplió la misión final de frenar el tráfico sin que hubiera que lamentar hasta ese momento problema grave alguno.

En el texto de la ficha de Adif se puede leer: “Caída central LZB Urda, con fallos de transmisión generalizados Meta 40 y Meta 0”. A continuación, la empresa pública constata en este parte de incidencia que “se revisan LTV [limitación temporal de velocidad] del tramo, encontrándose todas señalizadas”. A partir de este punto, en el que la situación está bajo control pese a perderse la señal del sistema de seguridad, se añade que “tras sufrir fallo de velocidad Meta 0, se circula con BSL [sistema de señalización a través de balizas laterales] hasta recuperar transmisión fuera de la central”. Es decir, se espera que una vez rebasada la estación de Urda, los trenes puedan volver a guiarse por el sistema LZB.

“La incidencia coincide con fallos en las comunicaciones GSMR en el punto”, indica Adif en la ficha de las 8.30. El GSMR o Global System for Mobile Communications-Railway es el estándar internacional de comunicación inalámbrica diseñado específicamente para el sector ferroviario. Además de quedar inhábil el LZB, se describe el fallo en las comunicaciones y, además, “se produce pérdida de información intermitente momentánea en los circuitos de vía de Urda”. Tercer problema concatenado, al que se suma un cuarto: “Coincide con pérdida de tensión a la salida de la estación de Urda en ambas vías y ocupación CV237”. Los cuatro fallos concretan la pérdida del LZB.

Una revisión posterior del sistema, explica un portavoz oficial de Adif, aclara que “todas las comunicaciones entre el centro de control de Atocha y los maquinistas se realizaron sin problemas”. Aunque se incluyó la referencia al GSMR en la ficha de incidencia, conocida de puertas adentro como GIFO, “se ha verificado lo ocurrido y confirmado que el contacto entre Atocha y los maquinistas no falló y que en ningún caso tuvo una relación directa con el accidente”.

Hasta ese punto en crisis de la línea Madrid-Sevilla llegó en torno a las 8.35 un equipo de mantenimiento de Adif para intentar levantar el sistema LZB, del que dos ordenadores iban a permanecer bloqueados hasta el momento de la colisión, a las 8.53 horas. Se intentó incluso rearmar el sistema usando un solo ordenador, pero tampoco fue posible. La investigación policial y técnica deben verificar ahora el estado de los equipos, a los que se prohibió el acceso a la empresa encargada del mantenimiento, Hitachi Rail, en cuanto el caso cayó en manos del juzgado de instrucción de Orgaz.

Mientras el personal de Adif atendía esta incidencia, de las que el ministro Puente relató ayer en rueda de prensa que se han dado en lo que va de año 170 de distinta naturaleza que han tumbado al LZB en la misma línea de alta velocidad (dijo que el 75% por causas ajenas a Adif), un tren de Iryo queda paralizado ante la estación de Urda y pese a dos intentos de la maquinista, le es imposible reiniciar el sistema LZB y continuar la marcha. Todo ello es comunicado a las 8.41 y 8.48 por la conductora al centro de control de Adif en Madrid-Atocha. Desde 25 kilómetros detrás sí avanza un AVE de Renfe, con amparo del sistema de seguridad BSL y con orden de marcha normal. Durante 17 minutos de trayecto alcanza hasta 200 kilómetros por hora sin que su conductor supiera en ningún momento que encontraría un obstáculo en la vía, el tren de Iryo. El choque que deja un balance de 69 víctimas mortales, se produce a las 8.53. La Autoridad Independiente para la Investigación Técnica de Accidentes (AITAT) estima en un primer informe que el AVE alcanzó a la unidad de Iryo a una velocidad de 160 a 200 kilómetros por hora.

El ministro Puente reconoció el miércoles, y reiteró ayer, que el control de la circulación de Adif “tuvo tiempo para evitar la tragedia”. Esa compañía pública depende de su ministerio. También concedió que se aplicó erróneamente el protocolo de circulaciones en caso de caída del LZB y la existencia de obstáculos en la vía. Pese a la orden de reanudación de la marcha que recibió el AVE de Renfe, la velocidad de avance nunca debió rebasar los 40 kilómetros por hora, lo que en el argot ferroviario se conoce como marcha a la vista.

En descarga de cualquier dificultad que pudiera haber tenido la unidad de Iryo para proseguir su viaje hacia Sevilla, Puente afirmó que el tren que tenía detrás nunca debía haber sido liberado hasta que el primero hubiera recuperado la marcha.

World.title: El guardia civil Salvador rescató a Almudena del vagón 1 del Iryo, el más afectado del accidente: “Solo había silencio”
World.content:
Salvador Correa patrulla desde la siete de la mañana. Es guardia civil, como su padre, de quien tomó el oficio y el nombre. Trabaja en la Unidad de Seguridad de Toledo y está preparando un puesto de control con su compañero, cerca de Illescas, cuando reciben un aviso: ha habido un alcance de dos trenes cerca de su posición. “No puede ser otro Adamuz”, se dicen entre ellos. Pero se mentalizan para un escenario como el de hace nueve meses. Se ponen dos pares de guantes cada uno, unos simples de látex y otros de material duro para evitar cortes. Tardan unos 20 minutos en llegar a Urda. Desde el coche ven a gente caminar con maletas, como “en shock”. Hay efectivos que atienden a heridos atrapados dentro de los convoyes. “Allí olía a lo que había pasado, a los frenos”. Ellos se acercan a un vagón al que todavía no ha accedido nadie. El vehículo está volcado sobre el talud. No lo saben, pero es el más afectado del accidente, el vagón 1 del Iryo, que iba en la cola y fue engullido por el AVE. Muchos de los 69 fallecidos del accidente están dentro, ya sin vida. Salvador se adentra por el suelo, por un hueco de unos 40 centímetros. Tiene que quitarse el chaleco antibalas porque si no, no cabe. Dentro ve los cuerpos inertes. “Solo había silencio”.

Tratan de buscar a alguien con vida, con muy poca luz. Hablan a los pasajeros. Les tocan para que reaccionen. Nadie responde. De repente, sí. Una mujer que los escucha empieza a chillar. Se acercan. Es la única. Salvador cree recordar que estaba en el asiento 5. Está totalmente cubierta de fusejale. “Lo que tenía encima era el AVE”. En las fotografías posteriores al accidente se ve al vagón 1 del Iryo, el último, como si estuviera dentro del primero del AVE, que lo arremetió por detrás y se lo comió. Nunca antes en la alta velocidad española un tren había alcanzado a otro en el mismo cantón. Salvador sigue con la mujer. Solo ve su mano y apercibe una pulsera verde. Se la agarra. “Siempre hubo relevo con esa mano, esa mano nunca se soltó”.

Llegan tres bomberos. Entre todos se coordinan para ir agarrando su mano y para retirar el amasijo de hierro, aluminio, plástico... que la mujer tiene encima. Ella no puede moverse. Salvador empieza a ver las heridas en sus piernas. Lleva unos calcetines granates. Por fin su cara. “Tenía los ojos claros, azules”. Al guardia civil se le clava su mirada. Empiezan a hablar con ella. Es importante que siga hablando sin parar para no desfallecer. “Le dije que estuviese tranquila, que se relajase. En ese momento no sientes ni dolor, el cuerpo es inteligente”. Ella cuenta que se llama Almudena, que tiene 32 años y que la pulsera es de una hermandad de Sevilla.

Cuando creen que ya pueden sacarla, algo lo impide. Es su pelo, es lo último que sigue atrapado. Buscan unas tijeras. Ha pasado algo más de una hora desde que Salvador encontró a Almudena. En todo ese tiempo, el guardia civil no piensa “en nada”. Está con el piloto automático, deshaciendo el puzle del AVE que se ha formado sobre Almudena. “No recuerdo de qué color tenía el pelo”. Se lo cortan y unos sanitarios se la llevan en camilla por el hueco de 40 centímetros que queda entre el vagón 1 del Iryo y el suelo. Es la última vez que Salvador ve a Almudena. No sabe si saldrá con vida.

Es en torno a mediodía. Salvador se desplaza hasta el vagón del AVE que arrasó con el vehículo del Iryo en el que iba Almudena. Ya han sacado a los pocos supervivientes que había. El trabajo del guardia civil consiste solo en extraer cuerpos. Así hasta las siete de la tarde. Cuerpos y más cuerpos. Salvador estuvo en la dana realizando funciones de seguridad. Aquello lo describe como una película, pero el accidente de Urda le impacta mucho más. Llega a casa por la tarde con la impotencia como una losa sobre su espalda. “¡He trabajado 12 horas y nadie ha vivido!“. Solo le queda la esperanza de haber ayudado a Almudena. Pero no sabe cuál ha sido su destino. Le atormenta. Tira de contactos en el hospital para localizarla. Solo tiene unos pocos datos: se llama Almudena, tiene 32 años, los ojos azules y una pulsera verde de una hermandad de Sevilla. De la angustia no consigue cenar. Angustia por todo lo que ha visto en los dos vagones con más víctimas mortales, que prefiere no describir. Y por Almudena. Recibe una llamada antes de irse a dormir. ¡Está viva!.

Al otro lado del teléfono habla Julio. Es el prometido de Almudena. “Solo lloraba, nos daba las gracias, nos decía que somos unos héroes, que habíamos salvado al amor de su vida”. Ella ha sido intervenida, pero “saldrá adelante”. Las 12 horas sin descanso de Salvador han tenido algo de sentido. Al día siguiente no trabaja; le toca descansar. Mantiene conversaciones con Julio. La pareja es de Sevilla, pero viven en Madrid. También los padres de Almudena. Ella viaja a la capital andaluza normalmente un par de veces por semana en tren por trabajo. Como el día del accidente. Desde que Salvador la saca del vagón 1 del Iryo y es trasladada por los sanitarios, está ingresada en la Unidad de Cuidados Intensivos del Hospital Universitario de Toledo. Es uno de los ocho pacientes que continúa en la UCI de ese centro, a los que se suman otros siete en otros hospitales. Almudena tiene heridas y contusiones graves. “Pero se recupera”. Puede hablar, recuerda todo lo que pasó y sabe quién es Salvador.

Es viernes. Salvador ha vuelto a Urda por la mañana. Trabaja en funciones de seguridad en el dispositivo para retirar los trenes. Por la tarde ha quedado con Julio en visitar a la familia de Almudena en el hospital. La primera que lo ve es la hermana de la chica, a la que una enfermera le indica: “¡Este es el que ha salvado a tu hermana!“. Le da un gran abrazo, ella tiene que marcharse y le guía con el resto de la familia. El prometido de Almudena lo abraza también. Ambos lloran juntos. Salvador trae regalos y un mensaje para la mujer que rescató hace dos días del peor vagón de uno de los peores accidentes de trenes de España. “Que ha tenido una gran suerte, que da igual cómo esté ahora, que va a vivir, que se tome una cerveza cuando salga de allí para celebrarlo”. Quiere que Julio se lo diga a Almudena. Le entrega los regalos: varias pulseras y una camiseta de la Guardia Civil, además del parche del cuerpo que llevaba en la camisa el día del rescate.

El Guardia Civil Salvador Correa, en el Hospital de Toledo, este viernes. Carlos Rosillo

La familia traslada a Salvador su agradecimiento con más abrazos y palabras de cariño. Él tiene 37 años y novia. Nació en Pamplona, creció en Málaga y, tras varios destinos, recaló en Toledo en 2023. El nombre y el oficio que tomó de su padre cobran hoy más sentido que nunca. “La madre de Almudena me ha dicho: ‘¡Salvador, eres el salvador de mi hija!”. El guardia civil está sentado delante del Hospital Universitario de Toledo. Julio le ha regalado la pulsera de la hermandad de Sevilla de parte de Almudena. La que tenía en la mano que no soltó en la hora de rescate. Tiene los ojos vidriosos mientras relata el encuentro que acaba de ocurrir junto a la UCI. No se explica por qué Almudena sobrevivió a la dramática suerte del vagón 1 del Iryo.

Un compañero ha contado a Salvador que otro hombre de ese vagón 1 del Iryo reaccionó después también y que fue llevado a un hospital. Este periódico no consigue dar con su paradero. Sí ha confirmado que Almudena iba en el vagón 1 del Iryo. Que tiene 32 años y vive en Madrid. Su familia no quiere hablar por ahora con la prensa. Salvador espera ver a Almudena cuando salga de la UCI. “Todos hemos vuelto a nacer. Yo también, porque fue la vida que me llevé”.
