World.title: [Time Trowel] Ube is taking over the world. So why are Filipinos still obsessed with rice?
World.content:
While the Philippines remains heavily reliant on rice despite being a major importer, recognizing and investing in alternative root crops like ube and taro can enhance food security and agricultural diversity

A trowel (/ˈtraʊ.əl/), in the hands of an archaeologist, is like a trusty sidekick – a tiny, yet mighty, instrument that uncovers ancient secrets, one well-placed scoop at a time. It’s the Sherlock Holmes of the excavation site, revealing clues about the past with every delicate swipe.

Long before ube became fashionable in cafés from Los Angeles to London, Filipinos had already given it a place in halo-halo, one of our most beloved desserts. The combination of shaved ice, sweetened fruits, beans, and milk has long included ube halaya, sometimes accompanied by ube ice cream for those who believe one serving of ube is never enough. Now, the rest of the world has discovered this purple yam, transforming it into lattes and pastries that sometimes contain more food coloring than actual ube.

The enthusiasm has attracted investment. The United States Department of Agriculture has committed $34.1 million to develop the Philippine ube industry through a five-year program expected to support 12,500 Filipino farmers. This is welcome news, particularly if it increases farmers’ incomes. Still, I find it amusing that a crop cultivated in the Philippines for generations is suddenly attracting millions of dollars because international consumers have developed an appetite for purple desserts. More importantly, the investment raises questions about how we value crops and determine agricultural priorities, especially in a country where food security has become almost synonymous with rice production.

Filipinos have an enduring love affair with rice. Someone who has eaten bread for breakfast and noodles for lunch might still complain about not having eaten rice all day. Government agricultural policies reflect this preference, with billions of pesos allocated to rice production. Yet the Philippines is the world’s largest rice importer. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, Filipinos consume approximately 329 grams of rice daily, or 120 kilograms annually per person. That is a considerable amount of rice for a country struggling to meet domestic demand.

Root crops, meanwhile, are frequently associated with poverty or food shortages. Kamote has even become a term for incompetence, an unfortunate reputation for a crop that has fed generations of Filipinos. Our preference for rice has influenced how we value other staples, including those cultivated long before rice became central to Philippine diets.

Archaeology offers another perspective on Philippine food history. There is no securely established archaeological evidence of wet-rice cultivation in the Philippines earlier than approximately 700 years ago. For much of Philippine history, communities relied on other food sources, including taro and yams, which played important roles in early Philippine agriculture. Our ancestors had more options on their plates than our contemporary obsession with rice might suggest.

Our archaeological research in Ifugao has challenged the popular claim that the Cordillera rice terraces represent 2,000 years of continuous wet-rice agriculture. Evidence indicates that intensive wet-rice cultivation expanded approximately 300 to 400 years ago, partly in response to Spanish colonial intrusion. Earlier agricultural systems included taro cultivation, supported by Indigenous knowledge of land management. Ifugao communities were producing food long before rice terraces came to dominate the landscape. Their agricultural history extends beyond the terraces that tourists photograph today.

This history has implications as the Philippines confronts climate change. Typhoons can destroy rice crops within hours, while drought threatens irrigation supplies. Certain varieties of yams and sweet potatoes tolerate periods of limited rainfall, while underground storage organs may survive wind damage. Although root crops are also vulnerable to flooding and prolonged drought, cultivating different crops could reduce dependence on rice. Given our annual encounters with typhoons, placing so much of our food security in one crop seems an unnecessary gamble.

ALSO ON RAPPLER

Root crops contribute to household nutrition in several ways. Ube provides carbohydrates and dietary fiber, while orange-fleshed sweet potatoes contain beta-carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A. Including these crops in everyday meals can improve dietary diversity and provide an alternative to rice. Their nutritional benefits, however, depend partly on how they are prepared. Ube ice cream and sugar-laden lattes are hardly substitutes for nutritious meals. Adding ube to a dessert does not turn it into health food, regardless of what social media influencers might claim.

Indigenous communities have maintained knowledge of root crop cultivation that agricultural institutions could learn from. Across the Philippines, farmers cultivate varieties of taro and yams adapted to local environments. Some communities also maintain knowledge of wild yams requiring processing before consumption. These practices developed through generations of experimentation and have supported households during periods of scarcity, often without the institutional recognition afforded to rice cultivation.

Commercialization raises questions about the future of this agricultural diversity. Export markets favor varieties selected for yield or processing characteristics. Farmers may consequently abandon cultivars that do not meet commercial requirements, including those adapted to particular environmental conditions. It would be ironic if ube’s international popularity eventually contributed to the loss of varieties.

The Philippine government’s decision to restrict exports of fresh ube and planting materials reflects concerns about protecting domestic production. Protection should also extend to farmers who have maintained these resources. Communities should participate in commercialization decisions and benefit from the use of their agricultural knowledge.

Agricultural research could use the enthusiasm for ube to investigate root crops beyond export markets. Universities and government agencies could document varieties maintained by farming communities and assess their responses to changing climatic conditions. If millions of dollars can be mobilized because people abroad enjoy purple pastries, perhaps we can also invest in crops that could address food insecurity at home.

I am certainly not proposing that Filipinos abandon rice. Anyone who has attempted to replace a Filipino household’s rice with boiled kamote knows how that conversation might end. Some might rather skip the meal entirely. Our preference for rice, however, should not prevent us from recognizing crops that sustained Philippine communities long before intensive rice agriculture became widespread.

For now, I will continue enjoying halo-halo with a generous serving of ube halaya. Perhaps the next time someone pays six dollars for an ube latte in Los Angeles, they might consider the Filipino farmers whose agricultural knowledge has sustained its cultivation for generations. I hope the international enthusiasm improves their livelihoods and encourages investment in other crops that have long fed Filipino communities. Taro and other root crops may never achieve ube’s celebrity status, but they were feeding people long before anyone thought of putting a yam in a latte. – Rappler.com

Stephen B. Acabado is a professor of anthropology at the University of California, Los Angeles. He directs the Ifugao and Bicol Archaeological Projects, which emphasize community

engagement in archaeological research. He grew up in Tinambac, Camarines Sur. His latest book, Stirring the Pot and the Past: Food Stories and Philippine History, co-authored with John Sherwin Felix, explores how centuries of cultural exchange have shaped Filipino cuisine and identity.

World.title: They came home to the Cordillera and found more than they expected
World.content:
TRADITION. A woman serves freshly brewed coffee from a traditional clay pot using a coconut-shell ladle at Awichon Cultural Village in Lubuagan, Kalinga, on October 19, 2026, during the Discover More to Love Homecoming Caravan.

For Cordillerans returning from overseas, a four-day journey becomes a chance to rediscover their roots, meeting the people who keep the region’s culture, farms, and communities alive

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – At 27, Izadee Nabunat has spent much of her life in Australia knowing she is Cordilleran. But she still has questions about the ancestral homeland she calls home.

Three days into a journey across the Cordillera, she stood before fellow travelers, tourism officials, and cultural performers at Mount Data Hotel, struggling to put the experience into words.

“Being a Cordilleran who grew up overseas, there has always been curiosity within me in regards to our culture and history,” she said.

The journey had answered some of those questions, she explained, but had also made her want to learn more. Then she turned to the Department of Tourism (DOT) officials who had organized the trip.

“DOT, if your target was our hearts, I can confirm you’ve captured ours completely.”

Izadee Nabunat, a Cordilleran from Sydney, Australia, treks through the UNESCO-listed Nagacadan Rice Terraces in Kiangan, Ifugao, on October 18, 2026, reconnecting with her heritage during the Discover More to Love Homecoming Caravan. All photos by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

Nabunat was among the overseas Cordillerans who joined the Discover More to Love Homecoming Caravan from October 17 to 20.

The four-day journey brought balikbayans, tourism stakeholders, and media partners through Ifugao, Kalinga, Mountain Province, and Benguet, beginning with a festival in Baguio City and ending at a flower farm in Atok.

For participants returning from overseas, it was an opportunity to reconnect with their heritage. For the communities hosting them, it was also a chance to show what tourism could contribute to local livelihoods and the considerable work involved in preserving cultural traditions.

Beyond the festival performances

The journey opened on October 17 with the fifth Cordillera Festival of Festivals, when more than 500 performers representing the region’s six provinces and two cities brought their respective celebrations to Baguio’s Session Road.

From the thanksgiving traditions of Apayao’s Say-am and Benguet’s Bindiyan to the cultural presentations of Ifugao, Kalinga, Mountain Province, Abra, Baguio, and Tabuk City, the performances introduced visitors to the region’s diverse communities.

It was a lively beginning, with the rhythms of gongs, colorful traditional clothing, and stories expressed through music and dance.

But the following days would take the participants beyond staged performances and into the communities where many of those traditions continue to be practiced.

Their first provincial destination was Kiangan, Ifugao.

On October 18, the caravan visited the Nagacadan Rice Terraces, one of the five terrace clusters inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as the Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras.

The terraces were in their post-harvest period, far from the lush green landscape often featured in travel s.

Community guides explained the agricultural cycle, irrigation, heirloom rice, and the work required to maintain the fields.

Among them was Johntrey “Dandan” Dinamling, a young resident who had put his schooling on hold to help his family farm and was gaining experience as a tourism guide. It was one of his first experiences guiding visitors.

His story offered a glimpse of the choices facing young people in farming communities. Maintaining the terraces requires labor and traditional knowledge, while families must also find ways to earn enough to meet their needs.

Tourism presents another source of income, particularly when visitors engage local guides, purchase community products, and spend time learning from residents.

The caravan also encountered traditional Ifugao houses, weaving, and local food, including binakle, a rice cake wrapped in banana leaves.

At one traditional house, visitors joined their guides in singing the Tuwali folk song “Itetem ta humgopak,” meaning “Put the ladder down so I can enter.”

Threads of tradition take shape on a loom at Mabilong Weavers Village in Lubuagan, Kalinga.

For Nabunat, the experience in Kiangan proved especially memorable.

She recalled how the group’s guide later asked participants to identify their favorite part of the journey.

They could not choose.

“Simply there was no way to choose a single moment,” she said.

The families keeping traditions alive

From Ifugao, the caravan traveled to Tabuk City on October 18, before continuing to Lubuagan, Kalinga, the following morning.

At Mabilong Weavers Village, visitors watched artisans create traditional Kalinga textiles, observing the intricate work behind patterns that carry cultural meaning.

The group later visited Awichon Cultural Village, established by the late National Living Treasure Alonzo Saclag and his wife, Rebecca Saclag.

Recognized in 2000 for his contributions to Kalinga performing arts and dance traditions, Saclag devoted much of his life to promoting the culture of his people.

His wife continues to share that work with visitors.

A craftswoman demonstrates traditional beadmaking at Awichon Cultural Village in Lubuagan, Kalinga.

Rebecca Saclag personally guided the caravan through traditional houses, weaving and beadmaking activities, and other features of Kalinga community life.

She explained that their family had helped recreate traditional houses so younger generations could see the forms of architecture that have become less common as households build modern homes.

“Ginawa namin para makita ninyo (We did it for you to see),” she told the visitors.

She also showed the group wild fruit trees she had planted during the COVID-19 pandemic, recalling the difficulty of finding fruits rich in vitamin C.

Her stories brought an intimate dimension to Awichon. Cultural preservation involves the efforts of families who spend years building, collecting, teaching, and sharing what they know.

The visitors also enjoyed local dishes prepared by the Pasil Slow Food Community, accompanied by cultural performances.

Later that afternoon, the caravan reached Bontoc, Mountain Province, where the Bontoc Museum offered another encounter with the region’s history.

A cultural welcome preceded the visit, which included traditional houses, rice granaries, and displays explaining Bontoc customs and community institutions such as the ato, historically a gathering place for elders and community affairs.

Traditional stone-and-thatch structures and a sculpted figure are among the outdoor displays at the Bontoc Museum.

By evening, the group arrived at Mount Data Hotel in Bauko.

It was there that Nabunat, representing a Philippine Cordillera organization based in Sydney, expressed her gratitude for the journey.

“We truly felt at home in every city and barangay across the provinces,” she said.

She also spoke of responsible tourism and the possibility of helping promote the Cordillera to overseas communities.

Her enthusiasm was evident. But beyond the warm welcomes and cultural experiences was a question that tourism destinations across the region continue to confront.

How can growing visitor numbers translate into lasting benefits for residents while protecting the resources, traditions, and everyday life that make these places worth visiting?

The caravan’s final stop offered a practical example.

From stopover to destination

On October 20, the participants arrived at Northern Blossom Flower Farm in Atok, Benguet.

The farm’s sweeping mountain views were familiar to many visitors through photographs and social media, although its famous flower displays were not yet at their peak.

Owner Mellany Ganayan explained that the main blooming season generally runs from December to June. The farm grows more than 30 varieties of flowers, including hydrangeas, carnations, snapdragons, and calla lilies.

Before becoming a tourist attraction, Northern Blossom was primarily a commercial flower farm.

That changed after photographs circulated online and television programs featured the property in 2018, attracting visitors eager to experience Atok’s landscape.

“We were known as a stopover before,” Ganayan said, referring to Atok’s former role as a place travelers passed through on their way to Bontoc or Sagada.

“But now we’re not just a stopover. We are a destination.”

The growth in tourism has brought employment and business opportunities.

Even between peak blooming seasons, Northern Blossom Flower Farm in Atok, Benguet, offers sweeping views of the Cordillera mountains.

Ganayan said the farm once had around seven workers, but now employs more than 30. It also provides seasonal opportunities for student guides and workers.

She recalled that Atok had about 11 lodging establishments and homestays in 2023, compared with approximately 47 at the time of the visit.

As more tourists began arriving, she said, residents saw opportunities to improve their houses and offer accommodation.

The figures reflect Ganayan’s account of local tourism growth.

Yet increased visitor numbers also mean greater demands on resources, particularly water.

Ganayan said warmer daytime temperatures and dry periods have increased the farm’s irrigation needs, while tourists add to water consumption.

She illustrated the problem with a simple calculation. If 1,000 visitors each used three liters of water for a toilet flush, that would mean 3,000 liters consumed. Two flushes per visitor would require 6,000 liters.

For a farm whose primary business still depends on growing flowers, that is a considerable amount of water.

Ganayan said they are exploring additional water tanks, water-saving toilets, and the reuse of wastewater for irrigation.

Northern Blossom also closes on Sundays, partly to give workers and the surrounding community time for church and other personal activities.

The farm’s experience shows both sides of tourism growth.

More visitors can mean more jobs, homestays, and income. But sustaining those benefits requires planning, investment, and consideration for the community’s needs.

Coming home, and wanting to return

By the time the caravan ended in Benguet, the participants had spent four days meeting people whose daily work sustains the places that attract visitors.

They had walked through rice terraces maintained by farmers, watched weavers at their looms, listened to cultural workers share their knowledge, and learned how a flower-growing community was adapting to increasing tourism.

For Nabunat and the other overseas Cordillerans, the journey was particularly personal.

They had returned to familiar mountains but encountered stories and traditions they had not fully known.

Traditional Kalinga dishes prepared by the Pasil Slow Food Community are served in clay pots lined with banana leaves at Awichon Cultural Village in Lubuagan, Kalinga.

At Mount Data, Nabunat said the experience had deepened their interest in their heritage and strengthened their desire to help promote the region overseas.

She also expressed hope that tourism could create opportunities while respecting the culture and way of life of host communities.

The enthusiasm of returning Cordillerans is an opportunity for the region, although turning it into lasting benefits will depend on how communities are supported and how tourism develops.

Back in Atok, Ganayan and her workers were preparing for another flowering season, with irrigation, maintenance, and water conservation among their concerns.

The next blooms were still weeks away.

For the balikbayans, meanwhile, the journey had ended with new memories, more questions about their heritage, and reasons to come home again. – Rappler.com

World.title: Tovera-led La Salle wins 3rd straight as rival Ateneo falls in OT thriller
World.content:
RIVALS. La Salle’s star rookie Joaquin Tovera shoots over Ateneo captain Ian Espinosa during the two teams’ rivalry match in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament.

Super rookie Joaquin Tovera shines with a heroic performance as La Salle trumps rival Ateneo in overtime to stay undefeated in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament second round

MANILA, Philippines – La Salle rookie Joaquin Tovera again stayed ahead of his learning curve in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament as he led the Green Archers to a thrilling 76-73 overtime escape of rivals Ateneo Blue Eagles at the Araneta Coliseum on Saturday, October 31.

Before succumbing to a non-contact ankle roll in the final minute of a heated extra period, Tovera willed La Salle with game-highs of 21 points and 6 assists to go with 7 rebounds as the Green Archers broke a standings deadlock with the Blue Eagles to go third at 6-4.

Veteran guard JC Macalalag led a balanced scoring effort behind Tovera with 11 points in nearly 39 minutes of action, as six other La Salle players tallied at least 5 points.

“When the game went to overtime, we just reminded everybody about what we discussed before the game and we talked about our dreams,” said Archers head coach Topex Robinson.

“In every moment, the strongest dream will win that moment, so we all dream about playing in the De La Salle-Ateneo rivalry. These guys just showed up and they believed in what we prepared for.”

Ateneo young stars Jared Bahay and super rookie Kieffer Alas paced the heartbreaking loss with 18 points apiece — with all their efforts nullified as they failed to link up on a basic inbounds pass that gave the ball back to the Green Archers with 3.3 seconds left in overtime.

Play Video

Shawn Tuano added 12 points and 6 rebounds, while Travis Roberts likewise scored 12 on a 5-of-17 clip, as the Blue Eagles tripped down a 5-5 slate for fifth place in a hyper-competitive field still featuring seven realistic Final Four contenders.

Rising NU keeps UST skidding

In the previous game of the loaded double-header, the NU Bulldogs strengthened its hold of second place with a scrappy 75-71 escape of the reeling UST Growling Tigers for a 7-3 record — half a game behind 7-2 UP.

Head coach Jeff Napa once again worked his magic on big men as star foreign student-athlete Mo Diassana tallied a huge 16-point, 19-rebound double-double, backstopped by 14 markers and 6 boards in just 15 minutes from MVP candidate PJ Palacielo.

Burly big Kenshin Padrones added his own double-double of 13 points and 12 rebounds, while Tebol Garcia topscored the NU back court with 12 points, 7 boards, and a game-high 6 assists, making up for MVP frontrunner Reinhard Jumamoy’s lackluster 6-point showing.

Amiel Acido and Mark Llemit paced the losing cause with 13 and 12 points, respectively, while star center Collins Akowe was limited to 11 points on 2-of-7 shooting with just 5 rebounds in 33 minutes.

Amid a heavily-contested elimination round, UST plummeted to a 4-6 card at seventh place with a costly third straight loss, while still being just two games behind No. 3 La Salle.

The Scores

First Game

NU 75 – Diasanna 16, Palacielo 14, Padrones 13, Garcia 12, Jumamoy 6, Reyes 6, Francisco 5, Cartel 3, Alfanta 0, Miranda 0, Figueroa 0, Solomon 0, Serrano 0.

UST 71 – Acido 13, Llemit 12, Akowe 11, Chio 11, Porter 8, Buenaflor 6, Jumawan 5, Sevilla 3, Cañete 2, Danting 0, Alao 0, Manding 0.

Quarters: 24-18, 40-39, 57-57, 75-71.

Second Game

La Salle 76 – Tovera 21, Macalalag 11, Dungo 8, Amos 8, Agunanne 8, Marasigan 6, Pablo 5, Abadam 5, Quines 2, Gagate 2, Cortez 0.

Ateneo 73 – Bahay 18, Alas 18, Tuano 12, Roberts 12, Kapihe 6, Baruwa 3, Espinosa 2, Rogers 2, Bongo 0, Cainglet 0, Espina 0, Leal 0.

Quarters: 17-20, 41-37, 51-48, 66-66 (reg.), 76-73 (OT).

– Rappler.com

World.title: France braces for fresh unrest, government vows tough response
World.content:
POLICE PREPARATIONS. French gendarmerie and police officers gather near Arc de Triomphe on the day of a demonstration organized by labor unions as part of nationwide protests called by the 'Yellow Vests' movement joined by French high school and university students against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in Paris, France, October 31, 2026.

Some 150 gatherings are planned across France, the interior ministry says

PARIS, France – France deployed a 70,000-strong police presence to contain a widely expected bout of fresh unrest on Saturday, October 31, in the latest nationwide protests driven by anger over living costs, public services and President Emmanuel Macron’s government.

The demonstrations, which fall on Halloween, come two weeks after riots and looting caught security forces off guard, leaving damaged shops, public buildings, and businesses in cities across France. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has vowed not to let a repeat happen.

“Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble,” Nunez told a news conference earlier this week as he set out details of security arrangements for a day he described as carrying “a very high risk” of unrest.

France’s top administrative court confirmed on Saturday a march between the emblematic Paris squares of Republique and Bastille will be banned, rejecting a challenge by unions. Demonstrations will instead have to be held on boulevards on the eastern fringe of the city, away from the main shopping areas in central Paris.

Authorities are also alert to the possibility that rioters could use Halloween masks to conceal their identities. Nunez noted that laws already allow police to ban face coverings when public order is at risk.

Some 150 gatherings were planned across France, the interior ministry said.

The US Embassy advised travellers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings are planned.

The protests gathered pace in late September as Macron’s minority government launched 2027 budget talks. Facing public debt approaching 120% of economic output and rising borrowing costs, the government is under pressure to rein in spending, narrowing its room for manoeuvre.

Students angry at the dilapidated state of many schools, crowded classes and a university admissions system widely seen as unfair, have been joined by trade unions and a re-emergent “Yellow Vest” movement demanding action on the cost of living.

Protests spread across Europe

The protests have inspired youth-led protests across Europe, with demonstrations planned in more than 30 German cities on Saturday.

The French government’s promises to reform education and ease fuel costs have failed to calm discontent.

“When I was little, I was told young people were the future,” said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student in the Paris suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne who plans to join his third consecutive weekend of protests.

“Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing.”

The unrest has handed a political boost to far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of April’s presidential election, while potential centrist successors to Macron remain divided.

The troubles are the latest blow to an economy which, data on Friday showed, was already shrinking in the third quarter.

The Chamber of Commerce estimates losses to retailers exceed €1 billion ($1.1 billion). Other estimates put the total at double that when including uninsured damage and lost revenue.

Along Paris’ main shopping boulevards, early Christmas lights glow around boarded-up windows and security grilles. Among the shops targeted in previous unrest were outlets belonging to luxury brands including Hermes, Louis Vuitton, and Burberry.

The government is pushing ahead with a controversial law making rioters liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused either by themselves or by groups they are deemed to be part of. Rights groups and some lawyers say the measure risks undermining the right to peaceful protest. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Hope and help’: How the Philippines fights to lower breast cancer deaths
World.content:
While treatments for late-stage breast cancer have reached the Philippines, medical professionals point out that making them available is vastly different from making them affordable and accessible

MANILA, Philippines – There’s a bold ambition in global cancer research to eliminate breast cancer as a cause of death.

And it’s this goal that has transformed cancer treatment over the years, even making Stage 4 or metastatic breast cancer — when the cancer has spread to distant organs like the bones, lungs, liver, or brain — more manageable.

“It’s important for people to know that metastatic breast cancer is not a death sentence,” said Dr. Marvin Mendoza, head of medical oncology and ambulatory infusion therapy unit of the National Kidney and Transplant Institute.

“It’s really very different from before, like the ’90s. We now have a lot of options.”

“The medical advancement in cancer is really fast. There’s a lot of investment in innovative medicine,” added Dr. Kriska Lim, medical affairs head of oncology for AstraZeneca Philippines.

“Most people think when it’s metastatic breast cancer, they won’t get treatment anymore. But even people with this cancer can live meaningful lives if they get the right treatment and the right support.”

But there are still a lot of hurdles doctors and breast cancer advocates face when dealing with Filipino patients.

For instance, some patients diagnosed at advanced stages abandon standard treatment and turn to alternative remedies, believing these will cure them. Others refuse biopsy on a suspected tumor, fearing the procedure will cause it to spread.

Kara Magsanoc-Alikpala, co-founder of the ICanServe Foundation — which helps breast cancer patients by connecting them to medical specialists, educational resources, and support groups — said there are many misconceptions in local communities.

“Common ‘yung nakakahawa ang breast cancer (The belief that breast cancer is contagious is common). A lot of husbands distance themselves, it’s so common in communities,” she shared.

“There’s also the use of underwire bra and deodorants, we still get that. And the biopsy, ’pag ginalaw, kakalat (if moved, it might spread), it’s so common.”

The lack of breast cancer awareness and education remains one of the reasons the Philippines ranks poorly in global breast cancer statistics.

In the US, around 66% of breast cancer patients from 2019 to 2023 were “diagnosed at a localized stage, meaning the cancer had not spread outside the breast.” This early detection results in a higher survival rate, according to the United States Cancer Statistics.

Unfortunately, that isn’t the case in the Philippines.

“We’re so far from that. We’re the total opposite,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala. “Around 65% of breast cancer here is diagnosed at an advanced stage, Stage 3 or 4.”

Breast cancer remains the most common occurring cancer among Filipinos, according to the 2024 statistics of the International Agency for Research on Cancer of the World Health Organization (WHO).

It’s the second highest cause of death among Filipino cancer patients in both sexes at 12.9%, just behind lung cancer (13.6%).

In Asia, the Philippines also ranks in the top six for both breast cancer incidence and mortality in 2024, according to WHO.

“We really want breast cancer, and all cancers in general, to have enough attention. In AstraZeneca, our bold ambition is to eliminate breast cancer as a cause of death,” said Lim.

“Recently, breast cancer is no longer the top cause of death. For it to happen, there’s a lot of things we have to look into. We recognize that it’s not enough that we bring the medicines in, it’s not enough that we invest. We’re supposed to work with like-minded organizations and really help the country move forward.”

“We do have advanced lines of treatment for metastatic breast cancer. It’s not just chemotherapy. There are a lot of targeted therapies now made available,” added Mendoza.

“Of course, made available is different from made affordable and accessible. But it’s one thing that they’re already here. We have to do the work to make it affordable for more patients, because treatment can take years or even a lifetime.“

Medical professionals and advocates admit there are still many gaps even as the government expanded the PhilHealth Z Benefit, the health package that covers catastrophic and high-cost medical conditions.

“The biggest program is the PhilHealth Z Benefit package, but the sites and hospitals that offer it are still limited. That’s why the lines are so long,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala.

Other government programs to help alleviate medical costs include the YAKAP program, which covers cancer screening tests, and the Cancer Assistance Fund under the National Integrated Cancer Control Act, which covers specialized treatments and palliative care.

“There are many initiatives from the government, medical society, and private institutions, but it has to reach the communities. That’s the main barrier,” said Mendoza.

“If people don’t know about the program and initiatives, how to access them, it doesn’t complete the loop. There are still many people who haven’t been reached.”

While a lack of awareness about government programs often leads to late diagnosis and poorer outcomes, navigating the required paperwork once assistance is found presents an entirely different challenge.

“Kailangan pa rin ng kumpas ng gobyerno para mas ma-improve pa (The government needs to provide direction to improve it),” said Mendoza.

For now, some private institutions try to fill in the gaps, with the ICanServe Foundation, for instance, running its Ating Dibdibin (Take Your Breast Care to Heart) flagship program.

“We partner with local government, usually a city, then we institutionalize the program. It’s a community-based breast cancer control program with the aim of saving lives,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala.

“We bring services to the barangays instead of expecting them to go to the hospital. It’s proactive, going house to house, checking on women, because sometimes they don’t know where to go. We make sure there’s a clear pathway, there are patient navigators to hand-hold the patients.”

Lowering breast cancer deaths in the Philippines through early detection remains the key message among advocates, who hope that conversations would go beyond the Breast Cancer Awareness Month every October.

“The government should really have a national campaign. It’s the same message every year — early detection,” said Magsanoc-Alikpala.

“We really need to be intentional in the way we promote our message, not only early detection, but there’s hope even if your cancer is diagnosed at a later stage.”

“I want everyone to know there’s hope and help,” she added.

“There’s the medical world, their supportive care. The government has some help — it’s not enough, but it’s a big help as well. There are foundations willing to help patients. But take charge of your health. Get screened. When you’re young, that’s the best time to find out.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Scams from false claims: How to spot them
World.content:
Here’s a guide to identify whether the post you’re seeing on social media is a phishing site or scam

MANILA, Philippines – False claims and online scams are working hand in hand to trick users on social media.

From false advertising to fake government aid, false news peddlers include links in their posts that redirect users to spoofed websites to steal sensitive information.
