What the law says

Article 13 of Georgia’s Law on Combating Corruption restricts public officials from engaging in business activities and managing private companies. The aim is to separate public and private economic interests and reduce the risk of conflicts of interest.

At the same time, the law allows public officials to own shares in commercial enterprises, which gives them a different legal status from that of a company director.

Transparency International Georgia argues that simultaneously holding public office and managing a private company creates corruption risks. The organisation calls on the government to take action in accordance with the law.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s ferroalloy exports to Spain fall 41.4% in eight months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 1. Kazakhstan’s ferroalloy exports to Spain fell by 41.4% year-on-year in volume terms during January-August 2026, reaching 14,184 tonnes compared with 24,196 tonnes in the same period of 2025, according to Trend’s calculations based on data from the Bureau of National Statistics of Kazakhstan.

In value terms, ferroalloy exports to Spain declined by 37.0% year-on-year to $19.95 million from $31.65 million recorded in the first eight months of 2025.

In total, Kazakhstan exported 1.05 million tonnes of ferroalloys in January-August 2026, down 16.8% compared with 1.26 million tonnes in the same period of 2025.

In value terms, ferroalloy exports declined by 6.16% year-on-year to $1.36 billion from $1.45 billion. China remained the largest destination for Kazakh ferroalloys, receiving 631,220 tonnes worth $704.5 million during the first eight months of 2026.

Japan ranked second, importing 127,485 tonnes valued at $213.2 million. Other major destinations included the United States, with 72,179 tonnes worth $135.7 million; Germany, with 28,042 tonnes worth $53.5 million; Russia, with 37,759 tonnes worth $47.7 million; Italy, with 20,716 tonnes worth $33.5 million; and South Korea, with 22,518 tonnes worth $31.3 million. Indonesia, Spain, the Netherlands and the Czech Republic were also among the main buyers.

In August 2026, Kazakhstan exported 102,127 tonnes of ferroalloys worth $145.49 million.

Kazakhstan’s foreign trade turnover reached $102.96 billion in January-August 2026, up 12.8% in nominal terms compared with the same period of 2025.

Exports totaled $60.39 billion, increasing by 19.5% in nominal terms, while imports reached $42.57 billion, up 4.5%.

Crude oil and crude oil products obtained from bituminous minerals accounted for 49.8% of Kazakhstan’s exports in January-August 2026. Other major export commodities included refined copper and unwrought copper alloys (6.4%), radioactive chemical elements and radioactive isotopes (5.1%), copper ores and concentrates (4.4%), and ferroalloys (2.2%).

Passenger cars and other motor vehicles accounted for the largest share of imports, at 3.3%. Other major imported commodities included telephone equipment (2.7%), pharmaceutical products (2.5%), petroleum gases and other gaseous hydrocarbons (2.4%), and electric generating sets and rotary converters (2.2%).

Italy was Kazakhstan’s largest export destination, accounting for 18% of exports, followed by China (17.6%), Russia (8.5%), Türkiye (7.9%), France (6.1%) and the Netherlands (5.9%).

Russia was Kazakhstan’s largest import partner, accounting for 31% of imports, followed by China (29.8%), Germany (4.6%), the United States (3.9%), South Korea (2.5%) and Türkiye (2.1%).

World.title: Uzbekneftegaz reports 5.9% industrial output growth in nine months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 1. Uzbekneftegaz reported industrial output worth 41.8 trillion soms (about $3.5 billion) in January-September 2026, up 5.9% year over year, as the company expanded production of petroleum products and other industrial materials.

This was stated in the press release by Uzbekneftegaz.

The company produced 773,500 metric tons of gasoline, 759,700 tons of diesel fuel, 210,600 tons of jet fuel and 452,700 tons of liquefied gas during the nine months. Its output also included 135,100 tons of sulfur and 101,300 tons of polyethylene granules.

According to Trend’s calculations, the six listed products totaled 2.43 million tons. Gasoline and diesel together accounted for 1.53 million tons, or approximately 63.2% of the combined volume. These figures cover only the products listed and do not represent the company’s total industrial output.

Uzbekneftegaz is also planning to expand its product range by launching domestic production of synthetic oils, refined paraffin and linear alkylbenzene (LAB), a raw material used in household chemicals and synthetic detergents.

The company expects the new products to replace some imports, support domestic manufacturers and create opportunities to expand exports. However, it has not announced production launch dates, planned capacities or investment requirements for the projects.

Ahead of the winter season, Uzbekneftegaz also reported that gasoline inventories at its oil depots were 2.5 times higher than a year earlier, indicating a larger stockpile than in the same period of 2025. The company did not disclose the absolute volume of the inventories.

The production expansion and planned introduction of new refined products form part of Uzbekistan’s efforts to strengthen domestic supply and broaden the range of higher-value industrial goods.

World.title: Iran's Bushehr Province exports $3.59B in goods in seven months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 1. A total of 7.3 million tons of products, valued at $3.59 billion, were exported through the customs offices of Iran's Bushehr Province to 33 countries from March 21 through October 22, 2026.

This was reported by the General Customs Administration of Iran's Bushehr Province, citing the remarks of the provincial customs supervisor, Reza Mehrjuyi.

He added that there are 13 active customs offices operating in the Persian Gulf region of Bushehr Province.

The customs representative pointed out that, during the specified period, the majority of exports through Bushehr Province’s customs offices were destined for China; specifically, 62% of the total exports handled by these offices were sent to China.

Mehrjuyi said that, over the course of seven months, goods valued at $13.2 million were exported to Qatar through the province's customs offices. These exports primarily consisted of agricultural products, food items, and minerals.

He noted that exports from Bushehr Province to Russia consist mainly of fish and fish products, including shrimp.

"Despite the current challenges facing Iran's international trade, priority remains placed on ensuring that the country's needs are met in a timely manner and that raw materials are delivered to manufacturing enterprises," he remarked.

According to Trend’s analysis of statistics from the Customs Administration of Iran, trade turnover through the customs offices of Bushehr Province from March 21, 2025, through March 20, 2026, amounted to 31.2 million tons, valued at $16.3 billion. During this period, 30 million tons of goods worth $11 billion were exported, while 1.2 million tons of goods valued at $5.3 billion were imported through the customs offices of Bushehr Province.

World.title: Georgia's gas imports from Azerbaijan rise 5.3% to $178.4M in eight months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 1. The value of natural gas imports by Georgia from Azerbaijan reached $178.4 million in the first eight months of 2026.

This was reported by Azerbaijan’s State Statistics Committee.

According to the data, compared with January-August 2025, the value of imports increased by more than $8.9 million, or 5.3%.

The volume of natural gas imported by Georgia from Azerbaijan amounted to 1.6 billion cubic meters, up 81.9 million cubic meters, or 5.3%, year-on-year.

Overall, Azerbaijan exported approximately 16.378 billion cubic meters of natural gas worth $5.711 billion to eight countries from January through August 2026. According to Trend’s calculations based on data from the State Customs Committee, compared with the same period in 2025, the value of exports decreased by $286 million, or 4.8%, while the volume fell by 75.1 million cubic meters, or 0.5%.

Meanwhile, Azerbaijan imported natural gas exclusively from Iran during the first eight months of 2026, totaling 215.022 million cubic meters worth $14.471 million. From January through August 2025, Azerbaijan imported 233.303 million cubic meters of natural gas worth $36.321 million from Russia and Turkmenistan.

As a result, the value of natural gas imports decreased by $21.850 million, or approximately 60.2%, while the volume fell by 18.281 million cubic meters, or 7.8%, year-on-year.

From January through August 2026, Azerbaijan produced 33.407 billion cubic meters of natural gas, down 177.4 million cubic meters, or 0.5%, from 33.584 billion cubic meters in the same period of 2025.

Marketable natural gas production amounted to 25.610 billion cubic meters, a decrease of 221.5 million cubic meters, or 0.9%, compared with 25.831 billion cubic meters a year earlier.

Thus, total natural gas production declined by 0.5%, while marketable gas production fell by 0.9%.

According to the State Statistics Committee, the total value of output in Azerbaijan’s extractive industry amounted to 26.9 billion manats ($15.8 billion) from January through August 2026. Production in the sector decreased by 1.1% in real terms compared with the same period of 2025.

Natural gas accounted for 26.18% of Azerbaijan’s total exports during the first eight months of 2026.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan expands Bishkek-Kuntuu-Shopokov road to four lanes
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Ministry of Transport and Communications of the Kyrgyz Republic

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 1. Reconstruction of the Bishkek-Kuntuu-Shopokov road is underway in Kyrgyzstan, with the 12.4-kilometer route being expanded to four lanes.

According to the Ministry of Transport and Communications of the Kyrgyz Republic, workers are continuing to lay the second layer of asphalt using stone mastic asphalt technology along the section between kilometers 5 and 6.

More than 30 units of specialized machinery and over 70 workers are currently involved in the project.

The Bishkek-Kuntuu-Shopokov road is one of the important transport routes in the Sokuluk district. The reconstruction aims to improve road infrastructure, create more convenient conditions for traffic, and enhance safety for residents and drivers.

Furthermore, the quality of the road construction work is being monitored by the Ministry of Transport and Communications of the Kyrgyz Republic.

Trend estimates that the reconstruction of the Bishkek–Kuntuu–Shopokov road could improve traffic flow and transport connectivity in Sokuluk district. Widening the road and upgrading its pavement are expected to facilitate vehicle movement, improve driving conditions, and reduce the likelihood of disruptions caused by inadequate road infrastructure. The improvements could also make journeys more predictable for residents and commercial transport operators.

According to Trend’s calculations, if the upgraded road reduces average travel time by an estimated 5–10%, regular users could benefit from shorter journeys and lower time-related transport costs. If traffic demand subsequently increases by around 3–5% annually, the expanded road could provide additional capacity to accommodate growing vehicle flows.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: November 1, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 1. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist," on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Trend presents the chronicle of the Second Karabakh War for November 1, 2020:

- President Ilham Aliyev received a delegation led by the Turkish Foreign Minister.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry released information on the latest situation in the frontline as of November 1.

- A list of destroyed military equipment of the Armenian Armed Forces was announced.

- Armenia violated a ceasefire on the state border.

- The Armenian Armed Forces shelled the territory of Tartar and Aghjabadi districts.

- A video of the destruction of Armenian military trucks loaded with ammunition was released.

- Two ‘Grad’ missile systems of the Armenian Armed Forces were destroyed.

World.title: Two more Azerbaijani judokas become European Champions as National Team tops overall standings
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 31. Azerbaijani national team members Ajdar Baghirov and Kenan Nasibov have won gold medals at the European Judo Championships among athletes under 23 (U-23), held in Naples, Italy.

According to the Azerbaijan Judo Federation, Ajdar Baghirov, competing in the under-100 kg weight category, defeated Germany’s Yannis Baschin in the final to claim the European title. On his way to the decisive bout, the Azerbaijani judoka defeated Ivan Kutenkov (Ukraine), Borna Butijer (Croatia) and Ronald Pröl (Austria).

Kenan Nasibov, competing in the over-100 kg category, also finished the day undefeated. He defeated Serbia’s Vidak Maljevic in the final, successfully defended his title and became U-23 European champion for the second consecutive time. On his way to the final, Nasibov overcame Luka Ivankovic (Croatia), Yan Rigo (France) and Morteza Suhani (Germany).

Thus, the Azerbaijani national team finished the individual competition with three gold medals and took first place in the overall team standings. Earlier, Islam Rahimov (under-66 kg) had also become U-23 European champion for the second consecutive time.

World.title: FBI accuses North Korea of Binance hack
World.content:
The FBI has accused North Korea of stealing $US6.3 billion n ($6.9 million) in virtual assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what is thought to be the biggest crypto heist in history.

In a statement, the US bureau said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the "malicious cyber activity".

On Thursday, $US6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack.

The FBI's statement came as Binance offered reassurances it was covering the losses from the hacking attack, saying it has used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90 per cent of what was stolen.

The FBI made the announcement on Saturday, local time. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.

"The FBI maintains its commitment to protecting the virtual asset community by identifying, mitigating, and disrupting North Korea's illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities," it said.

It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called Ethereum.

Zhao Changpeng is the founder and chief executive officer of Binance. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

The FBI said it expects TraderTraitor would now attempt to convert the assets using de-centralised finance (DeFi) and "instant swap services".

"It is expected these assets will then be further laundered," it said.

They are the same actors behind a $US1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.

'Cat and mouse game' of tracking assets

Crypto expert and chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs Ari Redbord said he expected the hackers would break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months.

A crypto expert says he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them. (Unsplash: Executium)

"It's bank robbery, in this case, at the speed of the internet," Mr Redbord said.

"However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds.

"It's just this cat and mouse game."

90 per cent of assets recovered, Binance says

On Saturday, Binance said it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen, to cover 90 per cent of the missing assets.

"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X.

It said the outstanding 10 per cent consists of tokens that are less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts.

Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but said in its latest update that they were on track to resume Sunday.

Reuters/AFP/AP

World.title: Fifty years on, Julius Dam continues to sustain outback communities
World.content:
In 1971, a devastating drought exposed a serious problem in the outback mining city of Mount Isa. Despite having a major dam, the city was running short of water.

Lake Moondarra, built by Mount Isa Mines in 1958 on the Leichhardt River north of town, was Australia's largest, privately-funded water scheme at the time.

But as the city and its mining industry grew, the drought exposed a need for another reliable water source.

The solution was unveiled five years later with the completion of Julius Dam, about 70 kilometres north-east of Mount Isa, at the junction of the Leichhardt River and Paroo Creek.

The North-West Star declared "No more water worries" when Julius Dam was officially commissioned on October 8, 1976. (Supplied: North-West Star)

An engineering solution built for the outback

Constructed by Thiess Brothers, Julius Dam required hundreds of workers, including people from Scotland, England and Ireland, some of whom lived on site with their families.

Building a structure with a 220-metre spillway in remote Queensland had significant challenges.

Hundreds of workers helped construct Julius Dam between 1973 and 1976, overcoming the challenges of building in remote North West Queensland. (Supplied: Sunwater)

Engineers chose a concrete multiple-arch and buttress design that reduced the amount of material needed while maintaining the dam's strength.

The design helped overcome the difficulties of building in the outback, according to current operator Sunwater.

"Because of its remoteness, because of the difficulty of getting materials in, that's the reason they decided to go with that structure," north region general manager of operations, William Weaver said.

Julius Dam's distinctive multiple-arch and buttress design reduced the amount of concrete required for construction. (Supplied: Sunwater)

Sunwater says it remains the only dam of its kind in Queensland.

But another feature caught the attention of University of Queensland geotechnical engineering professor Alexander Scheuermann.

"The first thing I thought when I saw the dam was, 'Where's the spillway?'" he said.

Professor Alexander Scheuermann says Julius Dam's unique design allows floodwater to flow directly over its structure. (Supplied: Alexander Scheuermann)

Unlike dams with a separate spillway, Julius Dam's concrete, 18m wide arches allow excess water to flow directly over the structure.

"When the water rises higher than the dam is, it simply overtops the dam without harming the structure," Professor Scheuermann said.

Julius Dam: By the numbers Construction: 1973–1976

1973–1976 Dam wall length: 399 metres

399 metres Maximum height: 34 metres

34 metres Spillway length: 220 metres

220 metres Span of each arch: 18.3 metres

18.3 metres Concrete used: 45,000 cubic metres

45,000 cubic metres Storage capacity: 107,500 megalitres (Sunwater)

107,500 megalitres (Sunwater) Design: Multiple-arch and buttress

Multiple-arch and buttress Main contractor: Thiess Brothers Sources: Original Julius Dam engineering plaque and Sunwater.

A reliable water source for the North West

Julius Dam can hold 107,500 megalitres of water, equivalent to about one-fifth of Sydney Harbour's volume.

While originally developed to supplement Mount Isa's water supply, its role has expanded over the past five decades.

The 113-kilometre North West Queensland Water Pipeline, completed in 1998, supplies mining operations including the Ernest Henry copper and gold mine near Cloncurry.

Another 38km pipeline was completed in 2010 following a drought, providing Cloncurry with an additional year-round water supply.

Lake Moondarra remains Mount Isa's main water source, with Julius Dam providing supplementary water when needed.

Julius Dam's built-in spillway allows excess water to flow directly over its concrete arches during periods of heavy rainfall. (Supplied: Sunwater)

Despite the region's long dry periods, Mr Weaver said Julius Dam had spilled every year for the past decade.

He attributed its reliability to seasonal monsoonal and cyclonic rainfall regularly replenishing the Leichhardt River catchment.

"What Lake Julius does is it gives you that real assurance and real surety of supply," he said.

"And that's allowed Mount Isa and its industry to grow."

William Weaver says Julius Dam remains a vital water source for North West Queensland. (Supplied: Sunwater )

Built to last another 50 years

While Julius Dam has operated for five decades, Professor Scheuermann said ongoing maintenance would be essential to its future.

He said dams could remain operational for more than a century, but changing rainfall patterns, extreme weather and future water demand would need to be considered as infrastructure aged.

"So you need to have the skilled labour and also the engineers who are able to assess the safety of the dam."

Julius Dam spilling before construction was completed in 1976. (Supplied: Sunwater)

Mr Weaver said a seven-person team based in Cloncurry operated and maintained the dam and its associated pipelines.

For a structure tucked away in a remote stretch of the Leichhardt River, its contribution reaches far beyond the water it holds.

"It's one of those little hidden gems that most people don't even know exists because it's tucked away in the middle of nowhere," Mr Weaver said.

"So it's a hidden gem, but it certainly does a great job."

World.title: WA rapper pays tribute to family's land rights battle, defends lyrics
World.content:
When Western Australian rapper Kurrungaya Bieundurry stumbled across a photo of his grandfather standing proudly as part of a landmark land rights protest, inspiration struck hard.

WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are advised the images in this article contain people who are deceased.

He knew immediately he wanted it as the cover of what would become his debut album, Bunuba Baby.

That album reached number 2 on the Australian hip hop charts within a week of its August release and has since been nominated for a major Australian music award.

It draws on his family's fight for land rights which he hopes will encourage younger mob to connect with their culture.

Bieundurry, known professionally as Kayps, had already written two songs for the album when he found the photo of his grandfather, who helped organise a blockade against an oil company wanting to drill a sacred site.

That moment, known as the historic 1979 Noonkanbah protest, galvanised the Kimberley land rights movement.

Kayps was immediately drawn to this photograph taken during the Noonkanbah blockade, featuring his grandfather. (Supplied: KAYPS)

"The mob up there — including my grandfather who is in that photo and a lot of my uncles and great-uncles as well — stood and locked arms and refused to let these big drilling trucks come in,” he said.

Ultimately the company broke the blockade but as Kayps notes, "they found nothing after they tore up all that land."

The album's artwork represents three generations of his family.

Police broke up the blockade at Mickey's Pool on Noonkanbah Station, arresting 22 people. (Supplied: Michael Gallagher)

"My dad painted the Pirlirr — the Indigenous symbol — on the cover art. That's his design, that's our family symbol," he said.

Now he's exploring his own identity and uncovering his political voice.

Community music roots

Born in Broome and raised in Wangkatjungka, a remote Kimberley town of around 200 residents, Kayps remembers his upbringing as the "perfect community environment".

"Every Friday, all the family would catch up at maybe one of the 20 houses in Wangkatjungka, just sitting around, everybody's singing," he said.

Kayps' grandmother was a blues artist and his father a guitarist and singer. (Supplied: KAYPS/Billy Zammit)

"You're looking at over 50 to 75 people meeting somewhere on this rundown basketball court in the middle of Wangkatjungka."

That sense of community and its shared love of singing country, blues and gospel music has driven him ever since.

Kayps and his family moved to Perth when he was about five, but it wasn't until he was 13 that he discovered the world of hip-hop.

Rising rapper

To afford music production software, he busked at the Kalamunda farmers market, playing the didgeridoo.

Rapping on his own beats, he performed to a live crowd in Fremantle for the first time later that year.

Kayps is performing his album part of a national tour. (Supplied: KAYPS)

"I got the loudest cheer of the night and that was the coolest thing for me ever," he said.

But during high school he found himself struggling as the only black student in his year.

Kayps says it was challenging moving to a predominantly white community in Perth. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

"I wanted to get braids to express myself ... and they were like 'oh that's too extreme', which is like the nice way of saying it's too black," he said.

"Being so far away from home — it's really hard, especially when you have no other representation for yourself."

Changing his tune

Kayps, 21, said the lyrics on Bunuba Baby have evolved and are more politically charged than his previous work.

He acknowledged earlier projects like 'Nuisance' and 'Mimosa' were "abrasive", featuring misogynistic and violent lyrics, and reflected his young age.

"I can't stand listening to them," he said, describing them as "disrespectful" and "awful".

Kayps says his voice has evolved on the new project. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

He said other songs like 'Blackfella', which he made aged 13, were a product of the music he was consuming at the time.

Late night conversations with his uncle and father — discussing issues in the community, his culture and responsibilities — shape his newer work.

Kayps doesn't shy away from controversy on Bunuba Baby, especially his lyrics about police.

The artist says his poltical voice has grown stronger in recent years. (Supplied: KAYPS)

"A lot of the lyrics of police are intentional because that is a sub-branch of the systemic oppression that First Nations people face," he said.

"Indigenous deaths in custody as well, the statistics are there."

Connecting with culture

He hopes Bunuba Baby inspires younger people to explore connecting with culture, particularly those who have grown up away from country.

"I hope mob will walk away from it [the album] feeling like it's not too late to go on that journey," he said.

" If you feel disconnected and want to reconnect, do it at your own pace. "

Kayps says he no longer pretends to be a scary rapper when posing for photos. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Back home, Kayps hopes to conduct workshops in Fitzroy Crossing's Night Place, with one strong message for community.

"You are your own person at the end of the day and how you choose to represent that is purely up to you," he said.

Kayps has been nominated as triple j's unearthed artist of the year, with Bunuba Baby up for Australian album of the year at the J Awards.

World.title: Six dead, four injured in horror weekend on Victorian roads
World.content:
Six people have died and four others are seriously injured after a spate of horror crashes on Victorian roads since Friday.

Four people died on Saturday, including a pedestrian and a motorcyclist.

Two motorcyclists in their 20s died on Friday.

The first incident occurred on Friday afternoon in Footscray when a 25-year-old motorcyclist died after colliding with a car at the intersection of Ballarat Road and Dawson Avenue.

The driver of the car, a 59-year-old Mount Waverley man, was arrested and interviewed at the scene before being released pending further enquiries.

Later that evening, another motorcyclist died in when he crashed with a car on the Black Spur in Healesville about 7:15pm.

The rider, a 21-year-old from Somerville, died at the scene. Police will prepare a report for the coroner.

On Saturday, a 75-year-old woman died after being hit by a vehicle at a pedestrian crossing at Dennington, near Warrnambool, just after midday. She died at the scene.

The 53-year-old male driver of the car provided assistance to the woman and will be interviewed by police.

About 6:20pm last night, a 26-year-old Nunawading man died after losing control of his motorbike and crashing into a tree in Blairgowrie, near the Mornington Peninsula.

A woman has died at Dennington, near Warrnambool, this weekend. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

The bike's passenger, a 29-year-old Blairgowrie man, was flown to hospital with life-threatening injuries where they remain in a critical condition.

At roughly the same time, police were called to a fatal crash between two cars in Maryborough in western Victoria.

One of the drivers, a 47-year-old man from Maryborough, died at the scene. His passenger, a 75-year-old woman from Maryborough, was flown to hospital where she remains in a serious condition.

About an hour-and-a-half later, the driver and sole occupant of a ute died after crashing into a tree in Werribee in Melbourne's west. The man has yet to be identified.

227 people have died on Victorian roads this year, 20 less than the same time last year.

Teenager hospitalised after e-bike crash

Victoria Police are also investigating a crash between an e-bike and a car on Saturday in Moolap, near Geelong.

A 17-year-old boy was flown to a Melbourne Hospital with life-threatening injuries. He remains in hospital in a serious condition.

Another 17-year-old male was taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries, while the driver of the car, who stopped at the scene, was not injured.

Meanwhile, a 20-year-old Warrnambool man was yesterday charged over a collision that allegedly killed 70-year-old local cyclist Clive Coomber on Hopkins Falls Road in Cudgee in March.

Police said the man was charged with a number of offences, including culpable driving causing death, and failing to stop and render assistance.

He was bailed and is to front the Warrnambool Magistrates' Court on December 4.

World.title: Country town reliant on backpackers warns visa changes will cripple business
World.content:
In Paul Fowler's country pub, more than half a dozen backpackers make up over 70 per cent of his workforce.

Italian travellers keep business ticking over from the front of house all the way through to his busy kitchen.

It is a similar situation at many businesses across Manjimup, 290 kilometres south of Perth in southern Western Australia, with the tourism and agricultural centre heavily reliant on backpacker labour.

Seventy per cent of the staff at Paul Fowler's pub are backpackers. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Both Mr Fowler and his workers have backed calls to scrap the federal government's controversial changes to Australia's working holiday visa program.

"It's only going to make things harder, and it takes away our ability to function," he said.

Before the working holiday visa changes were announced, Mr Fowler bought a second pub in the neighbouring town of Pemberton, which he planned to staff with backpackers.

Viola Argenta, Ilaria Dalla Valeria and Mattia Ballarini all work at a pub in Manjimup. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Mr Fowler said that business was now under threat.

"We probably go through 50 to 80 workers a year, all backpacking workers, and so without the backpacking staff, we won't have a workforce here at all," he said.

" We could have more workers now if we could get them, but they're not here. "

Paul Fowler says his pub in Manjimup couldn't run without backpacker labour. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

The federal government's decision to initially slow down visa applications in August was heavily criticised by farming and regional communities across the country.

The decision to allocate fewer second and third-year visa extensions prompted WA's Premier Roger Cook to ask federal Immigration Minister Tony Burke to reconsider the restrictions.

Manjimup is a regional hub for tourism and agriculture. (ABC South West: Andrew Williams)

A spokesperson for the Department of Home Affairs said the reduction would ensure the program's long-term sustainability, and it would work with affected industries to access the labour they need.

Back in Manjimup, those impacted say the move fails to account for the benefits backpackers provide beyond their first year.

Roberto Spadotto wants to build a life in Manjimup. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Roberto Spadotto came to Manjimup to work as a farmhand, picking avocados and broccoli as part of his visa obligations.

After completing his 88 days and being granted an extension, he started managing Mr Fowler's pub along with his partner Giulia Colombo, whom he met while completing his farm work.

"That's where I met Giulia … one of the worst and best days of my life because picking broccoli is very tough, but I enjoyed it and I had a good outcome," he said.

After spending about four years in the region, the Italian couple were hoping to put down roots.

"I love the area, love the region, never really thought about moving somewhere else," he said.

"And now we're planning to stay, settle, and build a new life here in Australia."

Backpackers shipping out

Fellow Italian traveller Valerie Casto completed her farm work in a seedling nursery, before starting work as a chef once her visa was extended.

Valerie Casto says second and third-year visa extensions incentivise backpackers to do hard jobs. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

She said the incoming changes were turning some of her friends off coming to Australia.

"Half a year of a farm job can be very, very hard," Ms Castro said.

"And some people don't know if it's worth it, if at the end the visa is not granted."

Gavin Booth says backpacker workers are already leaving Australia. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

It is an experience all too familiar for truffle farmer Gavin Booth, who produces the valuable fungus on a property in neighbouring Pemberton.

He relies on backpackers for sporadic and seasonal work.

"We had a girl who's worked for us for a couple of years, a French backpacker, and she was on her third year visa when she found out she would have to go into a 5,000-space lottery," he said.

"She just said, 'Stuff this, I don't want to do this' and left.

"She was happy to come here and earn the money, to spend the money in this economy, and now she's left for Bali."

World.title: Third weekend of protests in France as youth-led rallies sweep Europe
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of protesters, inspired by frustrated high school students, have taken to the streets across France in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.

Youth-led protests were also held elsewhere in Europe on Saturday, including in Germany and Portugal.

France's protests were overwhelmingly peaceful, but gatherings in Paris and other cities ended in clouds of tear gas and scattered fires set by small groups on the margins.

About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country after Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder.

Protesters included a mix of high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living. (Reuters: Abdul Saboor)

The Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge to protect stores, government buildings and tourist areas in the city centre.

Authorities reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Saturday night, with the government estimating that 320,000 people protested nationwide.

Mass protests on October 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew 550,000 people around the country, and demonstrations on October 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates.

Organisers' turnout estimates are higher.

The march remained peaceful for hours before clashes broke out at its end point. (Reuters: Abdul Saboor)

Diverse grievances

Multiple groups marched together in Paris, including high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.

Unpacking the European protests Footage of mass protests in Europe has been flooding newsfeeds for weeks, with demonstrators taking to the streets across the continent.

Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said he lived in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats".

An information technology worker protested in solidarity with the students and her mother, who was struggling with a minimum wage job.

A grey-haired woman carried a sign reading, "The Old are Fed Up Too."

The rallies were started last month by high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students.

Labor unions and others angry at the leadership of President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.

On Saturday, a joyful crowd streamed for hours along avenues on the edge of Paris, but clashes broke out where the march ended.

Some protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police, who responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas.

Many peaceful marchers left the march, coughing and eyes streaming with tears.

Paris police barred people from entering the Place de la Republique and Les Halles neighbourhoods from 11 pm to 6 am Saturday and Sunday, and unaccompanied minors faced a separate 9 pm curfew around the Champs-Elysees.

Scattered fires were set by small groups on the margins of the Paris protest. ( Reuters: Abdul Saboor)

Protests in Germany, Portugal and the Netherlands

In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life", and against any return of military conscription.

Organisers said tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country. Official figures weren't immediately available.

Fires were lit in the streets of Frankfurt during a nationwide protest by campaign group Gen Z regelt. (Reuters: Kai Pfaffenbach)

In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.

"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.

Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said authorities had to invest more money in education.

"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

While most people rallied peacefully, some protests turned violent on Saturday night.

Some rioters smashed storefronts and looted stores in Frankfurt. (Reuters: Kai Pfaffenbach)

In downtown Frankfurt, some rioters smashed several storefronts and stole goods from inside. They also stole weapons from a gun store, which police were able to retrieve.

Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummelling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.

In Cologne, police ended a protest march early after protesters used pyrotechnics, threw stones at them and covered their faces despite a ban. Police used water cannons to disperse demonstrators.

In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades, and police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.

Elsewhere in Europe, people also protested against the housing crisis and for a better future.

Demonstrators gathered in Lisbon to protest Portugal's housing crisis. (Reuters: Rodrigo Antunes)

Thousands of protesters converged in downtown Lisbon to peacefully protest Portugal's housing crisis, holding up placards reading "Houses or Fire" and "We are not Afraid".

In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Saturday afternoon after online appeals for protests and fears of rioting and looting.

There were no major disturbances by midafternoon.

AP

World.title: Passengers give their verdicts on new Spirit of Tasmania
World.content:
The sky was clear and the sea calm when Spirit of Tasmania V arrived in Devonport at 6:19am on Sunday morning.

For a channel known for baring its teeth, Bass Strait had been kind to the passengers and crew.

This calls for a toast! (ABC News)

About 12 hours earlier, guests took selfies and drank wine on the pristine deck as the new ship left Geelong for its maiden passenger voyage.

As a guitarist wove through the crowd, dignitaries were singing the vessel's praises.

"We've stayed the course, and we've got it done," Tasmanian premier Jeremy Rockliff told ABC reporters, who were invited on the inaugural crossing.

Alison Jarman with Jeremy Rockliff, ahead of the inaugural voyage. (ABC News)

Standing beside the premier was an emotional Devonport mayor Alison Jarman, who likened the Spirit of Tasmania brand to the Sydney Opera House.

"She's iconic … and so are these two ships to our state," she said.

Oz McGuire's photo of Spirit of Tasmania IV in Devonport after its inaugural voyage. (Supplied: Oz McGuire)

The view from the deck as Spirit of Tasmania IV heads into Bass Strait. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Chris Carbone and Alison Jarman pose for a selfie. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

The new Spirits, which were beset by delays and cost blowouts, were built by Finnish company Rauma Marine Constructions.

"It's a historic moment for us … a beautiful collaboration," said the Finnish ambassador to Australia, Arto Haapea.

" It's a beautiful story. "

Arto Haapea was there to help celebrate. (ABC News)

Some of the food on display. (ABC News)

There are screens to keep the kids entertained. (ABC News)

Ship enthusiasts were not going to miss the historic occasion.

Mitchell Bruce, creator of the Ferries in Tasmania website, said he had been passionate about the Spirits for decades.

"Growing up in Tassie, going across on the original Spirit … it sparked an interest inside me," he said.

" It's great that we have these things from another part of the world that are servicing the island of Tasmania. "

Ferry enthusiast Mitchell Bruce was there to mark the occasion. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

The view of the vehicle gantry during embarkation, as seen by Mitchell Bruce. (Ferries of Tasmania: Mitchell Bruce)

A view of one of the lounge areas, as photographed by Mitchell Bruce. (Ferries of Tasmania: Mitchell Bruce)

A peek inside a cabin aboard Spirit of Tasmania IV, as photographed by Mitchell Bruce. (Ferries of Tasmania: Mitchell Bruce)

For many on board, the historic crossing was a journey home.

Celeste Ackerly, accompanied by her child and two pet dogs, was returning to Tasmania and had initially been unaware that she had booked on Spirit V's maiden crossing.

"It's pretty cool to know this is the first time," she said.

Celeste Ackerly travelled with her dogs. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Brian Munday was capping off a mainland road trip with a memorable night at sea.

"We've been all up Queensland, three and a half months on the road, and now we're heading home," he told the ABC.

" It's a nice ship. The finished product is good. "

Brian Munday liked what he saw of the ship. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

Sweety Neik, from Melbourne, was embarking on her first Tasmanian adventure, with Cradle Mountain and Hobart's Salamanca Market high on her to-do list.

"It's very exciting. I was looking forward to [October] 31," she said.

" I want to go and see how good Tasmania is. "

Sweety Neik is excited to see the sights of Tasmania. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

As the Sun slowly rose above Bass Strait this morning, with the north-west Tasmanian coast coming into view, Mr Rockliff and Transport Minister Kerry Vincent addressed the media.

"This is a pretty iconic moment, and I think everybody on board felt that last night," Mr Vincent said.

Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff with Minister of Infrastructure and Transport Kerry Vincent. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

There is hope that November 1, 2026, will mark a "new dawn" for a brand that has spent years in the headlines for the wrong reasons.

"This project certainly had its challenges," the premier said.

" But some very capable people picked up the mantle and got it done. "

Sandy Powell and Mackenzie Heard were invited on the inaugural sailing.

World.title: The unexpected neighbourhood pest terrorising this pensioner
World.content:
Every morning before 6am when pensioner Mal Richards walks down his driveway to collect the day's newspaper, his nemesis is waiting.

It's not a typical villain, but a beady-eyed, long-necked emu known by residents in this north Queensland community as Eric.

Eric the emu is a bit of a legend in Bluewater. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

Mr Richards said the female emu had been pestering him for the past nine months, leaving him trapped inside his home on Townsville's outskirts, afraid to venture into his garden.

"It stands around honking all day," Mr Richards said.

"I've got to do my daily chores and every time I turn around, he's under my feet."

The retiree said despite securing the property and locking his fence, Eric always finds a way through.

Mal Richards says he can't leave his house without the emu stalking him. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

"I know they kick badly and I've got to watch out. I'm a pensioner, right?" Mr Richards said.

"It seems friendly, but I don't trust them."

Mr Richards said he reported Eric to the Townsville City Council and the state government's Department of Primary Industries as well as the environment department but "they all pass the buck".

A Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation spokesperson said rangers had been monitoring an emu in Bluewater that "has not been seen to exhibit any concerning behaviour".

"Residents are asked to give the emu plenty of space and not to feed it or provide it access to food," the spokesperson said.

Mr Richards is frustrated authorities have been unable to help move Eric on, and he's not happy that Eric keeps pooing on his driveway.

Mal Richards tries to shoo Eric out of his yard. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

'Little legend'

The Bluewater community Facebook page is filled with posts of Eric sightings and several warnings for drivers to slow down while it is near the roadside.

"Everyone that sees [it] instantly falls in love with [it] <3," one local wrote.

"That's just Eric the Emu our mascot."

Another resident wrote that she saw schoolchildren at the bus stop forced to climb a nearby fence to escape Eric's attempt to come and say hello.

Mal Richards is scared of the emu's claws and big feet. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

Wildlife educator Jackie Hasling said Eric was known locally as an unusual emu, though she does not know why the animal is called Eric.

"She's certainly a little legend around Bluewater," she said.

Ms Hasling said Eric had been raised as a pet so was likely more friendly than non-domesticated emus.

In a statement, the council said local laws did not prohibit someone keeping an emu on blocks larger than 2,000 square metres, as long as applicable laws were met, including an adequate enclosure.

"I don't think Eric will be aggressive," Ms Hasling said.

Eric the emu under a mango tree in Mal Richards's yard. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

She said if an emu displayed threatening behaviour, the advice was to back away slowly and give it as much space as possible.

She said hold up a rake or a stick to appear taller and try put something, like a tree, between yourself and the bird.

As for the poo on the driveway? "Yep, that is definitely frustrating," Ms Hasling said.

With no-one taking action, Mr Richards continues to be followed around by someone else's pet emu.

World.title: ‘We are coming from hell’: The Ukrainian evacuees who escaped a kill zone
World.content:
WorldEuropeRussia-Ukraine war ‘We are coming from hell’: The Ukrainian evacuees who escaped a kill zone Carlotta Gall and Oleksandr Chubko Updated November 1, 2026 — 12:34pm ,first published November 1, 2026 — 9:47am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Northern Ukraine: A rasping scream rang out as a teenager recognised her father. He was one of the hundreds of people who had escaped: years of Russian occupation, months of hunger under a deadly drone war, and then a truce backed by a first lady and the Pope, and an odyssey back to their loved ones. A fleet of buses brought the evacuees from the embattled Ukrainian city of Oleshky out of the war zone on Saturday (Kyiv time), the passengers waving and wiping tears as they swung into the parking lot and ended their journey back. Draped in Ukrainian flags, the evacuees stepped down gingerly from the buses, weary after a 24-hour journey, which took them from the front line and through Russia and Belarus before returning to Ukraine. Many were gaunt from living months with little food, dark rings round their eyes from lack of sleep. Ukrainian serviceman Dmytro welcomes back his partner, Larysa, as evacuees arrive from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, in southern Ukraine. Getty Images “We are coming from hell,” said Oleksandr Styopin, 75, lighting a cigarette. “It’s a kill zone there.”



Trapped close to the front line, with Russian soldiers living among them, the residents of Oleshky have been living under occupation for more than four years since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. Their predicament worsened this year, when Ukraine drastically increased its drone attacks on Russian forces in the area, said Styopin, a retired electrical engineer. Loading The roads came under fire and supplies dried up as fewer and fewer drivers dared to risk the trip. Some residents tried to drive to the nearby town of Radensk to buy provisions, but many were killed on the road when drones struck their vehicles, he said. Bodies of Russian soldiers were left lying in the road, he said, since no one would risk collecting them.



Styopin would push his bike to a local store once in a while and stock up on as much food as he could carry. Once he passed the burned body of a girl beside her own bicycle, he said. “That was from a mine, I think,” he said. Some drones hovered close as if to look at him and then let him be, he said. An evacuee walks on crutches after arriving from Oleshky. Getty Images A local man rides a bicycle beneath anti-drone nets stretched over a street during the local ceasefire in Oleshky. AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka But they hunted down the Russian soldiers relentlessly, he said.



“They pinned them down so hard, they could not step out of the building,” he said of the Russian soldiers. A group of soldiers had moved into an apartment in his building, he said. Related Article Foreign relations US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Europeans, Australia object to Russia Some evacuees described the hardships they endured with a lightness that verged on humour as they recalled destruction and loss. “There was no electricity and no water. Then the house got bombed. Then the food ran out,” said Halyna Lohvynovska, 65. “We got used to everything,” her husband, Ivan Lohvynosky, said with a smile. Their house was hit several times, he said. “When something fell on your head, you moved to another room. When the house was destroyed more, you moved house.”



There were some young families and even young children among those evacuated. Vladyslav, 24, came out with his sister and mother. Thin and watchful, he declined to give his surname for security, he said. Red Cross volunteers move a man with a disability during the evacuation. AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka Pets were evacuated alongside residents. Getty Images The family had stayed in Oleshky because they had been scared that Russian authorities would prevent him from leaving; he was of the age to be drafted into the military in Ukraine.



They survived by growing vegetables in their garden and raising a few animals, he said. To some of their fellow evacuees, that was good fortune. Family members reunite. Getty Images Buses carrying evacuees arrive near Chernihiv, Ukraine. Getty Images “The past two years were terrible. We had nothing to eat,” said Anatolii Honcharov, 53. His 61-year-old brother, Valerii, had not heard from him for three years because communications were so bad. Only families who lived close to the river could pick up a Ukrainian cellphone signal.



Things became so dangerous in recent months, Styopin said, that he did not dare leave his apartment. He sat listening to the radio, a cigarette permanently clamped between his teeth, he said. His wife, who left at the onset of the full-scale invasion in 2022, joining their son in New York, called him many times urging him to leave. ‘For the last two months I was living with a drone above my head. It’s more than fear, it’s an internal dread that’s always present inside you.’ Oleksandr Styopin, 75 “If I try to leave, I will step on a mine,” he told her. “For the last two months I was living with a drone above my head,” he added. “It’s more than fear,” he said, “it’s an internal dread that’s always present inside you.”



But the plight of Oleshky drew international attention, helping to push for a rare localised truce in a war where each side has pressed for every advantage. Pope Leo, just three days after surgery for lung cancer, spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and called for a ceasefire to evacuate the city, and then US first lady Melania Trump announced a local truce last Friday. When the ceasefire began on Tuesday, Russian soldiers appeared to demine the roads and clear the streets of the dead. “The Russians cleared up everything,” Styopin said. “There was a destroyed armoured personnel carrier with bodies inside,” he added. “There was a body in pieces, half here and half there. The Russian took them all away.” Many residents did not trust the news of a humanitarian convoy. Several said they had tried to leave in convoys early in the war only to retreat after the vehicles came under fire.



But Styopin packed his things. Then, on Friday morning as he was leaving his home, a blast knocked him back. During the Russians’ demining, an explosion went off, and shrapnel ripped into his suitcase, he said. He went back to find another case and then rushed through heavy rain for more than a mile to the bus. An Oleshky resident waves after being evacuated. AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky “My heart was burning,” he said. “I thought I would crawl there in order to leave.” Vladyslav said he and his family feared to trust that they would truly escape.



“These last four days, we didn’t believe we would make it out,” he said. “We thought it was just another provocation — they would declare a ceasefire and then blow us up along the way,” he explained. “We were terrified, but we went anyway, because there might not be another chance.” Editor's pick Magazine

Sunday Life The November 1 Edition November 1, 2026 Many of the evacuees and their families said they were surprised at the scale of the seriousness of the operation to get them to safety, and said it raised hopes for an end to the war. Standing in the parking lot looking around, Vladyslav still looked uncertain. “I can’t quite make sense of my mood yet,” he said. “Happiness. Being back under my own flag, hearing my own language.”

World.content:
SportRacingMelbourne Cup ‘I don’t feel that’s good enough’: International manager hits out Melbourne Cup technology Peter Ryan November 1, 2026 — 12:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Joseph O’Brien’s racing manager Kevin Blake has called for emergencies to become part of the Melbourne Cup after stewards scratched Defiantly on Saturday due to concerns about his gait. The stewards had to make the decision three days out from the race due to the need to lock in the field of 24 at 4.30pm on Saturday, despite the fact the horse may have made the necessary improvement in the remaining two days to take his place. Kevin Blake (left) suggested the technology used for the Melbourne Cup needed to be updated. Getty Images Emergencies are considered impossible because betting technology can’t handle late inclusions to a field of 24. It means if there are late scratchings between 4.30pm Saturday and the race start, fewer runners will race rather than the next qualified horses in the order of entry being granted a start.



Related Article Updated

Melbourne Cup Racing dodges another nightmare after mid-race fall; Derby Day trainer charged by stewards “We know it’s rigorous, we know it’s tough, and so we’re not going to cry about [the decision]. We’re all big boys and girls, but probably the main takeaway from it is they probably need to sort out their emergency situation,” Blake said. “I’m a guest here so I don’t want to be telling people what to do, but for the reason to be that the technology can’t cope with more than 24 runners in 2026 … I don’t feel that’s good enough.” Defiantly’s withdrawal gives stablemate Kizlyar a start, meaning the O’Brien stable still has five runners – but it robs the race of a natural leader, with the four-year-old gelding a noted frontrunner. Blake said the jockey Dylan Brown-McMonagle, who had been booked to ride Defiantly, would now jump on Sons And Lovers, who was the best drawn of their five starters with barrier three.



He said local jockeys James McDonald and Craig Williams would need to weave some magic to their mounts Trustyourinstinct and James J Braddock in a good spot after they drew barriers 18 and 24 respectively. Related Melbourne Cup Pick your winners with our 2026 Melbourne Cup sweep McDonald is the in-form jockey after an exhilarating Derby Day where he won four races including the Derby and Trustyourinstinct is sure to win support due to his presence in the saddle. “James is going to have to work his magic to get in and get cover [and] get him racing efficiently, but he is a very classy horse unexposed to the trip,” Blake said. “[He] looks to have a leading chance in the book, so you just hope he gets a kind spin from the draw.”

World.title: Inside the scramble to contain the largest crypto heist in history
World.content:
BusinessMarketsCryptocurrencies Inside the scramble to contain the largest crypto heist in history Ben Weiss , Muyao Shen and Olga Kharif November 1, 2026 — 12:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The biggest crypto hack in history began with a rehearsal. As trading hummed along on Binance, hackers were quietly running sequences of code on accounts they controlled on the Ethereum blockchain — just a couple of dollars or so at a time. According to cybersecurity analysts, they were testing a program designed to seize control of accounts owned by the world’s largest crypto exchange and smuggle their contents elsewhere. Just after 4pm (New York time) on Thursday, they attacked. Binance, the largest crypto exchange in the world, was hit by a massive hack late last week. Getty Images In short order, the infiltrators drained more than $US6 billion ($8.9 billion) from wallets across at least four different blockchains, setting off a worldwide effort to contain the damage.



From New York to Abu Dhabi and Kyiv, security researchers and Binance executives scrambled to trace the stolen money, freeze accounts and understand how the attackers had breached the exchange and pulled off a heist that has shaken confidence in the crypto industry as it tries to earn greater acceptance in finance’s mainstream. “It’s the largest bank robbery in human history,” said Ari Redbord, global head of policy and government affairs at TRM Labs, a blockchain analytics firm. Redbord’s firm was one of several that mobilised after the attack started. “I literally haven’t slept and I haven’t stopped.” Related Article Cryptocurrencies ‘Biggest hack in history’: Crypto giant freezes assets after $8.9b heist As Binance publicly said it could easily reimburse any losses from the hack on Friday, employees were privately expressing doubts to one another that they’d be paid bonuses this year, according to people familiar with the matter.



The crypto industry is no stranger to malevolent actors. Only a month ago, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget was subject to a cyberattack that drained $US388 million. In February 2025, hackers stole nearly $US1.5 billion from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit. But the scale of this week’s attack shocked even industry veterans. Just as the exploit was unleashed, Taylor Monahan, who’s based in Los Angeles as a researcher at the non-profit security firm, SEAL, was on a group chat with other crypto investigators when someone at blockchain security firm zeroShadow sent a message about strange transactions at Binance. “I’m going to remain optimistic that everything’s fine,” Monahan told herself. But she knew that if things weren’t OK, they were very bad. “It’s like a hack — like, a really big one.” By 4.38pm, Monahan suspected the worst and contacted Tether, the firm that issues the USDT dollar-backed stablecoin. “In our souls, we knew it was a hack,” she said. Tether responded immediately but didn’t acknowledge that there was an infiltration. Less than 30 minutes later, the firm began the process of freezing the transactions on its blockchain, as did Circle, issuer of the USDC stablecoin. Scrolling X



Yi He, Binance’s co-founder and co-chief executive officer, was at home in Abu Dhabi when she first noticed something wrong. The executive had logged off work and was scrolling through X before going to bed about 12.30am in Abu Dhabi (4.30pm in New York). Posts on the social media site alerted her to trouble. Alarmed, she logged back on and saw that Binance’s security and wallet teams – which are empowered to act on hacks without executive sign off – were already at work, trying to stop more losses. Within minutes, the company created a war room that swelled to about 100 people around the world. Yi and hundreds of Binance employees would stay up through the night, co-ordinating efforts within the company and with other crypto firms and law-enforcement agencies including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the US Secret Service. Binance’s co-founder and co-chief executive, Yi He, was alerted to the trouble by posts on X. Natalie Naccache At 5.15pm (New York time), Binance publicly acknowledged it was aware of a “potential security issue” and that it was investigating the rumoured breach.



At 5.18pm, Circle chief executive Jeremy Allaire announced the stablecoin company had frozen more than $US800 million associated with a “potential exploit involving Binance”. Seven minutes later, Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino announced that his firm had frozen more than $US1.5 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack”. Related Article Cryptocurrencies Inside a billionaire’s paradise with crypto’s most powerful ex-convict Soon, crypto companies of every stripe started flooding social media to promise onlookers that they were safe. Binance competitors, including Kraken, Coinbase and Bybit, proclaimed they were unharmed. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs, Chainalysis and Elliptic have all said North Korea is behind the heist. They observed funds stolen from Binance commingle with crypto seized in the Bitget hack, which researchers had already attributed to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. At the weekend, the FBI also blamed North Korea for the hack.



Chainalysis labelled the hack as “the largest in the history of crypto, and one of the single-largest financial crimes of all time”. Still, even as the heist became more widely publicised, hackers continued to drain funds from Binance. The code attackers used gave them access to blockchain accounts owned by Binance and let the hackers empty them, all while exchange funds kept replenishing the accounts. Estimates of the amount stolen crept higher, eventually reaching $US6.3 billion. Mainstream crypto The attack comes at an inopportune time for an industry that is getting unprecedented support from the US government. The Trump administration has been pushing for mainstream adoption of cryptocurrencies and blockchain technology, including through its regulators. In September, the Securities and Exchange Commission approved a rule that allows for public company stocks to trade on blockchains. The Binance hack could undermine those efforts, experts fear. Odysseas Lamtzidis, founder of blockchain security company Phylax Systems, was on a plane travelling to Miami from New York when he saw a Telegram chat discussing the attack. “It was very scary. I remember breathing heavy because it was huge amounts of capital moving around, and people on the plane were asking if I was OK,” he said.



‘It’s still a Wild West.’ Odysseas Lamtzidis, founder of Phylax Systems, He watched as the attackers moved from one wallet to the next, and kept posting on X to alert users. “I think this is very scary for organisations and adoption of crypto because these types of events should be impossible to happen, not improbable,” he said. “It’s still a Wild West.” Binance co-chief executive Richard Teng. Dominic Lorrimer Yi and her co-chief executive, Richard Teng, on Friday confronted the potential reputational damage the attack could do. In a video posted on X, Yi promised Binance would continue to work with law enforcement to find the attackers. The company has vowed to reimburse any users who lost funds in the hack.



“We won’t let the hackers take away the momentum this industry deserves,” she said in her video post, speaking in Mandarin. “Of course, there are areas where we could have done better. We should have invested more in security earlier, and set stricter standards. Going forward, we won’t hold back, whether it’s investing in security or fighting hackers.” On Saturday, the company said it had restored 90 per cent of the tokens which hackers had stolen, pledging to reinstate customers’ ability to withdraw funds the following day. Related Article Opinion

Cryptocurrencies Trump has made billions from crypto. It just backfired on him Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Asked about employees’ bonus concerns, a spokesperson said Binance didn’t expect any impact there either. In the midst of the turmoil, some traders found opportunity.



Morten Christensen, a cryptocurrency trader who also runs AirdropAlert.com, a site that tracks cryptocurrency giveaways, made tens of thousands of dollars on Thursday. He was in Mexico, on a Discord call with six friends, brainstorming strategies to take advantage of the hack. They had decided to short cryptocurrencies, which were starting to drop in value when his wife walked into his office. He sent her back out. “Binance got hacked, babe,” he said. “Need to lock in.” With assistance from Ryan Weeks and Teresa Xie Bloomberg The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

Warning: This story contains distressing details and images. Two teenagers have been killed after their car crashed and caught fire south of Perth on Saturday evening. The police cordon on Saturday evening. 9News Perth The boys were in a grey BMW sedan with two other teenage boys as they drove north on Railway Parade in Bullsbrook about 10.20pm. It is understood the car was near the Twin Swamps Nature Reserve when it left the road and crashed into “several” trees.



Footage taken by witnesses appears to show the car caught fire shortly after the crash. Police said two 16-year-old boys died at the scene, and two 17-year-old boys were seriously injured. They were taken to Royal Perth Hospital for treatment, where they remain in a serious condition. The wreck of the car taken on Sunday morning. 9News Perth Police cordoned off Railway Parade and Warbrook Road while they investigated, with Railway Parade remaining closed until early on Sunday morning.



Detectives said they would be examining the cause of the crash, and asked anyone who may have had dashcam vision of the car prior to the incident to contact them. “Major Crash investigators are conducting an examination of the scene and are appealing for any witnesses to contact Crime Stoppers,” a WA police spokesperson said. The wreck of the car was taken from the site on Sunday morning.

World.title: ‘Not set in stone’: Bostock sets record straight about Sydney return
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Not set in stone’: Bostock sets record straight about Sydney return Christian Nicolussi November 1, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. St George Illawarra and Cronulla target Jack Bostock will meet with his management this week to weigh up his options, and he has not ruled out extending his stay at the Dolphins. One of 11 Kangaroos now free to accept offers from rival clubs, Bostock is doing everything possible to drive up his price following another three tries for Australia in their 66-6 thrashing of the Cook Islands on Saturday night. Loading Arguably the best winger in the game but someone who wants to play centre in the NRL, Bostock has been heavily linked with the Dragons, along with the Sharks and even Parramatta, who are also chasing fellow Kangaroo Bradman Best. Depending on what happens to Dolphins centre and primary Roosters target Herbie Farnworth, the Illawarra junior could even pop up on the radar of the NRL premiers.



When asked about relocating back home, Bostock said: “It’s definitely not 100 per cent set in stone [that] I’m coming to Sydney. I’m not sure where that’s come from. “I spoke to the Dolphins a couple of weeks ago and said I wanted to see my options and what I could do. Jack Bostock will meet with his management this week. Getty Images “It’s not set in stone I’m leaving the Dolphins. It’s a matter of going through the process. It’s hard to do while you’re in here because the task at hand is winning the World Cup. “Once I can sort out a time with my manager, we’ll sit down during the week, or have a phone call, and start figuring out what we’re going to do.



“We can see how many players are coming off on November 1. It’s been a running joke in camp about who is going where and what’s going to happen.” Kangaroos fullback Reece Walsh urged Bostock to come to the Broncos, especially now the club has signed Peter O’Sullivan, the recruitment chief who brought Bostock to the Dolphins. Loading Bostock, who also made his NSW Origin debut this year, is in line to earn as much as $900,000 a season. “What is he, 23?,” Walsh asked.



“He’s hardworking, can play many positions, and you can see he’s still growing into his body. “He’s an awesome talent who works really hard. He knows when to flick the switch, work hard at training, but he’s also a character off the field and has a laugh. Related Article NRL 2026 ‘It makes sense to us’: Meninga wants to reunite Burton and Sexton at the Bears “It’s interesting to see all the [contract] yarns getting thrown around; obviously there have been jokes and a bit of chat here and there, but I don’t think it’s hindered anyone’s training or connection or their presence in [Kangaroos] camp.” Some of the game’s biggest names are officially ready to open negotiations for 2028, none more so than Nathan Cleary. The Penrith playmaker, however, is expected to extend his stay with the club.



Sam Walker’s contract talks broke down with the Sydney Roosters, and he has been linked to Canterbury, especially if Matt Burton takes up a lucrative offer with Perth, whose coach Mal Meninga is eager to work with the five-eighth. Hudson Young is tipped to tour the PNG Chiefs’ Port Moresby base in the coming weeks now that his own extension offer with Canberra was officially spiked, while Harry Grant and Cameron Munster are prepared to test their worth before deciding whether they recommit to the Melbourne Storm. Meanwhile, Bostock’s hat-trick means he still trails Tom Trbojevic by one try in this tournament, as the Manly star also bagged another treble in Townsville. “He’s got me, hasn’t he? It would be silly to have a wager now; we haven’t had a bet, but he can score all of them, as long as we’re winning,” Bostock said. World.title: Wong warns new US strikes on Iran would worsen global instability, protests
World.content:
NationalForeign relations Wong warns new US strikes on Iran would worsen global instability, protests Michael Koziol November 1, 2026 — 11:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
