World.title: Porirua deputy mayor Kylie Wihapi dies
World.content:
Tributes are pouring in after the death of Porirua deputy mayor Kylie Wihapi, aged 45, on Saturday morning.

Mayor Anita Baker said she was numb with shock and disbelief at the sudden loss of a colleague she described as her "rock".

"She was such a vibrant, outgoing and generous person, full of life, warmth and a deep love for all of Porirua."

Wihapi's loss was huge, Baker said.

"I'm shattered like the rest of our council and I'm angry for someone to pass so soon. She just had a fall, hit her head."

Wihapi was "Porirua through and through", showing up for people "24-7", Baker said.

Wihapi embodied community spirit, wearing various hats as a netball coach and umpire, Rotarian, and supporter of kapa haka and charities, she said.

"She was there for every animal in our city - she was always saving a dog or a cat.

"She was the rock of our council; she organised all the functions and she was a party animal in the sense that she just loved life and made the most of it."

Ultimately, Wihapi was a wife and a mother, she said, offering her support to the family.

The outpouring of grief following Wihapi's death had been overwhelming and details of a live-streamed civic service would be announced in the coming days on the council's website, Baker said.

"The community is crying."

Baker said Wihapi had made history as Porirua's first elected Māori ward councillor.

"She brought wisdom, courage, compassion and an unmistakable energy to everything she did.

"I have lost a trusted adviser and friend, and her fellow councillors have lost a much-loved colleague.

Kylie Wihapi Supplied/Barbara Edmonds Facebook

"Kylie was Porirua through and through. She loved this city, believed in its people and worked tirelessly to make it a better place.

"We will miss her terribly," Baker said.

Te Pāti Māori co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer said she was "so very sad to hear of Kylie's passing".

"She was so passionate about Porirua, every conversation with her was of huge pride for the whole community.

"My deep condolences to her whānau... Moe mai rā e te taonga."

Labour MP Barbara Edmonds said she was "heartbroken" at the loss of "one of our most amazing local wāhine".

Barbara Edmonds and Kylie Wihapi. Supplied/Barbara Edmonds Facebook

"Kylie was everywhere and anywhere.

"Whether it was on the netball court as a dedicated referee, hosting her annual Pink Breakfast to raise funds for the Breast Cancer Foundation, co-ordinating her annual Christmas pet food drive, filling in for the mayor Anita Baker, coaching netball teams or following her beloved son Cooper on the rugby field sidelines."

Edmonds described her as "selfless" and "always keen for a dress-up".

"Her energy for life was just immeasurable. No matter what it was, Kylie always made time for the community of Porirua that she loved so much.

"Thank you e hoa for all that you've done for us and for Porirua. La manuia lau malaga."

Wellington City Council deputy mayor Ben McNulty said he was devastated.

"Kylie was an incredibly warm and welcoming person, and deeply passionate about Porirua.

"To her family, friends and wider community, I am so sorry for your deep loss."

Pāuatahanui general ward councillor Ross Leggett said Wihapi was a "true child of Porirua" and "gone far too soon".

"To say the loss of Kylie Wihapi... is a shock would be an understatement.

"I was elected to the council alongside her in 2016, and we were all the better for her openness, humour, warmth and sheer industriousness. She made a fine deputy mayor and gave so much to the city she loved."

The former mayor of Lower Hutt, Campbell Barry, said Wihapi's passing was not fair.

World.title: Hamilton takes F1 pole in Mexico, Piastri down in 13th
World.content:
Lewis ​Hamilton put Ferrari on pole position for the Mexico City Grand Prix on Saturday with Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli set to line up fourth on the grid for a ground-breaking race likely to make him Formula One's youngest champion at 20 years old.

Antonelli needs only a ninth-place finish at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez on Sunday ​to become Italy's first champion since 1953. ‌He was fifth fastest in qualifying but will move up a place due to Red Bull's Max Verstappen, in fourth, taking a grid drop.

The pole was a record-extending 105th of Hamilton's career and the Briton's first for Ferrari.

For Oscar Piastri, however, it was a very disappointing day as the Australian failed to make the final qualifying session and finished back in 13th.

"Thank you so much, it has been such a long ‌time coming," Hamilton said over the team radio. "Mega job, guys — I am so grateful for the hard work you guys put ⁠in."

The last time he took pole in a regular grand prix, ‌not including sprint races, was in Hungary in July ​2023 — a wait of 1,197 days.

It ‌also made the 41-year-old seven-times world champion the oldest pole sitter since American Mario Andretti, at 42, in Italy in 1982.

How Kimi Antonelli can win the F1 title in Mexico The Mexico City Grand Prix shapes up to be the coronation of Kimi Antonelli as an F1 champion. Here is how he can seal the world title.

Mercedes' George Russell, Antonelli's closest rival but 123 points behind his teammate with only 100 to be won after this weekend, was second fastest and Ferrari's Charles Leclerc third.

Both Hamilton and Russell have to win if either of the remaining contenders is to ​keep ‌Antonelli waiting another week for the title.

"I am happy. It has been a tricky few races for me and I'm still struggling to get on top of this car, to be honest," said Russell.

McLaren's Lando Norris, the reigning champion and ⁠last year's winner in Mexico, qualified sixth with Red Bull's Isack Hadjar ‌seventh.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson was eighth fastest ‌but also has a one-place grid drop for the clash with Verstappen in Friday practice.

That will mean he starts ninth with teammate Arvid ‌Lindblad eighth and Alpine's Pierre Gasly completing the top 10 on the grid.

Oscar Piastri struggles to explain things after he failed to make the top 10 in qualifying in Mexico. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

Antonelli was only seventh in the second phase, with Norris fastest and teammate Piastri knocked out in 13th ‌place in ​a blow for McLaren's hopes of ⁠edging back in front of Red Bull in the battle for third overall.

The Australian complained of lack of rear grip after being told he was out of the top 10.

Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso halted the first session when the team told him to stop in the stadium section with a suspected water pressure issue in the power ⁠unit.

The Spaniard was then noted for a general safety incident after he failed to reattach the steering wheel after getting out of the car.

Hamilton was fastest in that first ‌session, with Antonelli only ‌ninth.

Japanese Ryo Hirakawa, making his F1 race debut this weekend at the age of 32 and ​in place of Esteban Ocon, qualified 19th for Haas.

Mexican Sergio Perez, preparing for his 300th grand prix in front of his home crowd, and Cadillac teammate Valtteri Bottas filled the back row.

Reuters/ABC

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Formula 1 Mexico City Grand Prix on Monday, November 2, from 5:30am AEDT.

World.title: Time to make lopsided international women's rugby league a fair fight
World.content:
The Jillaroos will be expecting to rack up a cricket scoreline when they face Wales at Western Sydney Stadium this afternoon.

The Australians have only been beaten once in the past decade and are the raging favourites to win a fourth straight Rugby League World Cup title.

There have been lopsided scorelines across the tournament so far, bringing out the critics of the international game.

Men's international rugby league has come a long way in the past decade, largely thanks to changed eligibility rules and the increased number of Pasifika players in the NRL.

The women's game is coming from a standing start, and players and experts argue it is unfair to judge a fight where one side has a hand tied behind its back.

Bridging the gap

Tayla Preston is one of the stars of the NRLW, and the Canterbury Bulldogs captain is experiencing a whole new world as part of the Welsh side.

Tayla Preston is representing Wales at the tournament. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

She qualifies through her maternal grandfather and says it has been an "eye-opener" to see the differences between the game in Australia and Europe.

"I think it was about 90 per cent of the girls that have never been paid to play rugby league ever," Preston said.

"So to get them to come to a World Cup, get paid to play a Rugby League World Cup and verse the best of the best week in, week out, it's pretty special."

The Jillaroos and Kangaroos players will each receive equal payments of $40,000 at this tournament, but the rest of the countries, men's and women's, are well behind.

There is a gulf between Australia and the rest of the world in women's rugby league. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Preston says $15,000 is spread across the Welsh men's and women's teams, with most staff members volunteering for the tournament, and only several hundred registered women's players in the country.

"Compare it to the NRLW where we've got 360 contracted girls … I think it just shows the difference of where the games are at the moment. But we want to help bridge that gap," she said.

"I think that's the importance of showcasing the World Cup and seeing the differences there.

"When you compare the resources and what the girls have, they're making the most of what they do have and it shows that they're just playing for the love of footy and I think we [in Australia] weren't too far away from that probably about five, 10 years ago too.

"Hopefully we can get some more funding into the smaller nations, even like France as well and PNG. I think we're going to see a lot more athletes be able to have access to professionalism and training facilities and things like that to be able to build full-time programs as well."

Preston says there needs to be investment in smaller rugby league nations. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Preston says it's unrealistic to expect players to perform as full-time professionals when they are essentially part-timers.

But she doesn't think a truncated World Cup or shunning smaller rugby league nations is the answer.

"We've had some girls who have had to step away at times to be able to work; also, a lot of girls have had to take leave without pay just to play at the World Cup," she said.

"Obviously those challenges a lot of the public don't see and face. And so for us, it's just about playing with all our heart, and we want to just do it for the Welsh community back home and grow the game for them.

"I think the only way you can improve is by versing the best of the best and challenging yourself against the girls that are the elite professionals."

ABC Sport commentator Matthew Elliott agrees.

"A great experience for those athletes [is] to go back to where they came from and go, 'Wow, we need to improve,'" he said.

"We know ourselves in our own lives, sometimes when we have that level of disappointment, that gives us the opportunity to make a difference in our life, and I think it can make a difference to the sport."

Northern hemisphere woes

The men's game in the Pacific has boomed in recent years, with big-name players choosing to play for the countries of their heritage.

Former NRL player Christian Welch says the women's players don't have the same luxury.

"We've seen Payne Haas, Jerome Luai, the Hammer [Hamiso Tabuia-Fidow], incredible players who probably would be walk-up starts for Australia and New Zealand, generally the two biggest nations, they're able to make those [financial] sacrifices and represent their countries, Samoa and Tonga, Papua New Guinea, Fiji," he told Summer Grandstand.

"And it's great for rugby league. But when Jerome Luai is on $1.2 million, he can forgo a 40 grand payment and pick up three, four, five grand that Samoa will be paying him.

"Whereas the women, they're in a much tougher situation, NRLW salaries are much lower, the minimum salary I think is about $48,000.

"To ask a player to forgo $40,000 and 

"No-one begrudges the Jillaroos for getting $40,000, they deserve it, they're incredible and they're just so dominant. But at the same time the competitive balance is really suffering."

Fetu Samoa is a rising nation in women's rugby league. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The rise of Pasifika nations has been rugby league's great success story, but it has coincided with a decline in the game in the northern hemisphere, particularly England.

Once considered among the "big three" in the international men's game alongside Australia and New Zealand, England could miss the semifinals of this tournament.

England's women have never even been in the mix; their second pool game ended in a 78-0 defeat to Australia.

The NRL is seeking a stake in the Super League to help inject life back into the game there.

The men's RLWC is featuring 10 teams, reduced from 16 in 2022. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"I've been at Wembley and walked out there with 100,000 people [at a rugby league game]," Matthew Elliott said.

"There is a passion for it, but it's got to be fed and it's not being fed in the right way.

"It's up to the whole international game, including Australia, to find a way to build the sport overseas because we know when you get it right people love consuming it."

Welch also wants to see investment in the game more broadly.

"It's great to have Tonga, Samoa, Fiji, but they don't have the ability to host games or competitions or really drive much commercial revenue," he said.

Tonga fans have been out in full force for the men's team through this tournament. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

He said the Australian Rugby League Commission could get "creative" with the money coming from the new broadcast deal, and review taking the game to Las Vegas.

"It's been reported that it's profitable. I'm very sceptical. But I'd like to interrogate those numbers," he said.

"Are we spending our money to grow the game in America? Would we have better bang for our buck by maybe improving minimum standards and helping Tonga, Samoa, Fiji, particularly in the women's game?

"It's probably a less sexy version. You don't get the glitz and glamour of Las Vegas, but long term, is that going to help us better?"

World.title: De Minaur stuns new number one Zverev in Vienna
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has been left celebrating what could prove one of the most significant wins of his battling career, downing the about to be crowned world number one Alexander Zverev with a fearless display of attacking tennis to reach the Vienna Open final.

The Australian number one played a fabulous deciding tiebreaker, brushing off a couple of double faults to keep the pressure on the two-time major champion and eventually prevail 6-4, 1-6, 7-6 (4) to set up a championship match with Carlos Alcaraz at the Wiener Stadthalle.

Saturday's victory had extra importance as it pushed de Minaur back among the top-eight qualifiers to make the end-of-season men's championship, the ATP Finals, in the live "Race to Turin" with just the Paris Masters now to come as a qualifying event.

But for de Minaur, it will resonate even more as one of his biggest wins as he had never before beaten Zverev, who will become the world number one when next week's rankings come out, in an individual tournament, with his only previous victories having come in early-season team events and the exhibition-like Laver Cup.

"I'm super proud, super stoked of how I handled the moment. I was very calm, even though I threw in a couple of doubles there," De Minaur said, as he thought about how he had battled back to regain control.

Loading Instagram content

"All in all, I played a very aggressive deciding tiebreak. I played on my terms. I was going to go out swinging and playing the right type of tennis, and that's what made the difference today."

It was an exceptional display from the world number 10 as he played with a striking front-foot intensity that seemed to shock Zverev.

Germany's Alexander Zverev was unsettled by his opponent's tenacity and aggression. (Getty Images: PS Images/MB Media/Yigit Oerme)

The German's mood was fairly tetchy all afternoon as the Australian kept up his aggressive approach, complete with 25 winners in total.

Only when de Minaur's serving let him down in the second set did Zverev gain some familiar dominance, but the Sydneysider regrouped superbly in a high-quality deciding set.

The extent to which Zverev was rattled became obvious as he served at 5-6 to stay in the match and raged at the umpire Arnaud Gabas, who had rightly given him a time violation for his interminable ball-bouncing before serving.

Remarkably, Gabas decided to take back the sanction after Zverev had remonstrated but the fuss did not stop de Minaur's focus as he went on to win the first three points of the tiebreak with brilliant strokeplay that gave him control even when he coughed up his doubles.

Loading Instagram content

But if beating Zverev was special, then defeating Alcaraz, who had beaten Daniil Medvedev 6-4, 7-6 (2) in the earlier semi-final, looks set to be the ultimate challenge for the Australian.

Zverev finally hits number one After years being blocked from the top of the game by a series of tennis greats, Germany's Alexander Zverev finally clinches the men's world number one ranking.

The pair have met six times before, with de Minaur having lost all half-dozen, including at this year's Australian Open.

Asked what it would mean if he could win the ATP 500 event, de Minaur smiled: "It would be a pretty decent week, I would say.

"I'm just happy with what I'm doing, the way I'm competing, the way I'm going about my business. Just one foot in front of the other, doing what I can.

"Ultimately I'm playing some good tennis, looking forward to hopefully finishing strong this season."

AAP

World.title: Strategy, succession planning needed for Australia after Cape Town collapse
World.content:
Fans of cricketing omens were treated to a masterful piece of psychological theatre before play on the final day of the Cape Town Test.

A week shy of 15 years since he rolled Australia for 47 at the same venue, former South African fast bowling genius Vernon Philander accompanied Proteas coach Shukri Conrad to the middle of Newlands and helped choose the ball to be used on the final day of this thrilling Test series.

Barely half an hour into play, Philander's most gifted successor, Kagiso Rabada, had used it to remove three of Australia's top order. With that, the game and Australia's fading hopes of winning the series were already dead and buried.

Kagiso Rabada was near-unplayable at the start of the Australian innings, setting up South Africa's final day win. (AP: Halden Krog)

Chasing 288, which was always a huge ask, Australia buckled to be all out for 111, having earlier looked like securing its second sub-100 score in as many Tests.

The last Australian team to suffer that indignity at least had the good sense of doing it before the invention of television.

Whatever meagre sense of respectability Nathan Lyon and Pat Cummins restored with a 45-run partnership for the ninth wicket was cancelled out by the emphatic confirmation that Cummins had erred unaccountably by electing to bowl on day one and setting the stage for the impossible chase this one proved to be.

Proteas off-spinner Simon Harmer, who had quite boldly put Cummins on notice before this Test, spun his side to victory with 6-16 from 22 overs of wizardry.

Simon Harmer spun South Africa to victory on the final day, making breakthroughs when others could not. (AP: Halden Krog)

Yet for all the bravado and posturing in this series, it was Harmer's lack of words, and his fighting back of tears when he picked up the man-of-the-match award, that best explained what this triumph means to South Africa.

There will be earnest post-mortems conducted to figure out where else Australia went wrong on this tour. The national selection panel should be interrogated first, and at length, yet so should several experienced batsmen who batted brainlessly at the critical moments that consigned Australia to a 2-1 series loss.

As most astute judges foretold, poor Marnus Labuschagne flubbed what will surely be his final chance at Test level. From the sixth delivery of a frantic day, the dejected Queenslander was trapped in front by Rabada and burned one final DRS review before trudging off with the weight of the world on his shoulders.

Australia vs South Africa day five Here are the quick hits from day five of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.

Still, we should not flatter Australia so much as to think of their miscalculations and mistakes as the most decisive factors in the resolution of this brilliant Test series.

Brimming with world-beating talent and self-belief, South Africa was simply better organised and better performed in almost every facet of the game.

So many of its players — Marco Jansen and Temba Bavuma in the second Test, Harmer, Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder in this one — can now say they produced career-defining performances when it mattered most. Would a single Australian?

Perhaps it was inevitable that Rabada would do something special after missing out in the first innings, when illness shrunk his powers.

But Harmer, whose performance was the most anticipated factor in the final day of the series, was the one who really played out of his skin.

His spell of 3-5 from eight spellbinding overs before lunch left Australia a Philander-esque 7-60, and the other wicket to have fallen at that point was also his in spirit: desperate to get off strike, Cameron Green called for a quick single that was not there and barbecued Josh Inglis.

Green hung around for 110 deliveries either side of lunch, but Harmer got him too with a raging turner that zipped through the gate.

Some tough and maybe unpopular decisions now await Australian cricket — not knee-jerk reactions to public outcry, and not wholesale personnel changes for now.

But there are matters of strategy and succession planning far more complicated than Marnus's sad slump into redundancy.

The world-class bowling attack that has papered over the cracks in Australia's batting line-up for several years will be, by the end of the coming Australian Test summer, aged 39, 37, 36, and 33, with a 37-year-old its best backup.

Like the rest of Australia's much-celebrated bowling line-up, Josh Hazlewood (pictured) cannot go on forever. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

No matter how entitled each feels to his spot, and no matter how much career statistics and public sentiment justify that entitlement, some form of attrition is inevitable. Longer-term replacements urgently require game time in Tests, not cordial-mixing duties.

Cummins, who has the most left in the tank, and Lyon, perhaps the least, will be the unhappiest with their returns in this series — just six wickets each, at a cost of 54 apiece for Cummins and 43 for Lyon.

And it is hard to imagine South Africa picking someone to bowl a combined total of 25 overs in two Tests and bat at seven, as Australia did with Beau Webster.

It is not all doom and gloom, of course, and even in this game there were some positive glimpses into the post-Labuschagne, post-Smith era.

Matt Renshaw's tenacity and run-scoring at the crease has been one of the few Australian highlights of this series. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Matt Renshaw, streets ahead as the batsman of the series with 369 runs at 61.50, is a lock at the top of the order beside Travis Head. Proven performers now, Green and Inglis should be backed to succeed.

That leaves the number three and six slots to fill, with common sense suggesting Alex Carey needs to return to batting at seven.

That three has been made to appear such a fiendish problem is at odds with the solutions staring selectors in the face. Even in the era of "false threes", it is anathema to the history of the Australian Test team to pick anyone other than a top-order specialist in that crucial slot.

Steve Smith, if his appetite for a big finale remains, may need to be told it is his duty. If he or Australia decide it is time to move on, Kurtis Patterson is a mature and proven option who makes as much sense as Renshaw did for this tour.

As for six, it is a little early to tell exactly what, and how good, Cooper Connolly will be. But for generations it has been a spot that tends to be filled by a youthful player of promise and Connolly is both of those things.

Whichever way Australia goes with the above decisions, it is probably time that a coherent rationale for Test selection is more clearly communicated to contenders and even the public, because nobody who emotionally invests in Australian cricket is buying the strange stories George Bailey has been telling in recent times.

With all that, Australia now drops to third in the ICC Test rankings and New Zealand, who it faces in a Test series starting in 38 days, rises to the top.

If the Black Caps have prepared themselves for their challenge as diligently as South Africa did in this series, there will be plenty more difficult days ahead for Australia.

World.title: The Suns started their rebuild when half their roster were just kids
World.content:
Gold Coast finished on the bottom of the AFLW ladder in 2025.

It was the first season under new head coach Rhyce Shaw and it could have seemed like a terrible place for him to start.

The club was giving up the most points per game in history, 64.3, and losing by a record 37.8 points across the course of the season.

But this was all by design, for the Suns knew exactly what sort of talent was going to land on their doorstep via the draft in December, with a third of the list transformed in just one night.

So, the shift in game plan started before they even arrived, fast-tracking their impact in a big way.

The shift bore some startlingly poor results, but it was all for the greater good of propelling the Suns to their third-ever finals series just 12 months later.

Moving away from the contest

Rhyce Shaw has led a turnaround for the Suns. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman/AFL Photos)

For the bulk of their time in the AFLW, the Suns have been synonymous with hard, contested footy, rolling mauls and dour games. Picture Charlie Rowbottom with ball in hand with three players hanging off her.

It bore low-scoring, scrappy affairs where the side relied on resetting games by creating repeat stoppages.

For this reason, the average score the Suns were conceding from turnover in 2024, their last season under Cam Joyce, seemed reasonable at 27.2 points per game, but they were also giving up nearly four goals per game from stoppage.

Essentially, by minimising the opposition's chance to score from live play, they created more opportunities for teams to get busy out of stoppage.

In an effort to shift away from a stoppage-heavy, contested game style, Shaw needed to be willing to go backwards on the scoreboard to benefit in the long run.

They moved to a more controlled game style in 2025, to varying effect on the given day, and focused more on a kick-mark game and valued uncontested possession.

Suns' average scores against From turnover From stoppage 2026 23.1 12.0 2025 42.1 21.0 2024 27.2 23.7

Teaching those who were going to be around for the long haul how to effectively move from inside the contest to outside transition was always going to be crucial when integrating the likes of Sunny Lappin, Mikayla Nurse, Ava Usher and Dekota Baron in 2026.

To get the most out of these star teenagers, existing players needed to know how to best engage them.

But the growing pains of establishing this change meant they were badly hurt when they turned the ball over, giving up an average of 42.1 points from the source throughout 2025. This is what saw their points against balloon out to record numbers.

Throughout that 2025 season, the Suns also gave up 40.7 inside 50s per game, as well as 9.6 marks inside 50, and 23.2 shots on goal, all unwanted club records. But it all came from that desire to be productive in attack themselves.

Their contested possession rate was dropping, their average metres gained were up, and it might have been small flashes of evidence that they were tracking the right way, but Shaw stuck fat because he knew that a host of talented kids were going to take this game plan and run with it.

Shifting style Avg disposals Avg marks Avg uncontested possessions Avg metres gained Avg contested possession % 2026 282.2 51.1 163.1 3,727.7 42.0 2025 246.8 45.5 129.3 3,459.5 46.6 2024 223.3 39.6 108.3 3,334.7 50.6

Learning to score

Although Gold Coast's average score dropped from 28.3 to 26.6 from 2024 to 2025, the side actually kicked scores of 30 or more points five times last year, compared to just three the year prior. So, it was becoming marginally less consistent, but those stronger attacking performances, helped along by the addition of Havana Harris, were popping up more regularly.

There have been six occurrences in AFLW history of a club averaging a losing margin of 30 or more points, but of those six occurrences, the Suns last year averaged the highest score themselves. Another piece of evidence that the focus on attack was in fact working, it was just about improving that movement through the middle of the ground to really get things going their way.

In 2024, just two Suns, Tara Bohanna (nine goals) and Jac Dupuy (eight), kicked five or more goals across the season. Last year, there were three: Harris in her first season (11 goals), Dupuy (seven) and Jamie Stanton (six).

Havana Harris is a major goal-scoring threat. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman/AFL Photos)

Of those players, just one has played games for the club this year: Harris. Bohanna moved to Carlton for the 2025 season, Dupuy arrived at Hawthorn this year, and Stanton has been unable to break into the side, and has since announced her retirement.

This year, six Suns have kicked five or more goals, while 11 different players have kicked multiple goals. Harris still leads the way with 18, but Usher (11), Anne Hatchard, Alannah Welsh, Lappin (all eight), and Baron (six) have been busy up forward. Harris is the only one who was at the club last year.

But without the clear intention to move into more of a live-play style of footy, which creates greater opportunity to score, it's unlikely these players would have had so many chances to get busy in attack.

Now, Gold Coast is averaging the highest score in its history (49.7 points per game), from the most inside 50s it has ever generated (37.9).

Attacking is the best defence

By way of controlling the ball more effectively once outside of stoppage, and retaining the ball inside 50 once in the zone, Gold Coast's defensive performance has tightened up significantly. The return of classy halfback Daisy D'Arcy and addition of key defender Georja Davies has also contributed to the strengthening line.

This year the Suns are giving up the third fewest inside 50s in the AFLW, and conceding the fifth-fewest points. A far cry from the record-breaking points teams were putting on them last year.

Defensive lockdown Avg pts against Avg inside 50s conceded Avg marks inside 50 conceded Avg shots on goal conceded Avg goal efficiency conceded % 2026 36.8 30.9 4.7 12.1 17.1 2025 64.3 40.7 9.6 23.2 21.9 2024 51.7 37.6 6.7 17.3 19.4

It has been a masterclass in redeveloping a side at speed. Granted, Gold Coast had an advantage very few sides across history have had: the knowledge and understanding of who is going to be added to their list in the coming year.

But it required the bravery for things to get worse before they were going to get better. They survived the worse, and now celebrate the better with a final on the horizon, and a chance of reaching the top four still live depending on results across the last round of the home-and-away season.

World.title: Quick hits: Marnus's career on the brink, Warner aims cutting lunch-time spray
World.content:
David Warner labels his former teammates "disgraceful" and Marnus Labuschagne's career crisis continues to spiral as Australia endures a horror end to its tour of South Africa.

Here are the quick hits from day five of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Marnus on the brink after horror start for Aussies

It was the first over from hell for the Aussies, and one in which Marnus Labuschagne must have surely seen his Test career flash before his eyes.

All it took was three balls, and the tourists, chasing 288 at the beginning of day five, were one down.

Matt Renshaw, the hero from Durban, was out for a golden duck after a leg-side strangulation, with Proteas spearhead Kagiso Rabada only just beginning to find his groove.

Kagiso Rabada had the Aussies shell-shocked in the game's very first over. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

Walking to the middle with his place in the team long under the microscope, the stage was set for Labuschagne's long-awaited innings of redemption.

He found his way off a pair courtesy of a streaky boundary through gully, but a massive lapse in judgement spelled disaster for the Queenslander.

Labuschagne was given out LBW after shouldering arms to a ball that nipped back and thudded into pad, with his review futile in providing life support to a Test career so desperately struggling for air.

It has now been 49 innings and well over three years since his last Test ton.

Australia, remarkably, was 2-5 after six balls.

2. Green barbecues Inglis

Josh Inglis was well short of his ground. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

Just when it felt like it could not get any worse for Australia, it did.

Having joined Cam Green in the middle after Travis Head had become Rabada's third victim, Josh Inglis, fresh from his century on day three, was 4 from 17 deliveries when Green called him through for a single that was never there.

The towering all-rounder had set off after doing little more than pat the ball into the off-side, meaning Marques Ackerman could race around from silly point, collect the ball, and fire it into Ryan Rickelton behind the stumps.

The bails were dislodged with Inglis helplessly short of his ground, the horror mix-up only appropriate after the first hour that was.

3. Reverse does for Carey in Harmer double strike

Alex Carey has a complicated relationship with the reverse sweep. He clearly likes playing it, but it has often been his downfall.

So, with his side 4-42 on the deciding day of the series, and with the Newlands pitch turning sideways, it perhaps wasn't the time to bring out the cross-bat special.

But facing finger spinner Simon Harmer, Carey just couldn't help himself.

Down on his haunches, his top edge was gobbled up by a diving Marco Jansen, and the wicketkeeper-batter was out for 2.

Alex Carey was out playing a reverse sweep. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

In at No.7 and playing his second Test, Cooper Connolly never stood a chance.

The 23-year-old was dismissed just two balls later, done by flight and spin, edging behind to Rickelton while attempting a booming drive, leaving the Aussies deep in the mire.

4. Ex-players fume at day five disaster

As Australia went to lunch at 6-70, the recriminations were already in full swing.

On commentary for ABC Sport, former Australia fast bowler Jason Gillespie was close to speechless.

In the Fox Cricket Studio, former Australia opener David Warner wasn't.

"It's un-Australian. There is no fight whatsoever, it's disgraceful," said a fuming Warner.

"The batters have let the bowlers down all series.

"Yes, Matt Renshaw showed fight in that first Test, but I think the batters have been disgraceful, utterly disgraceful."

David Warner was livid with his former teammates. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

As we returned for the second session, ex-Australia batter Phil Jaques was still attempting to come to terms with what he had witnessed.

"Words can't describe how disappointing it is for Test cricket today," Jaques said on commentary for ABC Sport.

"I bounced out of bed this morning hoping for a really good day of cricket … and then Australia today just didn't show up.

"They've been found wanting on numerous occasions … it's just been pretty poor from Australia, to be honest, and really deflating as a cricket fan."

5. Aussies go 78 deliveries without scoring

With the result no longer in doubt heading into the second session, Australia changed tact.

Pat Cummins came out alongside Green following the lunch break and was determined to bat time, rather than score runs.

After Green had farmed the strike earlier in the day with Mitchell Starc, protecting him from the pace of Gerald Coetzee, he did the same with Cummins.

Simon Harmer claimed six wickets as the Aussies fell to a disastrous defeat on day five. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman/Gallo Images)

They turned the Test into a waiting game and had some success until Harmer, in the middle of a miserly spell, switched ends and threw a spanner in the works by ripping an off break through Green's defences and into his off stump.

Cummins was then joined by Nathan Lyon and finally scored his first run, ending a streak of 78 dot balls and receiving Bronx cheers from those in the stands at Newlands.

It was an embarrassing final nail in the Australian coffin near the end of an embarrassing day for a proud team.

World.title: World Cup player sidelined by gang war gets second chance
World.content:
The Lebanese rugby league team has broken ranks with an NRL club that refused to pick a player who had been sidelined over safety concerns due to his familial ties to the Alameddine crime family.

Mohamed Alameddine was sidelined by the Parramatta Eels this year after an alleged attempt on his father's life in broad daylight by the self-proclaimed "Coconut Cartel" crime gang.

The incident was one of several targeting his family members this year, including another failed assassination attempt at a junior rugby league game where a relative was playing.

Alameddine has no association with the crime family barring his last name, and police have previously said his relatives are being targeted purely because of their familial link to organised crime figures.

The talented winger, who is contracted to Parramatta until the end of 2027, was stood down from training with the Eels or playing in the side's reserve grade team in the New South Wales Cup.

One family, two rules

Zain Alameddine of the Bulldogs is still able to play, while his brother is benched. (Supplied)

Despite this stance from Parramatta, the ABC previously revealed Mohamed Alameddine's younger brother Zain had been allowed to develop with a lower grade team at the Canterbury Bankstown-Bulldogs.

Lebanon made the decision at this World Cup to pick Alameddine, however he has not played any matches so far.

Tonight is the last chance he has to be picked and he was listed among the reserves, unlikely to feature in the Cedars' campaign.

Tony Francis (centre) praised Alameddine's work ethic. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Gold Coast Titans winger Tony Francis was also selected in the Lebanon squad and said it had been a tough situation for a player whose future was in part out of his control.

"He's a very good player and it's unfortunate he can't get out there, but hopefully it all settles down and he's back on the field again," he said.

"He's a cracker bloke honestly."

Lebanon halfback Alex Conti told the ABC he was glad to call Mohamed Alameddine a teammate.

"He's having a great time, we've become mates and he's just a great kid" he said.

"He's been training well."

Decision's far-reaching consequences

The decision by Parramatta has meant Alameddine's pursuit of a professional rugby league career has effectively been in a holding pattern, despite no issues with his conduct or performance.

The ABC understands at this stage Parramatta has not offered Alameddine a contract beyond next year, nor has the club made a public decision about whether he would return to training in January.

There is a scenario where Alameddine could join another club as soon as next season, which would require the activation of a release mechanism in his contract.

However to do this, he would need to be paid for the 2027 season in full, either by Parramatta or another club.

Such a scenario could mean Alameddine's salary would count against the Eels' salary cap, despite him not playing at the club.

Due to the ease of public access to Parramatta's facilities and the regular training routine of an NRL club, concerns remain for the safety of Alameddine, his teammates and club staff.

The club has continued to have regular contact with police as well as with Alameddine's family to support the young player who remains a popular figure among teammates.

World.title: Melbourne Cup 2026: Field, barrier draw, form guide and betting
World.content:
6yo gelding (Great Britain)

Jockey: Dylan Browne McMonagle

Trainer: Joseph O'Brien

Sons And Lovers kicked off the year with success in Saudi Arabia. (Reuters/Action Images)

The honour of topweight this year goes to Sons And Lovers, one of five horses in the race for Irish trainer Joseph O'Brien, who won the Cup with Rekindling in 2017.

A consistent stayer across his 19-start career, Sons And Lovers began 2026 with a narrow victory over 3,000 metres in Saudi Arabia, and in July claimed the Prix Maurice de Nieuil (2,800m) in Paris, where he took the lead from the start and refused to be passed.

The six-year-old rounded off his Cup preparations with a second in the Kilternan Stakes (2,414m) in Ireland; behind him that day were stablemates and fellow Cup rivals James J Braddock and Goodie Two Shoes.

Sons And Lovers has the services of Dylan Browne McMonagle, whose initial Cup mount Defiantly was withdrawn by stewards on Saturday after failing a vet inspection.

Tech.title: Get in the spirit with these horrors from YouTube
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Rather than recommend a single horror film or an unsettling album for our final installment of spooky season recs, I present you with a small selection of creepy, disturbing, and just plain weird videos from YouTube. There’s a little something for everyone here. Whether you’re a fan of surreal art house shorts, cosmic horror, or classic viral clips, you’re bound to find something below that will get you in the Halloween spirit.

This 1983 short film from Cecelia Condit found its audience over 30 years later when it was uploaded to YouTube and eventually found its way to Reddit. If you’ve ever wondered what a feminist musical about cannibals directed by David Lynch would be like, wonder no more. Possibly in Michigan is only 12 minutes long, but it has inspired hours of YouTube videos dedicated to analyzing its deeply unsettling imagery and meaning.

The line between horror and comedy is razor thin, and Homemade Gatorade expertly threads that line. It’s bizarre, uncomfortable, and uncanny. It blends stiff animation with heavily processed video to create something quite unique. I’m never sure if I should be laughing or squirming in terror with every turn this road trip short takes.

Big budget cosmic horror films often make the same mistake — they try to show too much. What makes Portrait of God work is it knows less is more. So much of its short runtime is spent staring into an empty abyss. Or is it empty…

Speaking of staring intently at nothing and wondering if you did actually see anything, Heck is the short that eventually was turned into the experimental horror Skinamarink. Personally, I love Skinamarink, but I understand it’s not for everyone. 100 minutes is a long time to be staring into staticky corners of a drab suburban home. Heck delivers the same tension-building quiet, but in a much more digestible 29 minutes.

There’s not much to say about this one-minute loopable short from David B Earle. It’s the sort of video that did gangbusters on early YouTube. It’s all abstract creepiness and nightmare-fuel visuals. If you want the full effect and need something to put on the TV at your Halloween party, put on this four-hour looped version.

No Halloween is complete without this banger from Nick Lutsko.

Tech.title: Keyboards of The Verge
Tech.content:
What is a keyboard if not the original brain-computer interface? You can tap on a touchscreen or talk to the computer, but if your work involves getting information out of your head and into the computer, you’re probably spending a lot of time using a keyboard.

We’ve written about many keyboards over the years, from the legendary Optimus Maximus to the ultra-luxe Seneca to even stranger fare. But I wanted to know what my coworkers actually use. As I’d hoped, there’s a wide range. Some of us are strictly utilitarian, optimizing for ergonomics or functionality. Others obsess over every detail of feel, sound, layout, and looks. Still others — maybe the most enlightened — just use whatever’s in front of them.

NuPhy came up a lot. So did Keychron. The Apple Magic Keyboard has its stalwarts. The Kinesis Freestyle split is surprisingly well represented. And there are other, odder entries.

These are the keyboards of The Verge.

Jay Peters, senior reporter

Jay Peters’ Kinesis Freestyle Pro in a picture from 2021. Sadly, Gouda the cat passed away, but his spirit lives on through this photo. Image: Jay Peters / The Verge

I currently use the Kinesis Freestyle Pro, and I’ve used it for so long that I’ve forgotten when I first got it. In the late 2010s, I had wrist pain that led me to try a lot of ergonomic keyboards so I could keep using computers. The Freestyle Pro — with its optional tenting add-ons that give the keyboard a significant angle and the palm rest accessories — just feels the best under my hands. If this keyboard broke, I’d buy another one the same day.

Kallie Plagge, senior copy editor

For work, I use a simple Keychron K2. But for my gaming PC, I use the Logitech G713 wired mechanical keyboard — the one that comes with the cloud wrist rest. Did I mostly buy it for the wrist rest? Perhaps. But I do love the tenkeyless layout. My previous gaming keyboard had a number pad and two rows of programmable keys, which was cool, but I mostly used the number pad to type the alt code for em dashes. The G713, on the other hand, meets my gaming requirements without taking up half my desk. I’m not playing anything competitive on my PC that requires adjustable actuation points, so the GX red linear switches do the trick. (And they’re the right amount of clicky, unlike the overly loud ones on my K2.) So yeah, maybe I bought it for the sleek all-white look and the cute wrist rest, but it’s also a great keyboard, too.

Danielle Steussy, product manager

I’m using Apple’s Magic Keyboard with the numeric keypad. Some version of Apple’s keyboard has been on my desk for over 20 years, starting with the Apple A1048 that came with my first Mac in college. I loved that keyboard (the sound of my fingertips hitting the keys — swoon!) and I wore it down to the point of keys falling off. Since then, I’ve stuck with Apple’s wireless keyboards. Honestly, it’s a pretty keyboard, but otherwise unremarkable, and blends in with my desk setup (which also is kind of the point, right?). My biggest complaints are that the key legends wear off faster than I’d like and the Bluetooth connection isn’t totally reliable. It’s not my favorite Apple product (by far), but after two decades of muscle memory, I’m not switching anytime soon.

David Pierce, editor at large

I really want to be a mechanical keyboard guy. I love typing on mechanical keyboards! I love the clackiness, the way they look on my desk, the huge personality upgrade that comes with them. But then I start typing notes during a call, and someone goes, “Sorry, what’s that noise in the background?” and I bail on my mechanical keyboard. I used Logitech’s MX Keys S for the last few years, and love that keyboard, but recently replaced it with an Apple Magic Keyboard (black keys, number pad) because I got tired of typing my 1Password password all the time. I bought a $200 keyboard for the Touch ID button. Ugh.

Jacob Kastrenakes, executive editor

Come on, you know where the letters are. Photo by Jake Kastrenakes / The Verge

My keyboard is probably the single dumbest thing I have ever spent money on, but it brings me joy every time I look at it. The setup matches a Boop Redux case with the GMK Dots keycaps and Silent Bluish White (V2) switches. I didn’t so much want to get deep into the mechanical keyboard hobby as I wanted to have this exact keyboard after I saw images of the Dots keycaps on the (original) Boop case floating around in around 2022. It looks cool, right? (Right?) From a practical standpoint, this is fully a downgrade from the Apple Magic Keyboard I was using before: It’s bigger and louder, with fewer keys, and I probably type a bit slower on it, too, owing to the longer key strokes. It’s also a few hundred dollars more expensive. But you know what? I think it looks really cool.

Antonio G. Di Benedetto, laptop reviewer

I’ve changed the keycaps and switches on this TM680 so many times. Photo: Antonio Di Benedetto / The Verge

Since I review laptops and occasionally mechanical keyboards, I’m constantly changing what I type on. But one of my personal keyboards that remains close to my heart is my TM680 (aka the Gamakay LK67). It’s a cheap bare-bones 65-percent kit I bought from AliExpress in 2021. I was inspired by the video that YouTuber Scott “Keybored” Kim did on it, so I dabbled in modding it.

My old TM680 is easily outdone by just about any budget board these days. Many switches now arrive pre-lubed from the factory, and even a sub-$100 keyboard can sound and feel nicer right out of the box. But doing the mods myself felt special. I doubt I’ll ever bother with all that work again, because lubing and filming switches is just too tedious and time-consuming, but I’m glad I at least experienced it once. And no matter how many new keyboards I test, I intend on keeping my TM680.

TC Sottek, former senior editor

I used to buy pretty expensive gaming keyboards that I can’t even name now without digging deep through email archives for receipts. I know I once spent nearly $200 on a full-size Razer mechanical keyboard with a numpad that took up a ton of desk space. The key travel felt amazing and it had a great sound. But what I really remember was knocking over a full glass of water on it. Oops! Farewell, keyboard.

Unfortunately, this happened not once, not twice, but three times for me with relatively expensive keyboards over the years. Yes, I should have learned to contain liquids in bottles on my desk. But now I’ve settled for cheap–but–still-good options the same way I’ve done with the several pairs of earbuds I’ve ruined over the years. (Former serial AirPods Pro user here, now fully on board the Nothing Ear train.)

I’m currently rocking a Keychron K2 with a 75-percent layout. It took me a minute to get my 120-plus WPM back on a cramped keyboard, but now it works just fine and I like the look. I’ll probably splurge again someday on a really compelling set of keycaps.

Meredith Haggerty, senior reports editor

This but with crumbs on it. Photo by Becca Farsace / The Verge

I use the laptop that is attached to the M2 MacBook Air I was issued by my employer. It’s right there whenever I need it, but I think they should make a version that’s covered in way fewer crumbs.

Emma Roth, news writer

I have a toxic relationship with my keyboard, a Corsair K55 RGB Pro that I picked up for half the price at a thrift store a few years ago. It’s a decent, budget-friendly keyboard that’s fine to use for gaming and writing. But recently, it’s been getting on my nerves. The keys no longer light up when I turn my computer on, and it sometimes doesn’t sync properly with my Corsair iCUE software. I can’t see what I’m pressing unless the keyboard is lit up (the keys are translucent), so I’ve had to resort to unplugging the keyboard and plugging it back in when I turn on my computer, which usually does the trick. The issue is probably software-related, but I might just get fed up enough to buy myself a fancy new mechanical keyboard.

Andrew J. Hawkins, transportation editor

I have never been a keyboard guy. I was content to use the one attached to my laptop or whatever wireless Apple version I could get for cheap. But I changed when a coworker turned me on to the NuPhy Air75 mechanical keyboard. The keys feel great, the “clack-clack” sound is so satisfying, and the overall design is retro without seeming outdated. That big yellow spacebar, the delightfully orange Enter button, the subtly aquamarine Escape key — chef’s kiss. Connectivity is robust and the battery lasts for days before needing to be recharged. It took some getting used to, but I chalk it up to not being able to use my left ring finger while typing since breaking it in a freak scooter accident years ago. But that’s a different story.

Nathan Edwards, senior reviews editor

Bright orange makes the dopamine go brrr. Photo by Nathan Edwards / The Verge

Omnitype Bauer Lite (Design Lab Edition) $ 136 $ 136 A 65 percent gasket-mounted wired mechanical keyboard kit. Use the Design Lab to customize its top, bottom, switchplate, and accent colors, plate materials, and mechanical or electrocapacitive PCBs. (Switches, stabilizers, and keycaps sold separately) Read More $136 at Omnitype

These days I mostly swap between a Leopold FC660C and a couple of Omnitype Bauer Lites. The Leopold is a Topre board I’ve had since 2017; I’ve modified it a fair bit over the years, with silencing rings, a new controller board, and Ursa keycaps. I fell in love with the unbeatable tactility of Topre switches early, but I love the customizability of regular mechanical keyboards too, so I’ve spent a lot of time over the past decade trying to find something that combines the best of both.

Related This DIY kit turned my favorite mechanical keyboard into my favorite electrocapacitive keyboard

I got most of the way there with my first Bauer Lite a couple years ago; its Kailh Deep Sea Silent Islet switches are linear, but they’re the closest to Topre I ever found in an MX-compatible switch. (They’re basically identical to the ones in the HHKB Studio). It’s also fluorescent orange, which just makes me happy. I built another one recently with DynaCap electro-capacitive switches and MTNU Space Cadet keycaps. Do I need three wired 65-percent keyboards with very similar layouts and pretty similar typing feel? Probably not. But I have them anyway. Also several other keyboards.

Stevie Bonifield, news writer

I love trying out new mechanical keyboards (and have reviewed dozens of them), but for the last year straight I’ve been using a NuPhy Halo75 V2 as my daily driver. I’ve built several custom mechanical keyboards over the years, but I haven’t changed anything on this one yet. I may swap out the switches and keycaps at some point. NuPhy’s tactile Mint switches are fairly good, but I miss the Leobog Juggle V2 switches I have on a wired keyboard that used to be my daily driver.

I’ve been pretty happy with how the Halo75 sounds and feels out of the box. I also appreciate that the design’s simple enough to not be distracting while still having a few pops of color. The battery life could be a bit better, but there’s not much to complain about overall — the build quality feels solid, the keycaps and switches have held up well over months of heavy typing, and the Halo75 works smoothly with both Mac and Linux. It also has Bluetooth and 2.4GHz wireless connectivity, which was a must-have for me since I like to hop between multiple devices from the same keyboard.

I’ve had a great experience with the Halo75 so far, but I’d recommend it mainly for Mac users — macOS is where it really shines. It works fine for gaming, but I’d suggest configuring it with linear switches if you want to use it for gaming, rather than the tactile switches I went with.

Brad Bourque, commerce writer

NovelKeys NK65 with SA Mizu keycaps. Photo: Brad Bourque / The Verge

I started building mechanical keyboards a few years ago, and have a few in my quiver, but the one I use most often is a NovelKeys NK65 in white. This 65-percent keyboard is sturdy and compact, with just enough extra buttons for work or surfing the web, and arrow keys in case I want to sneak in some gaming. It’s a hot-swap board, so I change up the setup occasionally, but it’s currently equipped with SA Mizu keycaps and C3Equalz x TKC Dragonfruit tactile switches, with a matching desk pad and metal Escape key.

Adi Robertson, senior tech & policy editor

I’ve upgraded my writing equipment since 2021, when I proudly displayed an Apple Magic Keyboard on top of a piece of cardboard on top of a MacBook with several nonfunctional butterfly keys. And as much as I love collecting dedicated typing machines — I’ve got a Freewrite, a 1990 Smith Corona word processor, a beautiful 1930s Underwood manual typewriter, and an impressively awful faux-vintage one from the zombie-brand era of Royal, among others — I discovered my perfect work setup is low-profile mechanicals: clicky enough to be satisfying, short enough travel to not hamper my typing speed. (I’m still slightly faster on a chiclet keyboard, but I’ll take the hit.) I spent a few years with a NuPhy Air75, but fell victim to its fairly well-known swollen battery issues, so I’ve since switched to the Iqunix MQ80 — which has less of a fun retro color scheme, but a more satisfying heft. I love the idea of giving it a cool custom keycap makeover someday, but for now I’m too cheap and lazy, and perfectly satisfied with its Mirror’s Edge-y sci-fi white.

Sean Hollister, senior editor

I noped out of mechanical keyboards for years because they were too clicky! No good for my shared office space. Then, Verge alum Dan Seifert clued me into the near-silent Boba U4 switches, which I installed in a Keychron V1 (love the small size, love the QMK programmable lighting, love the volume dial!) and I almost never looked back.

I did have to re-spring and lube all the switches to get a familiar level of spring action, which was easy enough. Some of the switches have spontaneously stopped working over the past four years, but it only takes seconds to hot-swap another one in. And a family member bought me 8BitDo’s awesome Nintendo-themed wireless mechanical numpad, so I’m covered there too.

But I don’t think it’s endgame. When I switch back from my laptop, I often miss the faster, more effortless typing I can do on its lower-profile keys. Maybe it’s time for something new.

Robert Hart, AI reporter

I should preface this by saying I know absolutely nothing about keyboards. My standards for what I want are pretty modest: It should work, move easily around my desk, and not hurt my wrists. Looking cool doesn’t hurt.

I’ve cycled through a few over the years, mostly geometric oddities — sorry, ergonomic — like the Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Desktop and Logitech Ergo K860, which were rather unwieldy. I also tried ordering the Kinesis Freestyle Pro Jay uses, but gave up after the supplier tried to pass off clearly damaged kit (read: tangled hair clogging everything) as brand-new.

I’ve been using the Keychron K2 Pro for a few years now. It’s compact, looks great, and holds a charge well. It has no number pad, but that keeps things nimble, and it handily switches between multiple computers I use on the go. There are also fancy lights, though I usually turn them off. The main downsides are having to regularly Google the key commands needed to control it — a pain when those lights won’t stop strobing like a hyperactive Christmas tree. It supports key remapping, so I may attempt a new layout like Dvorak sometime soon.

Elizabeth Lopatto, senior internet typist

First of all, keyboards should be clacky. I want to sound like I am firing a machine gun while I write. Second, due to assorted repetitive stress injuries, my keyboard needs to be split. So I am typing with a light-up gaming keyboard — the lights are optional, I just like them — called the Kinesis Gaming Freestyle Edge RGB. Do I game? Uh, well, I do crossword puzzles. But the Cherry MX Blue switches guarantee I sound fucking productive while I do them.

Nilay Patel, editor-in-chief

Very boring Apple keyboards. Every five years the right side of the spacebar stops working and I buy a new one. Full-size. Numpad for life.

Tech.title: Happy Pikmin Day Eve
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

This morning, Nintendo announced that tomorrow, November 1st, would be the first annual Pikmin Day. As part of the short Pikmin Day Direct, Shigeru Miyamoto shared new info about Pikmin 4 for the Switch 2, as well as an update for the mobile app Pikmin Bloom, and announced the Hello! Pikmin series of shorts.

Players will be able to use the Switch 2’s built-in microphone to issue voice commands to Oatchi, the space dog. Pikmin 4 will also have a Dandori Academy mode that will test players’ skills in specific challenges. There will be limited tests on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday, complete with leaderboards where players can compare stats. Pikmin Bloom will be getting a new feature called Secret Caves, where players can win treasure by battling enemies and exploring said caves.

Lastly, Miyamoto showed the first installment of a new series of shorts called Hello! Pikmin. A second episode will premiere tomorrow, with a third later in November. The series will then debut one short per month starting in December. The shorts build on the success of Close to You, a Pikmin animation released last year.

Tech.title: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi.

But I won’t be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home. It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it.

My version doesn’t sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio, but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home.

Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code.

Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C. Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud.

When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app.

Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos.

Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

But a few sessions of Claude Code filled in almost all those holes. All I had to do was plug the Waveshare back into my PC, then ask Claude to reprogram each thing I wanted.

When I complained to Claude that I couldn’t properly read or hear Muse’s replies to my asks, issues that others have mentioned as well, Claude built a conversation history page so I can swipe right to read what it said, and I plugged in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs that speaks its answers out loud. (The voice was the least soul-sucking of the ones in ElevenLabs’ free tier, my wife and I agree, even if it doesn’t match the Muse avatars’ cuddly vibe at all.)

Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

Thanks to Claude, I can now press a button to make my phone take a picture from across the room with a high-quality live preview, and my phone’s front-facing camera no longer displays upside down. Claude made fairly short work of adding a low-quality camera preview over Bluetooth, too, so I don’t need to be on home Wi-Fi to get photos from creative angles.

When I hit this button on my new remote viewfinder… Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge …my phone takes a photo. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

I asked Claude to make a whole batch of different avatars like the ones Meta showed off during Meta Connect, and to add a Tamagotchi-like minigame where they need food, play, sleep, and a bath. When the game seemed too simple to capture any attention, I had it add four different levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt. I decided treats should make a crunchy mess and get avatars dirtier when they eat them, and that too much play should tire out a pet. My wish was Claude’s command.

When I noticed I was accidentally letting go of the push-to-talk button too soon and making Muse choke on almost-empty audio, vibe coding fixed it minutes later by sending only audio over one second in length. The only obvious lag I’m seeing now is from Meta’s own servers — sometimes they’re responsive, sometimes they lag quite a bit.

Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge

It was so easy to let Claude reprogram the pendant that I asked it to build a few features specifically for this video in this story, including a working pocket watch face with three hands that actually tells the time. (That took it 15 minutes; now, when I say the hardware looks like a pocket watch, you can see what I mean!) It even found, downloaded, trimmed, and loaded video clips of Zuck introducing the Muse Charm and installed a video player so I could play those clips on the Waveshare.

I want you to understand I have no coding experience, and so I have no idea if any of this code is good. It might be fatally flawed. Nor do I trust Meta or its Muse agent with my email or my home network, particularly after hearing how it leaked one reviewer’s home address. (I put it on guest Wi-Fi from the get-go as a precaution.)

That means I don’t really know how useful a Muse Charm may or may not be for those who do know how to code and are willing to take a bigger leap of faith. But after nearly dropping a bulky little silver pendant a couple of times, one with no more Muse functionality than my phone (and quite a bit less without additional code), I’m thinking Muse itself isn’t the reason to buy a dedicated compute pocket watch.

The reason to have a dedicated piece of hardware is to do things you can’t do on the phone that’s already in your pocket, like coding the entire gadget to do whatever you want. Which makes me wonder: Will the actual Muse Charm be this freely programmable, or would the kind of people who’d buy one be better off with a development kit? I guess we’ll see when it ships.

Tech.title: Windows 11 tries new shortcuts for Xbox gaming mode and search
Tech.content:
The latest Windows 11 Insider build adds some powerful new search features and quick settings while in Xbox mode. The Xbox shortcuts let you control things like Bluetooth, WiFi, and power settings without having to exit gaming mode.

The search improvements are quite comprehensive. You can now filter results for files, actions, or web results. You can also use the search box to perform actions like changing the screen brightness or volume, and even perform actions on a connected phone, including making calls. Results can also offer much more detail, like when a file was last modified and its author, or pull in charts for stock prices and weather forecasts. And you can train Windows 11 search by clicking inline thumbs-up or thumbs-down icons to help it improve over time.

Tech.title: Best Buy is bundling a $100 gift card with touchscreen MacBook Pro preorders
Tech.content:
While the new touch-enabled MacBook Pro with the PROLED XDR screen is available for preorder across a few major retailers, Best Buy is sweetening the deal by including a $100 gift card. The gift card will be automatically added to your cart when you preorder one of Apple’s highest-end laptops available in 14- or 16-inch configurations, and even one of its 14-inch MacBook Pro laptops with the M6 chip. You can verify that it’s been added to your order in the “Complete your purchase” section of the checkout page.

My colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto got a chance to check out the new laptop at Apple’s event, and came away impressed by the Tandem OLED panel’s brightness and contrast, but described the update as “kind of boring” given the relatively small changes to the system otherwise. There are some unique changes to macOS that help make the new touch experience smoother, like magnifying the traffic light-colored buttons on windows when you move your finger near them. The PROLED laptops are also a bit thinner and lighter than standard models, and the Apple logo on the back glows like on older versions.

Tech.title: Vic Mensa can’t live without the Voice Memos app
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Vic Mensa is one of those people who has done so many things that it’s hard to remember where you were first introduced to him. Was it his debut mixtape Innanetape, which finally hit the major streaming services for the first time in September? Or maybe his house-influenced single “Down On My Luck”? Maybe you didn’t even realize that Mensa was a rapper. Maybe you know him from his roles on The Chi or Bel-Air. Or perhaps you’re mostly aware of him through his activism, social media presence (peeling oranges and waxing poetic), or his podcast The Vic Mensa Show.

Point is, the man wears many hats. Part of the secret to being so prolific, it turns out, is Voice Memos. Just capture those ideas before they disappear.

What is your most indispensable tool?

Voice Memos. Everything starts there for me. Songs, essay ideas, orange tree thoughts, voice notes to myself at some wild hour, little things my son says that I do not want to lose. My phone is a million distractions in one rectangle, but Voice Memos is one of the few parts of it that still feels honest. Just press record before the thought disappears.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

Instagram, for better or worse. That’s definitely where my voice has really found its legs. I started out peeling an orange and talking through whatever was on my mind, and it turned into this whole conversation with people about politics, history, music, grief, jokes, fatherhood, all of it. That response helped show me there was room for The Vic Mensa Show too. Instagram can be a circus, obviously, but it’s also a very valuable tool for connection.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

Maybe Meta glasses. Them motherfuckers seem like they’re being used for evil.

What creation are you most proud of?

Probably my upcoming album right now. It’s the first album that I’ve really taken myself completely seriously as a producer. The surrounding art, videos, design, clothing, and world I’m building around it is something that really excites me as well.

What do you do when you need to focus?

I either do my Shambhavi Mahamudra meditation that I learned from Sadhguru or the Wim Hof breathing method. Ideally, I’ll do the Wim Hof breathing method in the steam room and then the meditation.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Anything that touches your life every day. A good mattress. Good headphones. Quality food. Clothes you will actually keep for years. Experiences with your child. I have wasted money on plenty of dumb shit, so I am trying to be better about buying things that either last or make a real memory.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

Live from the contradiction.

What is the last GIF or meme you used?

Ummm… that is not Vic Mensa. Also, the letter casing here is pure chaos.

Tech.title: Apple CEO says the company doesn’t ‘want to ship AI for AI’s sake’
Tech.content:
In Brief

During a recent interview with Wired’s Steven Levy, Apple CEO John Ternus defended the company’s current position in the AI landscape.

Over the past couple years, Apple has often been described as behind on AI, especially as it delayed the release of a more powerful version of Siri, which finally launched this summer. But while Ternus — a longtime Apple executive who officially became CEO at the beginning of September — acknowledged that “everyone has an opinion,” he insisted, “I really like where we’re at.”

Ternus added that Apple is “absolutely going to leverage AI” in its new products, but he said, “We don’t want to ship AI for AI’s sake. When we’re doing it right, people won’t have to think about whether it was AI that made this happen or more traditional software. What matters is, did we build something that they really love?”

And when Levy pressed him on whether AI might affect Apple and its ecosystem more dramatically, with agents potentially making things like apps unnecessary, Ternus replied,”That could make life really easy, I suppose, but the creation of products is a deeply human and personal thing, something that we love to do.”
